metadata.title: Section 301 Duty Drawback Explained
metadata.author: USA Customs Clearance
metadata.shortDescription:
Paying Section 301 tariffs on China imports? You may be eligible to get up to 99% of those duties refunded through duty drawback. If you export, manufacture for export, or even destroy imported goods under Customs supervision, you could recover significant tariff dollars, including Section 301 duties.

Don’t leave money on the table. Visit https://USACustomsClearance.com to speak with a licensed customs broker and see if your imports qualify for duty drawback.

#Section301 #DutyDrawback #ChinaTariffs #Importing #CustomsBroker #TariffRefund #SupplyChainStrategy

segments.text: Section 301 duty drawbacks are refunds
associated with tariffs and customs
duties applied to China origin products
under the section 301 act. If you're
importing goods from China into the
United States, you've likely felt the
sting of section 301 tariffs. These
extra duties can add up fast, eating
into your margins and tying up cash
you'd rather use elsewhere. But what if
there was a way to recover most of that
money? Not in the distant future, but
right now with the right knowhow and
documentation.
That's where section 301 duty drawback
comes in. Let's break down what it is,
who can [music] claim it, the types of
drawbacks available, the process for
filing, the common pitfalls, [music] and
why it's more important than ever for
your business. First, let's clarify what
section 301 duty drawback actually
means. When you bring goods into the US,
you pay duties at the border. Section
301 tariffs are extra duties imposed on
China origin products as part of ongoing
trade actions. For many importers, these
tariffs are significant and can
dramatically increase landed costs. But
here's the good news. If those goods are
later exported, destroyed under customs
supervision, or used as components in
products that are then exported, you
could be eligible to claim a refund on
those duties. This refund is known as a
duty drawback and [music] yes, it
includes section 301 tariffs. So, who
can actually claim a section 301
drawback? The requirements are pretty
straightforward but strict. [music] You
must have imported goods that were
subject to section 301 duties. Those
goods must then be exported, destroyed,
or used to manufacture an export
product. And crucially, you need to be
able to connect the original import to
the export or destruction event with
solid records.
If you meet these criteria, you could
recover up to 99% of the duties you
paid, including those hefty section 301
tariffs. [music]
However, be aware that not all products
qualify. For example, if your goods are
also subject to anti-dumping or
counterveailing duties, you may not be
eligible for a standard drawback refund.
There are a few key types of duty
drawback you should know about. The
first is unused merchandise drawback.
This applies when you export the same
goods you imported without significant
changes. [music] Next is manufacturing
drawback which covers situations where
you use imported components to make
products that are then exported. Then
there's substitution drawback which
allows you to claim a refund even if the
exact imported goods weren't exported as
long as the exported goods are
commercially interchangeable and share
the same HTS code. Finally, there's
rejected merchandise drawback for goods
that are returned or destroyed under
custom supervision.
of these. Substitution can be especially
powerful since it lets you match exports
to imports even when inventory gets
mixed [music] as long as you maintain
proper classification records. Now,
let's walk through the process of
claiming a section 301 drawback. Step
one, identify your eligible imports.
You'll need to pull your entry records,
specifically CBP form 7501, to find
shipments where you paid section 301
duties. Step two, match those imports to
your exports or to products you
manufactured for export. This requires
careful documentation and if you're
using substitution, a clear link through
HTS codes. Step three, prepare your
claim. This involves gathering all
supporting documents, confirming
quantities and values, and ensuring you
use the correct HDS codes, including the
special chapter 99 code that flags
section 301 duties. Step four, file your
claim electronically through the ACE
system. Paper claims are no longer
accepted. [music]
Then it's a waiting game. First-time
filers may wait 6 to 12 months or more
for approval, though accelerated payment
options can get you cash in as little as
4 weeks if you file quickly and meet the
requirements. There are some crucial
risks and pitfalls to watch out for. Not
every good qualifies, so check for
exclusions and make sure your products
aren't blocked by anti-dumping or
counterveailing duties. Accurate HTS
classification is absolutely critical. A
mismatch can derail your entire claim.
Timing is also key. Drawback claims
generally must be filed within 5 years
of the import date. [music] And above
all, your documentation must be
airtight. Poor records mean no refund,
no matter how strong your case. So why
does this matter? Right now [music] in
the current climate, with supply chain
still in flux and tariff strategies
evolving, many US companies are just now
realizing they may be sitting on
significant amounts of refundable
duties. If you've been absorbing section
301 costs on China origin imports, don't
simply write them off. A properly
executed duty drawback can put real
money back into your business and
improve your cost structure without
having to change your supply chain. To
sum up, section 301 duties are eligible
for drawback refunds. Success depends on
accurate records, correct
classification, and timely filing.
[music] If you want help navigating
eligibility, strategy, or the filing
process, you don't have to go it alone.
Ready to stop leaving money on the
table? Explore how section 301 duty
drawback could transform your bottom
line. Subscribe now for more customs
compliance insights and actionable
strategies for your business.
USA customs clearance.com

metadata.title: What Is Duty Drawback? Get Up to 99% of Your Import Duties Back (Explained)
metadata.author: Evana
metadata.shortDescription:
Paid duties or tariffs on imported goods, then exported or destroyed them? You may be able to get up to 99% of those duties back. It's called duty drawback, and billions of dollars go unclaimed every year.

Jade Christopher, a licensed customs broker who has worked exclusively in duty drawback for 15 years, explains how it works in plain English: who qualifies, which duties come back (and why IEEPA tariffs don't), how far back you can claim, and how fast you can get paid.

👉 See what's on the table for you, free: https://evana.app

Chapters
0:00 Billions in unclaimed refunds
0:12 What is duty drawback?
0:44 Who qualifies?
1:32 Exported or destroyed goods
2:17 Which duties come back? (IEEPA, Section 301, 232, MPF/HMF)
2:51 How far back and how fast you get paid
3:20 Is drawback worth it? (clawing back what tariffs cost you)
3:49 Who it's for and the bottom line

Evana handles duty drawback end to end and works alongside your existing customs broker.

#DutyDrawback #Tariffs #Importing

metadata.title: IEEPA Tariff Refunds vs. Duty Drawback: What Importers Need to Know (2026)
metadata.author: Evana
metadata.shortDescription:
Tariff refunds took over the news this year, and most of the buzz is about IEEPA and the CAPE refunds. But there's a second, bigger refund most importers miss: duty drawback.

Jade Christopher, a licensed customs broker who has worked exclusively in duty drawback for 15 years, breaks down the difference: what the IEEPA refund actually is, why it's a one-time "blip," how drawback gets you up to 99% of duties back on goods you export or destroy (going back 5 years and ongoing), which duties qualify, and the three things every importer should do right now.

We're about to guide you through an exciting opportunity to reclaim money you didn’t know you were leaving behind — cash refunds through duty drawbacks. This essential guide is brought to you by the experienced team at USA Customs Clearance, where we simplify complex customs processes to help your business thrive.

usacustomsclearance.com

Video Overview:
Are you looking to maximize your import/export operations and reduce costs? Duty drawbacks can help you recover up to 99% of certain import duties, taxes, and fees. 

In this video, you’ll discover:

What Duty Drawbacks Are and Who Qualifies: Learn about this incredible program and whether your business can benefit from it.
The Step-by-Step Process to Claiming Your Refund: Get a clear understanding of what documents you’ll need and how to submit a claim.

Why Choose USA Customs Clearance?
Navigating duty drawbacks can be overwhelming, but you don’t have to go it alone. At USA Customs Clearance, we offer comprehensive solutions to help you reclaim your funds seamlessly:

Duty Drawback & Mitigation Services: We evaluate your current importing program to identify eligibility and maximize refunds.
Customs Brokerage Services: Simplify the entire process with our expert brokers who handle everything from tariff classifications to compliance checks.
Consulting Services Tailored to Your Needs: Whether you’re new to the process or need advanced guidance, we offer one-on-one consulting sessions to streamline your operations.

Explore Our Services:
We’re here to support you with all your customs clearance needs:

Importer Consulting Packages: Receive personalized guidance from a licensed customs broker.
Government Agency Compliance: Ensure your imports meet all U.S. regulations and avoid costly penalties.

Visit us today at usacustomsclearance.com for more and start getting the help your business deserves.

metadata.title: Understanding Duty Drawback: Recover Duties & Reduce Trade Costs
metadata.author: Gallagher Transport International Inc.
metadata.shortDescription:
Did you know businesses involved in importing and exporting goods may be eligible for a refund on certain duties, taxes, and fees through the Duty Drawback program? At Gallagher Transport International, we help companies understand and navigate this valuable trade opportunity.

Duty Drawback is a U.S. Customs program that allows importers, exporters, and manufacturers to recover eligible duties paid on imported products that are later exported, destroyed, or used in qualifying manufacturing processes. This can significantly improve cash flow and lower operational expenses for businesses engaged in international trade.

Common examples of eligible goods may include:
📦 Products imported and later exported
🏭 Imported materials used in manufacturing exported products
🔄 Unused merchandise returned or re-exported
🚢 Goods transferred through global supply chains

Many businesses miss out on potential refunds simply because the process can be complex and documentation-heavy. Proper recordkeeping, import/export matching, and compliance with customs regulations are essential for successful claims.

At Gallagher Transport International, our team helps simplify the Duty Drawback process by assisting with:

✔️ Customs documentation review
✔️ Claim preparation & filing
✔️ Trade compliance support
✔️ Import/export record management
✔️ Freight & logistics coordination

Whether you're a small importer or a large international distributor, understanding Duty Drawback could uncover valuable savings opportunities for your business.

🌎 Streamline your international shipping and trade processes with expert logistics and customs support from Gallagher Transport International.

segments.text: Duty Drawback is a US Customs and Border
Protection program that lets companies
reclaim up to 99% of duties and taxes
paid on qualifying imports. Duty
Drawback is a US Customs and Border
Protection Program that lets companies
reclaim up to 99% of duties and taxes
paid on qualifying imports. This program
has existed since 1789 to support
American manufacturing and exports by
reducing the tax burden on US exporters.
There are three main types of drawback
claims. The first is unused merchandise
drawback which applies when you import
something, don't use it and then export
it or destroy it under custom
supervision. The second is manufacturing
drawback where you import raw materials,
use them to make a product with a new
name or function and export that
finished product. The third is rejected
merchandise drawback. For items that
don't meet specifications or turn out to
be defective when they arrive. Before
you can file any claims, you need to
apply for permissions from US customs.
You can request a one-time waiver to
file a claim for something you already
exported or destroyed. There's also a
waiver of prior notice that lets you
file future claims without asking
permission each time. You can apply for
accelerated payment to get your refunds
faster once you submit your claims. The
timeline matters. You have 5 years from
the import date to submit your claim.
The process requires detailed
documentation including import and
export dates, product descriptions, and
tariff classification numbers. Each
claim is different based on your
specific circumstances. Gallagher
Transport offers customs broker services
specializing in duty drawback claims.
They have experience across multiple
industries, including FDA and EPA
regulated products. Their services cover
customs clearance, compliance reviews,
and logistics coordination by land, sea,
or air. They stay current with customs
regulations to help ensure your claims
meet all requirements. If you're
interested in learning whether you
qualify for duty drawback, their experts
can assess your situation and determine
what information you'll need to file a
successful claim.

During this period, drawback claimants could file new drawback claims under either the old law, known as core, or the new TFTEA law. The new drawback regulations, which incorporates TFTEA, were published on December 18th, 2018. Since February 24th of 2019, all drawback claims must be filed as TFTEA claims. So, what are the similarities and differences between core and TFTEA? First, I will tell you what is the same. Those filing direct identification unused and rejected merchandise drawback claims will continue to operate as they did under core. For those claims, you will still need to connect the exported part number to the imported part number and claim drawback on the value of the imported part following the allowable inventory methods. Direct identification manufacturing drawback claims will also operate as they did under core. You can claim drawback on exported products that are manufactured in the United States with the use of the imported material. You can also file drawback on merchandise that is destroyed under customs supervision. What has changed? TFTEA has redefined substitution unused drawback. Claimants will no longer need to link the import to the export by part number. Instead, they can file drawback based on the eight-digit HTS number. If two different products have the same HTS number, but one was exported and the other was imported, you can use them in a substitution unused drawback claim. Substitution manufacturing drawback has also changed. If the eight-digit HTS number of the component used in the manufacturing process matches the eight-digit HTS number of the merchandise that is imported, you can claim drawback on the imported merchandise. It does not matter whether or not the imported duty-paid merchandise was used in the manufacturing process of the exported product. You can still get the drawback. The regulations for substitution unused drawback include a new method for calculating drawback refunds. Claimants now have to determine the average unit value of the entry summary line number of the import, compare that to the value of the exported unit value, and use the value that is lesser in the drawback claim. ITM's drawback software determines which is lesser of the two. A new calculation is also used for substitution manufacturing claims. You now have to determine the average unit value of the entry summary line number of the imported merchandise. Compare that value to the unit cost of the component used in the manufacturing process, and use the value that is lesser in the drawback claim. Again, ITM's drawback software determines which is lesser of the two. Now, there are some limitations with NAFTA. Some substitution unused and substitution manufacturing drawback claims cannot include exports to Canada or Mexico. In addition, substitution unused drawback cannot include HTS numbers that fall under the other other categories. This means merchandise can't be substituted if the eight-digit HTS subheading or the 10-digit and the 10-digit HTS subheading both begin with the term other. But, you can file direct identification unused claims or unused merchandise claim uh I'm sorry, but you can claim direct identification unused claims on unused merchandise that is exported to Canada, exported to Mexico, or fall under the other other category. So, if you can't do it under our substitution claim, you can do it under direct identification. Uh in addition, TFTA has established the first filed rule. If an entry summary line number has been used in a substitution claim, merchandise under that entry summary line number may not be used in a non-substitution claim. Similarly, if a direct identification unused or rejected merchandise claim is first filed using that entry summary line number, then that entry summary line number cannot be used in a future substitution claim. You have to choose one or the other. The drawback refunds have also changed. Under core, manufacturing drawback claim refunds were limited to 99% of the duties paid on the imported merchandise. It did not allow for the recovery of other taxes and fees. TFTA authorizes drawback refunds for 99% of duties, taxes, and fees, including merchandise processing fee and the harbor maintenance fee paid on imported merchandise for both unused and manufacturing drawback claims. Unfortunately, you still cannot claim obtain MPF or HMF refunds for rejected merchandise drawback claims. The filing process under TFTA has also changed. Under core, drawback claim and drawback claims could be filed manually or electronically. Now, under TFTA, all drawback claims must be filed electronically within the automated commercial environment known as ACE. There are also changes in the record retention requirements. Under TFTA, all supporting records must be maintained for 3 years from the date of liquidation of the claim. In addition, forms that were once required are now obsolete. Under core, drawback claimants who are not the importer of record had to obtain a customs form called the delivery certificate for the purposes of drawback, which was also called a CD. You'd have to get this from the importer of record. That form is now obsolete. Drawback claimants still do have to get permission from the importer of record to use one of their import entries in a drawback claim, but the entry information can be provided using records kept in the normal course of business. Customs has also done away with the official drawback entry form, referred to as the Customs Form 7551, because drawback entries are submitted electronically now. Drawback bonds are still needed in order to receive accelerated payment of drawback claims, but the bond data is also submitted electronically. ITM can work with you to obtain electronic single transaction or continuous drawback bonds. One of the most dramatic changes under TFTA is the duty drawback time frames. Under core, there were different requirements for unused merchandise drawback and manufacturing drawback. Under TFTA, the time frame is both simply 5 years from the importation of the merchandise to the date of filing a drawback claim. The biggest advantage of the new time frame is that the drawback claimant can claim exports that are almost 5 years old rather than 3 years that was allowed under core. Under core, um, I'm sorry. Now that the drawback claims must be filed in ACE, Customs has created a series of validations that a claim must pass before being accepted. These validations ensure that the claims contain correct data. Under core, ACE's validations were only on the import entry level. Under TEFTA, ACE validations are on the line number level. So, data provided for a line number cannot exceed the duty claimed on an entry, the MPF claimed I'm sorry, the duty claimed on a line number, the MPF claimed on a line number, or the HMF claimed on a line number. Also, the HTS numbers provided must must match the HTS numbers listed on that line number for that import entry. Waiver of prior notice, as the name would suggest, waves the requirement of prior notice of intent to export merchandise. Without it, a company would need to provide CBP with advance notification of export in order to allow for Customs to inspect the merchandise. After an inspection or a waiver by Customs of an inspection, a drawback participant without waiver of prior notice privileges would also need to provide original export documentation with each claim in order to file for drawback. Securing waiver of prior notice eliminates the necessity of filing prior to export as well as the submission of original documentation. Therefore, an exporter can ship at will and claim the drawback within the regulated time frame allowed. A claimant will apply for a one-time waiver, which covers prospectively, and a retroactive waiver, which covers historical data. Both requests can be made in the same application and would require a complete and comprehensive set of trace documents. metadata.shortDescription:
Get #Section301 #duty refunds on Chinese goods with the #exclusions made available through December 31, 2022 (current as of the date of this video). In this video, customs lawyer Jason P. Wapiennik of Great Lakes Customs Law  explains the two ways an importer can get a duty refund if they paid duties and their product is eligible for an "exclusion" granted by the U.S. Trade Representative for goods originating from China. 

🙋‍♂️Section 301 Refunds: https://greatlakescustomslaw.com/section-301-tariff-exclusions-china/protest-for-refund-of-section-301-china-tariffs/
🚨Section 301 Exclusions: https://greatlakescustomslaw.com/section-301-tariff-exclusions-china/
🙋‍♂️Protests: https://greatlakescustomslaw.com/customs-violations/protest-customs-decisions-protest-filing/

All information in this video is current only as of March 28, 2022. Laws change. The video does not contain legal advice so do not rely on it; have your situation evaluated by a lawyer or other customs professional.

metadata.author: Tariffs Lawsuit
metadata.shortDescription:
Your business may already be owed money from tariffs it paid in 2025.

In this video, attorney Mikal Watts explains what importers need to know after the Supreme Court ruled that tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act - IEEPA - were never authorized.

If your company imported goods in 2025 and paid these tariffs, you may be eligible for a refund with interest. But the refund process through CBP’s CAPE system is technical, time-sensitive, and already causing many claims to fail before they are reviewed.

The Supreme Court has ruled. The money was collected under tariffs that were never authorized. The question now is whether your claim is handled correctly, and in time.

Get In Touch Today at TariffsLawsuit.com

metadata.shortDescription: CBP December Protest Webinar Description: On December 9, 2020, CBP provided the trade community a webinar covering topics specific to protests (19 U.S.C. 1514). This presentation is not intended to replace previously provided formal guidance to the trade community, nor is it intended to constitute legal advice.

metadata.title: Tariff Refund Update: Why Importers May Need To File Now
metadata.author: Tariffs Lawsuit
metadata.shortDescription:
Attorney Mikal Watts provides a June 2026 update on the ongoing tariff litigation involving tariffs levied under IEEPA, Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, and potential Section 301 tariffs.

Approximately $166 billion in tariffs were levied under IEEPA between 2025 and 2026 before the United States Supreme Court found that the Trump administration lacked authority under that statute. The Court of International Trade has since become a key forum for businesses seeking refunds, and the Trump administration has appealed the scope of the refund order.

Mikal also discusses the administration’s use of Section 122 tariffs, which may result in approximately $50 billion in additional tariffs during the 150-day period following February 20, 2026. He then explains why future Section 301 tariffs could lead to even more litigation and potentially hundreds of billions of dollars in additional tariff claims.

Watts Law Firm is representing importers and businesses seeking to recover tariffs paid under these statutory actions. If your business paid tariffs under IEEPA, Section 122, or future Section 301 actions, now may be the time to determine whether you need to file a claim in the Court of International Trade.

Note: This video is for general informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. Viewing this video does not create an attorney-client relationship.

metadata.title: You Paid the Tariffs. Target Just Got the Refund.
metadata.author: Finn's Fine Print
metadata.shortDescription:
Target just booked $301 million in tariff refunds in one quarter, on tariffs you helped pay. On Feb 20, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 that the law the president used (IEEPA) doesn't let him impose tariffs, and about $166 billion of those duties became subject to refund. But the refund goes to whoever is named on the customs paperwork, the importer of record. For anything you bought off a shelf, that's the store, not you.

We follow Dana (made up, but her receipt isn't). Her $60 space heater: the store imported it and paid the tariff, so the store holds the refund ticket and her receipt gives her no claim. Her jacket from overseas, where she paid an import duty at the door: the carrier filed the paperwork and collected the duty from her, the one place a refund has a road back to a shopper.

Who walked out with the money: Target (refunds were about 18% of its Q3 operating profit), Lowe's (by our math, EPS would have fallen about 10% without the refunds), TJX (an amount equal to about a third went to incentive pay and bonuses), Walmart (about $2.9 billion back by the end of July; it says a significant portion went mainly into price investment) and FedEx ($2.7 billion booked as owed to customers). By Nov 5, Customs had certified about $128.4 billion of refunds, interest included. Core-goods prices did not come down: up about 0.66% from February to October.

The fine print, precisely:
- The $166 billion is the IEEPA duties collected, all of it subject to refund. The Court said nothing about whether or how it goes back; Customs runs its own process.
- Feb 1, 2025 to Feb 19, 2026 is the period covered by the trade court's class of importers of record. It is the importers' period, not a claim window for shoppers, and shoppers are not in that class.
- Only FedEx has said, in its SEC filing, that it passes duty refunds back to customers who paid the duties ("To the extent customers have previously paid amounts associated with these tariffs, FedEx remits corresponding refunds as soon as practicable."). We found no such statement from other carriers in primary sources, and not every duty paid at the door was an IEEPA tariff. Check what your carrier says.

It booked $2.7 billion of that as money it expects to owe back to customers.
And FedEx says that where customers paid the duties,
it sends the refund back as soon as practicable.
When I read that line in FedEx's filing, it was the first sentence in this whole
story that sounded like somebody owed Dana anything.
Funny how that works.
The one time the bill had her name on it, the refund at least knows her address.
For everything she bought off a shelf, there's no form to fill in.
The price tag was the end of the paperwork.
So if those tariffs are gone, why didn't your price tags come down?
I went looking for the price cut.
Prices for goods, leaving out food and energy,
rose about 1.2% while those tariffs were on.
Since the ruling in February, they're higher than they were that month,
up about two-thirds of a percent.
Not even a small dip a store could point to.
Dana checked too.
The heater on the shelf is still sixty dollars.
Hers still works, so mostly she's just offended.
Part of the reason is that the tariffs didn't really vanish.
The same month, a global 10% tariff took over under a different law,
and in July another one replaced it, at 10 or 12.5%.
So the coat check is handing back last year's coat,
while a new one is already on the rack, and part of that one is probably in Dana's
prices too. And if a court ever knocks down one of those replacements too,
that refund would follow the same ticket.
Now, the strongest case for the stores.
Their margins got squeezed, they had to eat part of the old tariff,
and the refund partly pays them back for real costs.
The public data can't measure how big that part is.
But even when a refund lands as profit, no rule makes a price tag click back down.
Price tags work like a ratchet.
In other words, the cost got passed to you, at least part of it.
The refund, mostly, didn't.
So back to Dana.
Her receipt proves she paid sixty dollars, and it gives her no claim in the customs
refund, not a single cent.
It's now a very well-kept souvenir on her fridge.
The email is a different story.
She digs up the jacket's delivery email, finds the line that says import duty,
and looks up what the carrier says about tariff refunds.
Then she checks the date.
January, a month before the ruling.
That's inside the window, and the window is the whole game.
Check your own inbox for an import duty charge from early 2025 up to the ruling
last February.
If you paid one at your door back then, that email is your ticket stub,
the clearest path to a refund with your name on it.
Dana forwards hers to herself with the subject line,
mine. Because a refund follows the ticket, not the wallet.
Target's $301 million followed its ticket home.
Dana helped pay the tariffs, and what she got back is a warm apartment and one email
worth keeping.
That's the fine print.
And the next piece of fine print hiding in the prices you pay is in the video
on screen now.

About $166 billion has to be paid back, and what decides who gets it is a name on a customs form. By the end of this video, you'll know whose name is on that form, why your price tags didn't come down, and the one email in your inbox, the one with an import duty on it, that might actually get you money back. Last winter her space heater died, so she grabbed a new one at a big-box store for sixty dollars, kept the receipt, and plugged it in before her toes could freeze. I assumed the tariff on that heater was the store's problem. Then I followed the heater back to the port. At the port, whoever is listed as the importer pays the tariff, a tax on imports, to Customs. For Dana's heater, that's the store. By the end of 2025, the average tariff rate on imports had climbed from 2.6% to 13%. At that rate, a heater the store bought for thirty dollars carries about four dollars of tariff, paid at the dock. metadata.title: China's Retaliatory Tariffs, Section 301 Authorities, and Tariff Refund Litigation
metadata.author: Center for Strategic & International Studies
metadata.shortDescription: On this episode of the Trade Guys, Bill and Scott discuss the impacts of Chinese retaliatory tariffs on U.S. agricultural and other trade, the Trump administration's continued efforts to implement Section 301 tariffs, and the ongoing tariff refund litigation.
keywords: Center for Strategic and International Studies

segments.text: I'm Scott.
>> I'm Bill.
>> And we're the Trade Guys.
>> You're listening to The Trade Guys, a
podcast produced by CSIS, where we talk
about trade in terms that everyone can
understand. I'm Alex Kissling, and I'm
here with Scott Miller and Bill Reinsch,
the CSIS Trade Guys.
Thanks for listening to The Trade Guys.
On today's episode, we examine the
impact of China's retaliatory tariffs,
take a look at the Trump
administration's new use of Section 301
authorities, and unpack the latest
litigation around tariff refunds. All
that and more on this episode of The
Trade Guys.
Well, Bill and Scott, it's great to be
back with you after a few weeks of
episodes with some great guests, and I
want to dive right into our first topic
today by taking a step back and talking
through the effects of Chinese
retaliatory tariffs, particularly on the
US agriculture sector.
>> A new study from North Dakota State
University found that China's
retaliatory tariffs on US ag goods wiped
out an estimated 14.9 billion in export
sales over 12 months. So, Scott, let's
look under the hood here. What stands
out to you as you look through these
numbers?
>> This is basically a disruption of an old
relationship. The old relationship is US
soybean sales to China. This goes back
to basically China's growth in the early
part of this century, and one of the
things that happened as people raised
their living standards is they improved
their diet. More people were demanding
the addition of meat, in this case pork,
in their diet. And soybeans is primarily
a very efficient food for pigs. So, that
was an agriculture match made in heaven,
at least for the moment at the time, and
so the US found a great source of sales,
net sales, additional for their soybeans
and other products, and Chinese
consumers improved their diet as it
became more and more important element
of trade between the two countries and
as trade tensions rose, it became one of
the obvious places for trade pressure
and retaliation. And that's indeed what
happened with soybeans. China basically,
you look at it broadly, they changed
sources. They switched their purchases
from the United States to Brazil and
Argentina principally. This had an
immediate effect in slowing down sales
and therefore exports from US over the
course of crop cycle. Most of the
consumption of soybeans was the same
worldwide, but what happened is your
sourcing changed. So, China sourced
Brazil and Argentina principally instead
of the United States. US soybeans went
to Europe instead of China. Europe
previously had gotten soybeans from
Argentina and Brazil. So, there was a
change in the shipping patterns, but it
showed up in uh net losses as the uh
North Dakota State University survey
showed, net losses for US farmers. And
it was sort of broadly across
agriculture. There was a big drop in
total ag sales to China from 2024 to
2025, sales dropped from 24 billion to 8
billion. So, it's steepest one-year
decline. It certainly got the message
through. And it's one of those things
when you accelerate pressure on a
rival's economy, they have techniques
they can use back. So, this happens
pretty frequently. It was not
unexpected. And all I can say is that
the agriculture groups in the United
States tend to be strong supporters of
the president and they tend to be very
well represented in the US Congress. And
so, over time this will work itself out.
Certainly there were there were a lot of
state-by-state issues that these losses
materialized. And it's coming now at a
time when farm incomes are under a lot
of pressure. If you happen to drive by a
a gas station that sells diesel fuel,
look at the difference between diesel
and gasoline. Diesel's what does work in
the country. Gasoline's what gets you to
work, but diesel's over $5 gallon in
most parts of the country. Big
separation from regular gas. That's a
just indication of the pressures on the
energy supply system. Those will have
translated to farm country higher costs
because they use diesel for basically
everything from powering the tractors to
running their dryers and all sorts of
equipment.
>> Yeah, of course. Bill, what's your view
here?
>> Well, we're beginning now to see data on
the overall impact of the tariffs. And a
lot of the analysis so far up until this
study has really focused on the other
side, which is the increased costs to
Americans of items that are coming in
with higher tariffs that are therefore
more expensive. And I'll come back to
that. This is really the first truly
comprehensive study we've seen of
retaliation. And in fairness, I think a
lot of us, including me, expected more
retaliation in the beginning. We thought
that everybody would retaliate, or at
least I did. And it turned out almost
nobody did. The Chinese did, and the
Canadians did to a lesser extent, and
that was it.
Of course, the reality of the global
economy these days is if the Chinese
retaliate, that's a lot. And in this
case, it's 14.9 billion in lost ag
sales. And I think the salient thing
about that is this is not, I don't
think, a short-term phenomenon. These
markets are gone. You know, the Chinese
have shifted to Brazil and Argentina.
And I don't think they're necessarily
going to shift back. I mean, they'll
probably make some token shifts back.
They made a commitment last October to
restart some purchases because last year
they purchased zero. And the Trump
administration has indicated that they
committed to, I think, 17 billion in ag
imports for them, not just soybeans, but
all agriculture. I don't think the
Chinese have confirmed that number, but
you know, if you take it as a number,
that's significant. It doesn't get us
out of the overall ag deficit. And we've
discussed that on past episodes. We are
now in our fifth year, I believe, of
agricultural deficits after more than 70
years of surpluses.
So, we've kind of turned corner here
that's disquieting for the farmers. And,
you know, this if the Chinese actually
follow through on the 17 billion
commitment, that'll help.
But, it's not going to erase the
projected deficit uh for this year. And
then, uh Scott made the other important
point, which is on top of that, the
farmers are facing a boatload of
increased costs. Fuel costs, diesel
costs, and as mentioned, I think in the
last episode, when we were talking to
Nasim Fasal from the RP, cost of
fertilizer is going up, the cost of
fertilizer ingredients is going up, in
part because of the closing of the
Strait of Hormuz, and the cost of
equipment is going up because most farm
equipment, no surprise, is made out of
steel. And we now have, depending on
what country you're coming from, 50 or
25% or maybe 15% tariffs on steel and
aluminum. So, if you're buying a new
tractor, a new combine, a new uh
harvester, first of all, it's expensive
anyway, and what you're now having to do
is pay something that's essentially more
expensive because of the increased price
of raw materials. And that gets me to
the other issue because what's becoming
obvious is that there are real costs
here for Americans. And that what Trump
said from the beginning is, "Well, well,
the foreigners are going to pay." He
didn't say anything about retaliation.
And what we're discovering is that there
wasn't as much retaliation as expected,
but what there was has made a
difference, particularly to the farmers.
And we are seeing increased costs on the
import side that where the biggest cost
or the most important one has been on
intermediate goods. And Scott has
pointed out previously that intermediate
goods now were like half of our imports,
I think, something like that.
Intermediate goods are the parts and
components, the stuff that US
manufacturers use to make end products.
And so, what we've succeeded in doing is
making US manufactured products more
expensive because now their inputs are
more expensive. It makes it inflationary
for them to sell here, and makes them
harder for them to compete in the global
market.
>> Now, across the whole economy, this
tends to flatten out. There are two
groups that are tracking this. One of
them is just the US government collects
very good data on import tariffs because
they're collecting. So, we know what
collections are, and we know what total
imports are. You can calculate your
actual applied tariff rate. But, also
the Yale Budget Lab has done a really
good jobs since liberation day of
keeping track of average effective
tariff rates. When President Trump took
office in January 2025, both the Customs
Service and the Yale Budget Lab reported
2% was our typical tariff rate. So, 2%
of all imports was the tariff rate. So,
today, the actual, if you do the math,
which is total imports and then tariffs
as a percent, it's 7.3%. The Yale Budget
Lab has it at 11.8. But, both those
numbers are lower than a year ago. In
June of 2025, the Yale Budget Lab had it
at total tariffs 14% of all imports. If
you did the tariff math, it was closer
to 10%. But, both those numbers are now
down from 14 to 11.8 or from 10 to 7.3.
So, year on year, it's definitely higher
than it was when the president took
office by quite a bit, but it's
moderated versus year ago. Well, I have
to see if this works. Bill's absolutely
right. In some of the specific areas
where tariffs are the highest, like
steel and aluminum, there'll be big
differences and noticeable increases.
But, overall, the tariffs are moderating
slightly.
>> Just to sow more confusion on all this,
the Bloomberg number
is neither the Yale number nor your
other number. The Bloomberg number is at
the current effective tariff rate is
up from 2.3% in the beginning of January
2025. In other words, before Trump came
in, there was a peak, as Scott noted,
last June, basically May and June, and
it's since come down. They have it at
10.7, so it's
>> What's the difference between the two?
>> I think two out of three is above 10.
The other thing they have is a little
commentary here on absolute volume and
these are the 232 tariffs question
because those are the ones that are
sticking around. Those are not the IEPA
ones that have been invalidated. So cars
and car parts, $372 billion worth of
affected trade. Metals, and that's not
just steel and aluminum, but all metals,
$299 billion. Timber, $17.7 billion,
which is making our housing costs go up.
Trucks, I mean heavy trucks here, $27.7
billion. And essentially everything else
that wasn't exempted, $1.1 trillion. So
that's quite a bit. They also have just
odd fact to it. I've never seen this
before. An interesting little chart
about the status of Trump's threats. And
so they counted up every tariff threat
he's made and they decided there were 59
of them
since November 2024. And the disposition
is interesting. Although this doesn't
reflect the magnitude of the various
ones, but the number that have imposed
in full is only eight. Imposed
partially, two. Under investigation, 11.
That's probably smaller now because it
was before the announcement about the
forced labor investigations, which we'll
get to in a minute. Threats that have
not yet been imposed is the biggest
number, 23. And then threats or actions
that were repealed, three. And threats
that were withdrawn, 12. So it's a mixed
picture. It's a much more of a mixed
picture than one would think. Although
some of them are a lot bigger than
others, let's put it that way.
>> Yes. But it also is a reflection of the
fact that the president uses tariffs for
more than just trade protection, which
was the old way to think about tariffs.
He's using them basically to move
negotiations forward, as leverage here
and there.
>> Well, Scott, let me just go back. We'll
move on here, but you made the comment
that ag community, ag sector, you know,
there's strong supporters of the
president generally. They're well
represented in Congress. To what effect
if the Chinese market has moved
elsewhere? Like how beneficial is that
to them if China's moving their soybean
purchases to Brazil and elsewhere?
>> Well, I haven't seen anything that would
lead me to believe that their global
soybean demand is declining. You look at
soybeans as a world market, they're
probably about the same amount. I just
don't know. I haven't looked at that
data recently, but I sense no major
decline in the consumption of soybeans
worldwide. What it means for American
farmers is after spending 25 or 30 years
cultivating customers in China, they now
have to go out and cultivate new
customers.
>> Yeah.
>> And that's real work. That's important
work. Reliable suppliers are hard to
find. Reliable customers are treated
like gold by most companies who are
customer-facing. So, there is work to be
done in that area. And when you're
dealing with China's retaliation, first
of all, as Bill pointed out, it's large
in scale. And second, it's often driven
by other factors than individual
enterprises making decisions. It tends
to be a very sort of top-down operation.
So, there's recovery that will have to
happen. And there's real work involved
in satisfying a whole new set of
customers.
>> On the politics of it, right now it's
really anecdotal. There was a lot of
people asking about this in Iowa because
the Iowa primary was on Tuesday. And
there were some reports, you know,
talking to farmers about, you know, are
you less pro-Trump than you used to be
because of all this because it's been a
big issue. Iowa is, according to the
North Dakota study, one of the biggest
losers in all of this along with
California and couple others because
Iowa's soybeans and other commodity
crops. And it sounds like, you know, the
farmers are unhappy, but most of them
are saying we're sticking with Trump.
And this is one of their problems. Trump
knows this. They don't have a lot of
leverage because they voted for him
three times and he's pretty confident
they're going to do what he tells them
the next time. I mean, there'll be some
erosion. It'll probably be show up in
people staying home in the midterms
rather than voting the other way.
And there's been some work done on that
by people like Charlie Cook and then
Zogby, the professional pollsters,
who've pointed out that the easiest
thing to do if you're unhappy is just
you don't vote. And getting farmers that
have voted Republican for the last, you
know, 12 elections to suddenly switch
and vote for a Democrat
>> Unlikely.
>> is a much bigger stretch than just
deciding, well, I'm going to pick pass
this time. So, we'll see if it shows up
in turnout.
>> We'll find out in 5 months. But Bill,
you just teased our next segment here
and this is news from just this past
week. On Tuesday, the Trump
administration announced new tariffs of
10 to 12 and 1/2% on the EU and roughly
60 other nations. The administration is
imposing these tariffs under Section 301
following a forced labor practices
investigation. So Bill, give us a lay of
the land here. What's going on and
explain how the administration is doing
this under 301.
>> Yeah, well, that's an interesting
question whether they're going to get
away with it or not. I'll get to that in
a minute. Our bottom line from the trade
guys' perspective is we were half right.
We said that everybody was going to be
guilty and that's what happened.
Everybody was guilty. All 60 countries
are deficient on the forced labor trade
front either because they don't have
laws to prohibit it or if they've got
those laws, they haven't done enough in
the USTR's judgment to enforce those
laws. And so what USTR has issued, you
know, the 301 is a process and there's
all these hoops and hurdles you have to
go to. And to Ambassador Lighthizer's
credit, unlike what Trump often does,
he's not ignoring the hoops and hurdles.
He's following the procedures which will
allow them to avoid a court loss over
process. So, the proposed remedy is out
for comment. They're putting out in
draft. So, it'll show up in the Federal
Register in the next day or so. Request
for public comment and there's going to
be public hearings later this month.
It's on a fast track. So, they're going
through all the motions to let people
talk about whether this is a good idea
or what they should do instead. And then
I think what they're going to do is of
the 60 countries, I think there were 54
that were found not to have appropriate
laws and so they're getting the 12 and
1/2% tariff.
And then the remaining one, which It the
EU, which is important, uh were found to
have relevant laws, but do not do enough
to enforce them. Their tariff is 10%.
The interesting word in the announcement
is these were referred to consistently
as additional tariffs, which suggests to
me that they're going to be on top of
the existing tariffs. Now, what that
really means, I think as a practical
matter, is the Section 232 tariffs,
because the IAPA tariffs are gone thanks
to the Supreme Court. The 122 tariffs
are in effect, but they go away July
24th.
And given even the schedule here with
the comment period and the the hearings
and everything, I think these new
tariffs will probably replace the 122
tariffs, so they won't be on top of the
existing 10%. They'll just be a new 10%
or for some people a new 12 and 1/2, but
for a lot of items, they'll be on top of
the 232 numbers, I think, which means,
depending on which country you are, your
15 is going to go to 27 and 1/2 or 25,
and your 25 is going to go to 35 or 37
and 1/2. To be fair, there are a lot of
exemptions. There's a very, very long
list of exemptions that are framed
around stuff we don't make, stuff that
would cause a lot of increased cost
increases here if we ran into supply
shortages, stuff that is essential for
US production. And if you look through
the items, there's a number of
agriculture items beginning with beef,
appropriately, because beef prices are
way up, so we can't accuse them of
making that worse in this case. And
there's a lot of metal, steel, and
aluminum derivative products, downstream
products on the exclusion list. And
you'll remember that this has been a
bone of contention with manufacturers
for the reason I said earlier, that

Uh which means, as a practical matter,

the decision last year, which was Trump

court left the door open here, which was

And you know, "Here's the process you

They're into the next buying cycle. No

They were obviously they didn't agree

and
>> Yeah.
>> we do it. That's the situation most

>> Those of us who are married to a CPA do

I just want to note that.
>> It's less friction in your transaction,

you, I wish I was married to a lawyer
cuz it's they seem to do pretty well

>> Well, yeah, as I've been saying for

>> All right. Well, we have two other
