videos.full_text: I'm Scott. >> I'm Bill. >> And we're the Trade Guys. >> You're listening to The Trade Guys, a podcast produced by CSIS, where we talk about trade in terms that everyone can understand. I'm Alex Kissling, and I'm here with Scott Miller and Bill Reinsch, the CSIS Trade Guys. Thanks for listening to The Trade Guys. On today's episode, we examine the impact of China's retaliatory tariffs, take a look at the Trump administration's new use of Section 301 authorities, and unpack the latest litigation around tariff refunds. All that and more on this episode of The Trade Guys. Well, Bill and Scott, it's great to be back with you after a few weeks of episodes with some great guests, and I want to dive right into our first topic today by taking a step back and talking through the effects of Chinese retaliatory tariffs, particularly on the US agriculture sector. >> A new study from North Dakota State University found that China's retaliatory tariffs on US ag goods wiped out an estimated 14.9 billion in export sales over 12 months. So, Scott, let's look under the hood here. What stands out to you as you look through these numbers? >> This is basically a disruption of an old relationship. The old relationship is US soybean sales to China. This goes back to basically China's growth in the early part of this century, and one of the things that happened as people raised their living standards is they improved their diet. More people were demanding the addition of meat, in this case pork, in their diet. And soybeans is primarily a very efficient food for pigs. So, that was an agriculture match made in heaven, at least for the moment at the time, and so the US found a great source of sales, net sales, additional for their soybeans and other products, and Chinese consumers improved their diet as it became more and more important element of trade between the two countries and as trade tensions rose, it became one of the obvious places for trade pressure and retaliation. And that's indeed what happened with soybeans. China basically, you look at it broadly, they changed sources. They switched their purchases from the United States to Brazil and Argentina principally. This had an immediate effect in slowing down sales and therefore exports from US over the course of crop cycle. Most of the consumption of soybeans was the same worldwide, but what happened is your sourcing changed. So, China sourced Brazil and Argentina principally instead of the United States. US soybeans went to Europe instead of China. Europe previously had gotten soybeans from Argentina and Brazil. So, there was a change in the shipping patterns, but it showed up in uh net losses as the uh North Dakota State University survey showed, net losses for US farmers. And it was sort of broadly across agriculture. There was a big drop in total ag sales to China from 2024 to 2025, sales dropped from 24 billion to 8 billion. So, it's steepest one-year decline. It certainly got the message through. And it's one of those things when you accelerate pressure on a rival's economy, they have techniques they can use back. So, this happens pretty frequently. It was not unexpected. And all I can say is that the agriculture groups in the United States tend to be strong supporters of the president and they tend to be very well represented in the US Congress. And so, over time this will work itself out. Certainly there were there were a lot of state-by-state issues that these losses materialized. And it's coming now at a time when farm incomes are under a lot of pressure. If you happen to drive by a a gas station that sells diesel fuel, look at the difference between diesel and gasoline. Diesel's what does work in the country. Gasoline's what gets you to work, but diesel's over $5 gallon in most parts of the country. Big separation from regular gas. That's a just indication of the pressures on the energy supply system. Those will have translated to farm country higher costs because they use diesel for basically everything from powering the tractors to running their dryers and all sorts of equipment. >> Yeah, of course. Bill, what's your view here? >> Well, we're beginning now to see data on the overall impact of the tariffs. And a lot of the analysis so far up until this study has really focused on the other side, which is the increased costs to Americans of items that are coming in with higher tariffs that are therefore more expensive. And I'll come back to that. This is really the first truly comprehensive study we've seen of retaliation. And in fairness, I think a lot of us, including me, expected more retaliation in the beginning. We thought that everybody would retaliate, or at least I did. And it turned out almost nobody did. The Chinese did, and the Canadians did to a lesser extent, and that was it. Of course, the reality of the global economy these days is if the Chinese retaliate, that's a lot. And in this case, it's 14.9 billion in lost ag sales. And I think the salient thing about that is this is not, I don't think, a short-term phenomenon. These markets are gone. You know, the Chinese have shifted to Brazil and Argentina. And I don't think they're necessarily going to shift back. I mean, they'll probably make some token shifts back. They made a commitment last October to restart some purchases because last year they purchased zero. And the Trump administration has indicated that they committed to, I think, 17 billion in ag imports for them, not just soybeans, but all agriculture. I don't think the Chinese have confirmed that number, but you know, if you take it as a number, that's significant. It doesn't get us out of the overall ag deficit. And we've discussed that on past episodes. We are now in our fifth year, I believe, of agricultural deficits after more than 70 years of surpluses. So, we've kind of turned corner here that's disquieting for the farmers. And, you know, this if the Chinese actually follow through on the 17 billion commitment, that'll help. But, it's not going to erase the projected deficit uh for this year. And then, uh Scott made the other important point, which is on top of that, the farmers are facing a boatload of increased costs. Fuel costs, diesel costs, and as mentioned, I think in the last episode, when we were talking to Nasim Fasal from the RP, cost of fertilizer is going up, the cost of fertilizer ingredients is going up, in part because of the closing of the Strait of Hormuz, and the cost of equipment is going up because most farm equipment, no surprise, is made out of steel. And we now have, depending on what country you're coming from, 50 or 25% or maybe 15% tariffs on steel and aluminum. So, if you're buying a new tractor, a new combine, a new uh harvester, first of all, it's expensive anyway, and what you're now having to do is pay something that's essentially more expensive because of the increased price of raw materials. And that gets me to the other issue because what's becoming obvious is that there are real costs here for Americans. And that what Trump said from the beginning is, "Well, well, the foreigners are going to pay." He didn't say anything about retaliation. And what we're discovering is that there wasn't as much retaliation as expected, but what there was has made a difference, particularly to the farmers. And we are seeing increased costs on the import side that where the biggest cost or the most important one has been on intermediate goods. And Scott has pointed out previously that intermediate goods now were like half of our imports, I think, something like that. Intermediate goods are the parts and components, the stuff that US manufacturers use to make end products. And so, what we've succeeded in doing is making US manufactured products more expensive because now their inputs are more expensive. It makes it inflationary for them to sell here, and makes them harder for them to compete in the global market. >> Now, across the whole economy, this tends to flatten out. There are two groups that are tracking this. One of them is just the US government collects very good data on import tariffs because they're collecting. So, we know what collections are, and we know what total imports are. You can calculate your actual applied tariff rate. But, also the Yale Budget Lab has done a really good jobs since liberation day of keeping track of average effective tariff rates. When President Trump took office in January 2025, both the Customs Service and the Yale Budget Lab reported 2% was our typical tariff rate. So, 2% of all imports was the tariff rate. So, today, the actual, if you do the math, which is total imports and then tariffs as a percent, it's 7.3%. The Yale Budget Lab has it at 11.8. But, both those numbers are lower than a year ago. In June of 2025, the Yale Budget Lab had it at total tariffs 14% of all imports. If you did the tariff math, it was closer to 10%. But, both those numbers are now down from 14 to 11.8 or from 10 to 7.3. So, year on year, it's definitely higher than it was when the president took office by quite a bit, but it's moderated versus year ago. Well, I have to see if this works. Bill's absolutely right. In some of the specific areas where tariffs are the highest, like steel and aluminum, there'll be big differences and noticeable increases. But, overall, the tariffs are moderating slightly. >> Just to sow more confusion on all this, the Bloomberg number is neither the Yale number nor your other number. The Bloomberg number is at the current effective tariff rate is 10.7% up from 2.3% in the beginning of January 2025. In other words, before Trump came in, there was a peak, as Scott noted, last June, basically May and June, and it's since come down. They have it at 10.7, so it's >> What's the difference between the two? >> I think two out of three is above 10. The other thing they have is a little commentary here on absolute volume and these are the 232 tariffs question because those are the ones that are sticking around. Those are not the IEPA ones that have been invalidated. So cars and car parts, $372 billion worth of affected trade. Metals, and that's not just steel and aluminum, but all metals, $299 billion. Timber, $17.7 billion, which is making our housing costs go up. Trucks, I mean heavy trucks here, $27.7 billion. And essentially everything else that wasn't exempted, $1.1 trillion. So that's quite a bit. They also have just odd fact to it. I've never seen this before. An interesting little chart about the status of Trump's threats. And so they counted up every tariff threat he's made and they decided there were 59 of them since November 2024. And the disposition is interesting. Although this doesn't reflect the magnitude of the various ones, but the number that have imposed in full is only eight. Imposed partially, two. Under investigation, 11. That's probably smaller now because it was before the announcement about the forced labor investigations, which we'll get to in a minute. Threats that have not yet been imposed is the biggest number, 23. And then threats or actions that were repealed, three. And threats that were withdrawn, 12. So it's a mixed picture. It's a much more of a mixed picture than one would think. Although some of them are a lot bigger than others, let's put it that way. >> Yes. But it also is a reflection of the fact that the president uses tariffs for more than just trade protection, which was the old way to think about tariffs. He's using them basically to move negotiations forward, as leverage here and there. >> Well, Scott, let me just go back. We'll move on here, but you made the comment that ag community, ag sector, you know, there's strong supporters of the president generally. They're well represented in Congress. To what effect if the Chinese market has moved elsewhere? Like how beneficial is that to them if China's moving their soybean purchases to Brazil and elsewhere? >> Well, I haven't seen anything that would lead me to believe that their global soybean demand is declining. You look at soybeans as a world market, they're probably about the same amount. I just don't know. I haven't looked at that data recently, but I sense no major decline in the consumption of soybeans worldwide. What it means for American farmers is after spending 25 or 30 years cultivating customers in China, they now have to go out and cultivate new customers. >> Yeah. >> And that's real work. That's important work. Reliable suppliers are hard to find. Reliable customers are treated like gold by most companies who are customer-facing. So, there is work to be done in that area. And when you're dealing with China's retaliation, first of all, as Bill pointed out, it's large in scale. And second, it's often driven by other factors than individual enterprises making decisions. It tends to be a very sort of top-down operation. So, there's recovery that will have to happen. And there's real work involved in satisfying a whole new set of customers. >> On the politics of it, right now it's really anecdotal. There was a lot of people asking about this in Iowa because the Iowa primary was on Tuesday. And there were some reports, you know, talking to farmers about, you know, are you less pro-Trump than you used to be because of all this because it's been a big issue. Iowa is, according to the North Dakota study, one of the biggest losers in all of this along with California and couple others because Iowa's soybeans and other commodity crops. And it sounds like, you know, the farmers are unhappy, but most of them are saying we're sticking with Trump. And this is one of their problems. Trump knows this. They don't have a lot of leverage because they voted for him three times and he's pretty confident they're going to do what he tells them the next time. I mean, there'll be some erosion. It'll probably be show up in people staying home in the midterms rather than voting the other way. And there's been some work done on that by people like Charlie Cook and then Zogby, the professional pollsters, who've pointed out that the easiest thing to do if you're unhappy is just you don't vote. And getting farmers that have voted Republican for the last, you know, 12 elections to suddenly switch and vote for a Democrat >> Unlikely. >> is a much bigger stretch than just deciding, well, I'm going to pick pass this time. So, we'll see if it shows up in turnout. >> We'll find out in 5 months. But Bill, you just teased our next segment here and this is news from just this past week. On Tuesday, the Trump administration announced new tariffs of 10 to 12 and 1/2% on the EU and roughly 60 other nations. The administration is imposing these tariffs under Section 301 following a forced labor practices investigation. So Bill, give us a lay of the land here. What's going on and explain how the administration is doing this under 301. >> Yeah, well, that's an interesting question whether they're going to get away with it or not. I'll get to that in a minute. Our bottom line from the trade guys' perspective is we were half right. We said that everybody was going to be guilty and that's what happened. Everybody was guilty. All 60 countries are deficient on the forced labor trade front either because they don't have laws to prohibit it or if they've got those laws, they haven't done enough in the USTR's judgment to enforce those laws. And so what USTR has issued, you know, the 301 is a process and there's all these hoops and hurdles you have to go to. And to Ambassador Lighthizer's credit, unlike what Trump often does, he's not ignoring the hoops and hurdles. He's following the procedures which will allow them to avoid a court loss over process. So, the proposed remedy is out for comment. They're putting out in draft. So, it'll show up in the Federal Register in the next day or so. Request for public comment and there's going to be public hearings later this month. It's on a fast track. So, they're going through all the motions to let people talk about whether this is a good idea or what they should do instead. And then I think what they're going to do is of the 60 countries, I think there were 54 that were found not to have appropriate laws and so they're getting the 12 and 1/2% tariff. And then the remaining one, which It the EU, which is important, uh were found to have relevant laws, but do not do enough to enforce them. Their tariff is 10%. The interesting word in the announcement is these were referred to consistently as additional tariffs, which suggests to me that they're going to be on top of the existing tariffs. Now, what that really means, I think as a practical matter, is the Section 232 tariffs, because the IAPA tariffs are gone thanks to the Supreme Court. The 122 tariffs are in effect, but they go away July 24th. And given even the schedule here with the comment period and the the hearings and everything, I think these new tariffs will probably replace the 122 tariffs, so they won't be on top of the existing 10%. They'll just be a new 10% or for some people a new 12 and 1/2, but for a lot of items, they'll be on top of the 232 numbers, I think, which means, depending on which country you are, your 15 is going to go to 27 and 1/2 or 25, and your 25 is going to go to 35 or 37 and 1/2. To be fair, there are a lot of exemptions. There's a very, very long list of exemptions that are framed around stuff we don't make, stuff that would cause a lot of increased cost increases here if we ran into supply shortages, stuff that is essential for US production. And if you look through the items, there's a number of agriculture items beginning with beef, appropriately, because beef prices are way up, so we can't accuse them of making that worse in this case. And there's a lot of metal, steel, and aluminum derivative products, downstream products on the exclusion list. And you'll remember that this has been a bone of contention with manufacturers for the reason I said earlier, that they're complaining the inputs that they need to make their stuff, that they can't get here, has gone up way up in price. I think this is an effort to solve some of those problems. So, the net impact may be less than it might seem at first. I saw, I think, one story that estimated, it was not a thorough study, estimated that maybe half of the items that we import are going to be covered by this, and the other half are going to be exempted. So, it won't be a big deal, so they say, but it, you know, obviously, as Scott said earlier, if you're in one of the affected companies, it is a big deal. >> Mhm. >> Sure, because 10% or 12 and 1/2 is not peanuts. What's going to happen next, you know, he'll be sued, of course he'll be sued. You know, he gets sued for everything, so expect that. >> But these are more durable, right, in court? >> Well, that's an interesting question. I had thought so. My column this week discusses that a little bit, and I reference a piece by Alan Wolff, our friend Alan Wolff, the former Deputy Director General of the WTO, who wrote a piece. We both came to the conclusion that it might not be as much of a slam dunk as the administration thinks. >> Oh, interesting. >> Although for different reasons. Alan's reason was sort of constitutional. Get my column, if you're not, it's on the website. Go to the last line, click on the link to his piece and read it. It's very thoughtful. I don't really agree with it, but basically, he's arguing that the Constitution gives revenue authority to Congress, end of story, and this is an unconstitutional extension of executive authority that the courts ought to strike down, as they did with AIPA. So, maybe they will. I've taken a narrower view, and if you look at the Federal Register notice, you'll see that Ambassador Lighthizer has too. The statute says that in order to act, you have to find that a foreign act, policy, or practice is an unjustifiable, unreasonable, or discriminatory burden on United States commerce. And that falls into, like, multiple parts. Is it unjustifiable, unreasonable, or discriminatory, number one? And two, is it a burden on United States commerce? Because it can be unjustifiable and not make any difference, you know, or it can be a burden and not be unjustifiable, etc. So, you have to prove all these things. The administration is asserting them, and they've got a lengthy study for all 60 countries, which I've not looked at yet, to back it up. My suspicion is that if you are a smart lawyer and choose your plaintiff wisely and choose your countries wisely, you may be able to get the court to decide that in the particular case you're suing, this is not an unreasonable That's really the only word that the ambassador would use. This is not an unreasonable act, policy, or practice that burdens or restricts US commerce. For example, and this is already screams of outrage are already coming from the EU, with good reason, because they have a law on the subject. And this has been something that the EU has actually attempted to deal with through a number of measures that they've taken over the years. They would probably say that they are more aggressive on forced labor than we are. We would probably not agree with that. But to imply that they're deficient is obviously offensive to them. The chairman of the Parliament's trade subcommittee has said this is either ridiculous or absurd. I forget which word he used for this particular thing. So, they'll push back and they'll argue this is an unconstitutional extension of the statute that goes beyond the president's authority. Somebody's going to say to the court, you know, in a case like that, what you need to do is find that this is not an unreasonable practice. It does not burden or restrict US commerce, and the US trade got it wrong. I don't know if that'll prevail, and I think there's certainly going to be cases where it won't prevail. The administration says everybody's guilty. Well, it's wrong to say that everybody's innocent. There's a number in there that certainly are guilty. So, I think though, if you choose your victims wisely, I mean companies that's actually suffered with forced labor imports from the right country, or allegedly forced labor imports from a country that probably is doing something about that, I think some of these may be winners in court. >> Yeah. >> But not all of them. Alan says they're all going to lose. >> Yeah, point is, I think Bill, what you're describing is something that's very fact-intensive. This is not easy litigation. I tend to agree with more with you than Alan. Alan is a wonderful legal scholar, but I don't think the constitutional argument will be all that strong because 301 was created by the Congress. It's been a statute. It's a specific delegation to the US Trade Representative to deal with unfair practices. But when you get down to defining how unfair is unfair, that gets very fact specific. I think claims are going to be difficult to make. Also, keep in mind that while we have this proposed rule on forced labor up at the plate, over in the on-deck circle is the 301 on structural excess capacity. So, there's another bite at this apple, all of which make me believe Secretary Besson's original forecast, which is whatever the Supreme Court decides, we're not going to see a drop in revenue from tariffs. So, I think we're on this train for a while. And once again, look, forced labor or prison labor has been prohibited in for imports to the US since I think the McKinley Tariff Act of 1896. It's a common feature. Sometimes it gets expanded in its coverage. Our favorite Afflebauch, there was an expansion of the clause in the Trade Act of 1930, the Smoot-Hawley, that was never applied for by an individual firm about forced labor and then became this entire program. So, there's a lot of ground to be plowed. >> All right. Well, let's turn to our final topic today and take a quick look at some latest news on the tariff refund process. The DOJ is asking an appeals court to overturn rulings from the Court of International Trade. And Bill, as I understand it, this dispute is in part centered around whether or not the trade court has the authority to order refunds on a nationwide basis. Am I reading that right or where am I wrong? >> No, that's right. First, a short update. The refunds of unliquidated entries appears to be proceeding as planned. The CBP is providing updates to the court. I think they've now I don't remember the exact numbers, but I think they said something like maybe up to 20 billion has actually been paid out. The estimate of what needs to be paid out is still 166 billion. So, there's a long way to go, but wheels are turning, mechanisms are developing. You know, one of the problems has been companies that didn't sign up for the electronic funds transfer program that CBP has. Companies The ones that haven't done that are now doing that because they figured out they won't get their money ever for anything from CBP unless they do. That'll still take care of it in time. The new wrinkle involves entries that were finally liquidated. >> What does that mean? >> It means basically that Customs has I think 312 days after entry to formally liquidate the item. That means that they essentially clear it. Everything is settled. Amount of duty is determined. The duty is paid. Everybody's happy. And the books are closed on that particular entry. Because it takes a long time, I mean more than 300 days, for Customs to do that, they have a schedule and it sort of rolls out. One category of stuff is stuff that fell victim to the earliest tariffs Trump announced. The steel and aluminum ones in February of '25, which were under IPA. And then the liberation day tariffs in April. 312 days takes you into sometime before the Supreme Court decision. So, there was a number of that got finally liquidated before the court came in. The other category, which I don't know as much about, seems to be those that are informally liquidated that are which tend to be small numbers from small companies that are liquidated virtually when they enter. They come in, the duty's paid at the same time. And that's sort of the end of it. There's it's an informal process. This is not Walmart. This is individual entities. >> Yeah. Yeah. >> But the point is, in all these cases, liquidation is over. The administration argues that in that case, the only way that those people can get their money back is if a court orders them to get their money back, orders CBP to pay them back. Uh which means, as a practical matter, they have to sue. They have to go to court, file a lawsuit, win, and then CBP will pay up. The judge issued a universal injunction essentially ordering CBP to pay anyway. And the Justice Department is arguing that he doesn't have authority to do that, that the decision last year, which was Trump v. Casa, c a s a, removed the authority to issue this kind of universal injunction that covers everybody as opposed to just the handful of plaintiffs in the case. That'll be litigated, I think because the court the court left the door open here, which was you can file a class action lawsuit. And so one of two things will happen, either Court of Appeals will slap down the Justice Department's request and let the order stand. In the end, the Supremes are going to have to do what they should have done the first time, which is to lay out what they wanted to have happen. You know, and all they said was the tariffs are invalid, period. They could have gone one step further and said, "And here's who gets their money back." And you know, "Here's the process you need to follow to do that." But they didn't do that. It's going to come back to haunt them because it's going to end up in their lap, and they're going to have to answer those questions. So, they could have done it the first time, but it'll probably go down that road. The alternative is Justice wins, the smart lawyers are going to rally everybody in that category, file multiple class action lawsuits. They'll win because the Supremes have already invalidated the tariffs. It's not a mystery as to how the courts are going to rule. It just forces everybody to go through an extra step, forces them to hire lawyers, and therefore pay part of the revenue or the refunds to the lawyers. I think the Justice Department is banking on the thought that a lot of people won't bother, especially the small guys, because it's too much effort. >> That's exactly right. The small players have moved on. They've sold the goods. They're into the next buying cycle. No one wants to go back. >> Which means they don't have to give as much back. I can see it, but it's cynical, you know, it's not justice. And it's kind of annoying. I think, you know, way back in the beginning of this, what Scott and I both said was, you know, the administration could make this easier, they could make it hard. And they've chosen to make it hard. And the losers in doing that are not going to be the large companies that have in-house lawyers, and you know, major compliance operations for this is just one more task. The losers are going to be the small importers that, like Scott said, have moved on, can't afford to litigate, and they're just going to say, "Well, you know, I'll chalk that one up to bad experience." And it's too bad because they can't afford to lose. >> Yeah, Scott, is this the right strategy? >> It is consistent with the administration's behavior all along. They were obviously they didn't agree with the outcome of the the case, and they've not obstructed in any way, but they're just they're not making it easy on anyone, and they have a right to do that, but it is for me the flaw here is once the Supreme Court decided they were going to take the case and decide the case, to decide the case without a remedy is kind of opened the door for this activity. I think there's plenty of blame to go around, but once again, every once in a while, Alex, in my long life at work, I've overpaid taxes here and there, and at some point you just you don't worry about it. You find a pile of items that you could have taken as a deduction, but it's just too much work to talk to your CPA and go back, and >> Yeah. >> we do it. That's the situation most importers are in who are in this situation where they have a liquidated transaction. So, you move on. Life goes on. >> Those of us who are married to a CPA do not have that problem. I just want to note that. >> It's less friction in your transaction, that's for sure. Bill, after hearing you, I wish I was married to a lawyer cuz it's they seem to do pretty well here. >> Well, yeah, as I've been saying for years, they're always the winners. No matter what happens, the lawyers are the winners. >> All right. Well, we have two other winners to talk about today. One is our dear friend Evan Brown, who has been a huge part of this program for years. As we talked about a month or two ago, Evan has been accepted into a wonderful graduate program at Princeton. Today is his final recording of Trade Guys. He occasionally has jumped in as host here and done a much better job than I could ever do, and he has been such a great part of this team and the economics team at CSIS. So, Evan, we all want to wish you congratulations and wish you the best of luck. We're we're so proud of you and thank you for all you've done for the Trade Guys over the years. >> Thanks, Alex. It's been such a pleasure being a trade dude. >> Sure. >> I don't know if I'm a full trade guy, but wishing you all the best and hoping to keep in touch with Trade Guys fandom. >> Well, you'll always be a trade dude and Evan, congratulations. Yeah. >> In national security hierarchy, you know, there are sherpas and then there are yaks. Evan's been a yak for us and a very, very good one. >> Indeed. We'll miss you, but we're glad you're moving on to the career you want for yourself. So, congratulations. >> Very excited for you. >> It's been an honor. Thanks, guys. >> The second winner here is Trade Guy Scott, who has welcomed a new addition to his family. And Scott, we're so happy for you and your growing family. You're second grandkid, I believe, and very, very thrilled for you. >> Well, thank you. Yes, yes, Benjamin Charles Sunwood came into the world on June 2nd. He came home from the hospital with his mom today and so they're becoming new parents and mom and dad are happy, baby is healthy, everything we could ask for. So, we're richly blessed. >> That's wonderful. >> I haven't tried to get any sleep yet. But just wait. >> Yeah, sleep has been optional so far, but won't be forever. >> I'm about 8 years into parenthood and I'm still not getting sleep, so I don't know if there's light at the end of that tunnel for anyone. >> We also have a third winner of and that is our new producer Olivia who has joined the Scholl Chair team at CSIS and is going to be succeeding Evan as our producer. So, welcome, Olivia. We look forward to more working with you and having a trade what? Dude-ette? Is that the right term? I don't I'm not sure. >> Trade gal, maybe? >> Sure. Trade gal. Trade gal Olivia. >> We can do that. >> So, lots of good things happening here and it's always great to end on a on a positive note. So, Bill and Scott, it's great to be back with you. Thanks to all of our listeners, as always. We'll be back with you next week. Take care until then. >> Thanks for listening to the program, CSIS Pod. For more audio content, visit csis.org/podcasts. Thanks for listening.

metadata.title: HTS Codes Explained
metadata.author: USA Customs Clearance
metadata.shortDescription:
Finding the correct Harmonized Tariff Schedule, or HTS, code is one of the most important steps in importing products into the United States.

Your HTS code determines how U.S. Customs and Border Protection classifies your product, the duty rate you pay, and whether additional government agency requirements, tariffs, quotas, or trade remedies apply.

In this video, we explain:
• How HTS codes are structured
• What details Customs uses to classify products
• Why similar products can have different tariff codes
• How the wrong classification can cause delays, overpayments, penalties, or additional reviews
• How to research potential classifications using an HTS code lookup tool
• When to request a binding ruling from CBP
• When to work with a licensed customs broker

We also walk through an example showing how two similar stainless steel water bottles can receive completely different HTS classifications and duty rates based on one product feature.

Start your research with the free USA Customs Clearance HTS Code Lookup Tool and watch our instructional walkthrough to learn how to narrow your search.

A lookup tool can provide possible classifications, but it cannot guarantee that the code you select is correct. When you need greater confidence, our licensed customs brokers can review your product, identify potential government agency requirements, evaluate duty implications, and help you avoid costly classification mistakes.

Contact USA Customs Clearance today and let our team help you classify and clear your imports with confidence.

https://USACustomsClearance.com
(855) 912-0406

#HTSCode #CustomsClearance #Importing #CustomsBroker #USCustoms #InternationalTrade #TariffCode #ImportCompliance #CBP #SupplyChain

are tackling the absolute backbone of
international trade, demystifying HS

Whether you're managing complex global
supply chains or just handling the
occasional cross-border shipment,
getting a grip on this is, frankly,
non-negotiable. So, let's just dive
right in.
Picture this for a second. Two identical

exactly the same product, same weight,
the whole shebang. Yet, one of them ends
up getting hit with a massively higher

metadata.title: 7 Tips for the US Customs Broker Exam
metadata.author: Imports Academy
metadata.shortDescription:
Are you prepared for the US Customs broker exam? This exam is difficult! You can pass if spend the time to prepare for it, and we have 7 tips to help anyone pass the US Customs broker exam.

If you want to take the extra steps needed to help you pass, come check out our US Customs broker prep course at Imports Academy:
https://www.importsacademy.com/prep-course

Our online course covers all the 14 exam categories: classification, entry, practical exercises, broker compliance, bonds, free trade agreements, fines and penalties, valuation, drawback, free trade zones, intellectual property, marking, power of attorney and antidumping/countervailing duties.
*UPDATE* AS of October 2018, CBP has added a new category to the exam: ACE. 

Our course has printable study guides for each category, online quizzes, practice exams and educational videos. 

Learn more at Imports Academy: https://www.importsacademy.com/customs-broker-exam/
CBP Informed Compliance Publications: https://www.cbp.gov/trade/rulings/informed-compliance-publications
Past broker exam and answers: https://www.cbp.gov/document/publications/past-customs-broker-license-examinations-answer-keys

metadata.title: HTSUS Classification Webinar
metadata.author: Star USA, Inc.
metadata.shortDescription:
Accurate classification is all about the details. This conversation discusses the fundamentals of HTSUS Classification and why it matters to your organization. Avoid common mistakes and learn fundamentals to keep your company compliant.

The Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) is the legal basis for application of tariffs and duty rates. It also informs any tariff-related programs, including USMCA and other Free Trade Agreements, AD/CVD, Section 232, Section 301, and many more.

There are more than 18,000 HTSUS classifications across 22 Sections and 99 Chapters. The HTSUS is 10 digits long: the first six from the HS plus two at the Tariff-Item level where duty rates are applied and two more for statistical reporting.

Visit our website for slides and additional information: https://starusa.org/on-demand-webinars/htsus-classification-2/

metadata.title: Product Classification Under HTSUS Part 1
metadata.author: Law Office of Yuri Starikov, LLC
metadata.shortDescription:
Lecture series preparing examinees to pass April 2014 Customs Broker License Examination (CBE Exam).  

Class focuses on rules guiding product classification under Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States.  Classification number, also known as statistical reporting number, or HTSUS number is primarily determined under principles of General Rules of Interpretation.  Lecture deconstructs General Rules through general background discussion and application of the rules through examples from the past customs broker examinations. 

For more updated materials, please visit LAWCUSTOMS.COM/STORE

metadata.title: Tariff Engineering & Duty Reduction
metadata.author: JSJ INTERNATIONAL LCB
metadata.shortDescription:
Want to pay less in import duties — legally?
In this video, we explain Tariff Engineering — the strategic process of designing, modifying, or sourcing your products to qualify for lower tariff classifications — and how it can lead to massive savings on customs duties.

We’ll cover:
✅ What tariff engineering is and why it works
✅ Legal framework under U.S. Customs rules
✅ Real-world examples of duty reduction
✅ Compliance tips to avoid penalties
✅ How to work with a customs broker for best results

📌 Whether you’re an importer, manufacturer, or supply chain manager, this is your guide to reducing costs while staying compliant.

#TariffEngineering #DutyReduction #CustomsBroker #TradeCompliance #ImportExport #CBP #CustomsClearance #TradeLaw #DutySavings #TariffClassification #GlobalTrade #InternationalTrade #ImportExportBusiness #CustomsCompliance #CBPCompliance #LogisticsTips #TariffReduction #internationalshipping

01:19 – What is Tariff Engineering?  
02:20 – U.S. Customs legal framework  
02:41 – Examples of tariff engineering in action  
04:42 – How to apply duty reduction strategies  
05:30 – Compliance tips to avoid penalties  
06:00 – Tariff Engineering vs Fraud
07:20 – Final thoughts and key takeaways
07:50 – Outro

metadata.title: [CBLE] CBLE3: Broker Licensing, Supervision, and Power of Attorney (19 CFR Part 111 & 141)
metadata.author: VoraPrep
metadata.shortDescription:
This episode explains U.S. customs broker licensing, permit requirements, and the critical concept of responsible supervision and control under 19 CFR Part 111. It also details the validity and scope requirements for a Power of Attorney (POA) as outlined in 19 CFR Part 141.

Full transcript & study notes: https://voraprep.com/audio/cble-cble3-dialogue-cble-cble3-lesson-001
Practice questions & study guides: https://voraprep.com/cble

segments.text: Welcome back to VOR Prep Audio. Emma,
we've got a scenario that hits two of
the most fundamental topics on the exam,
broker supervision and the power of
attorney.
>> It's a classic pairing. They test your
understanding of a broker's internal
duties and their external authority from
a client.
>> Exactly. So, here's the setup. A
brokerage firm, Global Trade Solutions,
is opening an office in a new port.
Their main licensed officer, Anya
Sharma, is based 500 miles away and
she's put a junior unlicensed supervisor
in charge of the new office's daily
operations.
>> Okay, I can already see a potential
issue with supervision.
>> Right. And at the same time, they get a
new client, Tech Innovations. The
client's head of logistics signs a power
of attorney authorizing the broker to
handle customs for electronic
components, but it's missing a corporate
seal.
>> Two distinct problems to solve. One
about the broker's own house and one
about the legal paperwork from their
client.
>> So, where do we start? Let's begin with
the broker themselves. To even operate,
Global Trade Solutions needs a license,
correct?
>> That's the foundation. And CBP issues
two main types. An individual can get a
license after meeting the requirements,
being a US citizen over 18, good moral
character, and of course passing the
CBLE.
>> So, for a company like Global Trade
Solutions LLC, does the corporation
itself take the exam?
>> That's a great question and a common
point of confusion. No, the corporation
doesn't take the exam. A corporation to
get its license must have at least one
officer who is an individually licensed
broker. We call that person the
qualifying officer.
>> So, in our scenario, that's Anya Sharma.
She holds the individual license that
allows Global Trade Solutions to hold
its corporate license.
>> Precisely. Her personal qualification is
what qualifies the entire company to
operate as a broker.
>> The scenario also mentions they're
expanding into a new CBP port. Does the
national license cover that
automatically?
>> Not quite. In addition to the national
license, a broker also needs a permit
for each district where they conduct
customs business. So for this new
office, Global Trade Solutions would
have needed to secure the proper
district permit.
>> Okay, so let's assume they have the
corporate license and the new district
permit. Now we get to the heart of the
problem. Anya, the qualifying officer,
is 500 miles away. You said you saw an
issue there.
>> I did. It's about a core requirement
called responsible supervision and
control, or RSC. It's not enough for a
brokerage to just have a licensed person
on the payroll. That person, the
qualifying officer, must actively and
meaningfully oversee all the customs
business the company conducts.
>> What does active and meaningful actually
look like? It sounds subjective.
>> CBP has been pretty clear on this. Think
of a head chef for a chain of high-end
restaurants. The chef's name is on the
door, and she creates the menu, but she
also has to ensure the quality in every
single kitchen, every single night. She
can't just write the recipes and then
disappear. She needs systems, she needs
to train her staff, she needs to check
the results. That's RSC.
>> That makes sense. So what are the
specific ingredients CBP looks for in
that RSC recipe? Is it just about
training?
>> Training is a huge part of it. Making
sure all employees, licensed or not,
know what they're doing. But it's more
than that.
>> What else? Are we talking about things
like record keeping?
>> Yes, maintaining adequate records is
another key element. So is having clear
written procedures for how to handle
customs transactions from start to
finish. The whole team needs to be
following the same compliant playbook.
>> What about the financial side of things?
>> Absolutely. RSC includes demonstrating
financial stability and having
safeguards in place for any client funds
they might handle. And underlying all of
this is the expectation that the broker
maintains current knowledge of all the
complex customs, laws, and regulations.
>> So, back to our scenario. Anya is 500
miles away and a junior unlicensed
person is running the day-to-day. That
sounds like a big red flag for
responsible supervision and control.
>> It is. This is a classic exam trap.
Delegation is a necessary part of
business, but the qualifying officer
cannot delegate her ultimate
responsibility. If Anya is just a name
on a letterhead and has no direct
systematic oversight of that new office,
then Global Trade Solutions is failing
its RSC duty. CBP wants to see active
involvement, not just a license hanging
on a distant wall.
>> The consequences for that could be
serious, right? Like suspension or even
revocation of their license.
>> That's the risk. It's one of the most
serious compliance obligations a broker
has.
>> Okay, that covers the broker's internal
problem. Let's switch to the second part
of the scenario, the client paperwork.
The new client, Tech Innovations, sent
over a power of attorney or POA. What is
that fundamentally?
>> A power of attorney is the legal key the
client gives the broker. It's a written
document that authorizes the broker, who
is the agent, to act on behalf of the
importer, who is the principal. Without
a valid POA, a broker simply has no
legal authority to file entries or
conduct any customs business for that
client.
>> The scenario flags a few details. The
POA was signed by the head of logistics.
It was missing a corporate seal and it
had a very specific scope. Let's unpack
that. First, who is allowed to sign a
POA for a company?
>> The signatory has to be someone with the
authority to bind the company. This is
typically an owner, a partner, or a
corporate officer like a CEO or CFO. An
authorized employee, like a head of
logistics, can also sign, but their
authority must be verifiable.
>> And what's the significance of the
missing corporate seal? Is that a deal
breaker?
>> It can be. A corporate POA often
requires the corporate seal. If the
company doesn't have one or doesn't use
it, the POA should include a separate
certification. This certification states
that the person who signed the POA is a
corporate officer and was duly
authorized to sign on the company's
behalf. It's all about proving the
authorization is legitimate.
>> So, the missing seal on the Tech
Innovations POA is a problem that needs
to be fixed before it can be used.
>> Correct. They would need to get a
properly executed POA before they file
anything.
>> Now, for what seems like the most
critical part, the scope. The POA
granted authority for all customs
transactions related to electronic
components. What happens if Tech
Innovations asks them to clear a
shipment of, say, finished computer
monitors?
>> They can't do it. Not with that POA. The
authority granted is specific. This is
the difference between a general power
of attorney, which typically covers all
customs business, and a specific power
of attorney, which is limited. Theirs is
limited to electronic components.
>> So, a computer monitor, which is a
finished good, wouldn't be covered?
>> Exactly. It falls outside the scope of
electronic components. The broker must
honor the limitations in the POA. To
handle the monitors, they would need a
new broader POA from the client or an
amendment to the existing one. Exceeding
the scope of a POA is a major compliance
failure.
>> So, let's apply the full decision
framework here. If this were an exam
question, what's the final verdict on
Global Trade Solutions?
>> Walking through the steps, first we
identify the parties, which we've done.
Second, we assume they have the proper
license and permit. The real problems
start at step three, assessing
responsible supervision and control. The
remote qualifying officer with an
unsupervised junior employee strongly
indicates a failure of RSC.
>> And step four, the power of attorney?
>> The POA is deficient. The lack of a
corporate seal or certification of
authority makes its execution
questionable and its scope is narrow,
which creates a significant operational
risk if the client's business is broader
than just components.
>> Which brings us to the final step,
compliance and consequences.
>> The conclusion is that Global Trade
Solutions is non-compliant. They face
potential disciplinary action from CBP
for the RSC failure up to license
revocation. And any entries they might
try to file using that flawed POA would
be rejected, causing delays and problems
for their new client.
>> It really shows how these two areas are
interlinked. You can't do the work
without a valid POA, and you can't
manage the work without proper RSC.
>> That's the perfect summary. On the exam,
you have to check both, the broker's
internal controls and their external
authorization from the client.
>> So, to nail this on exam day, we need to
verify the broker's license and permit,
scrutinize the reality of their
responsible supervision and control, and
then dissect the power of attorney for
proper signature, seal, and especially
scope.
>> Exactly. Here's an analogy to hold onto.
The broker's license is your driver's
license. The permit is your permission
to drive in a specific city. Responsible
supervision and control is you actually
being a safe, attentive driver behind
the wheel. And the POA? That's the car's
owner handing you the keys and telling
you you're only allowed to drive to the
grocery store and back.
>> That clarifies it perfectly. You can
have the license, but if you're not
paying attention or you go somewhere you
weren't allowed, you're in trouble.
>> You've got it. And remember, these
concepts are foundational. If you need
more practice with scenarios like this,
Vora Prep is a full exam prep app,
lessons, practice questions, and an AI
tutor in one place. You can get started
at voraprep.com.
It's free to try.
>> Great advice. Thanks, Emma.
>> Anytime, Marcus. Keep up the great work,
everyone.

metadata.title: Recording Part 111 Modernization of Customs Broker Regulations
metadata.author: CONECT Recorded Webinars
metadata.shortDescription:
Part 111: Modernization of Customs Broker Regulations

The new Customs Broker Regulations went into effect on December 19, 2022 but guidance from CBP continues to be issued to clarify some of the issues.

This session will outline the most critical changes to the Regulations and discuss impact to Brokers and Importers:

 * What do Brokers have to do differently?

 * How will the new Regulations change brokers’ interaction 
           with importers?
  
The discussion will include changes to broker reporting requirements,

Power of Attorney (POA), Responsible Supervision and Control, and CBP’s updated guidance on implementing the Regulations.

 Speakers:
Ania Fuller, Director of Consulting and Regulatory Affairs, A.N. Deringer, Inc.

Robert Silverman, Esq. Partner, Grunfeld, Desidero, Lebowitz, Silverman and Klestadt LLP

metadata.title: ISF “10+2” Filing Explained | Importer Requirements under 19 CFR Part 149 | CBP Compliance Guide
metadata.author: JSJ INTERNATIONAL LCB
metadata.shortDescription:
VIDEO DESCRIPTION (Ready to Paste):

In this video, Licensed Customs Broker Jaime Salazar from JSJ International breaks down the Importer Security Filing (ISF), also known as the “10+2” rule, required by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) for all ocean-bound imports.

You’ll learn:
 • Who must file the ISF
 • What information is required
 • When the filing must be submitted
 • What to do if the information changes
 • Exemptions for bulk and break bulk cargo
 • Bond and power of attorney requirements

This content is based on Title 19 CFR Part 149 and is a must-watch for importers, freight forwarders, NVOCCs, and customs brokers handling vessel cargo into the U.S.

Chapters:
00:00 – Introduction
01:10 – What is ISF and Who Must File?
02:35 – The 10 Mandatory ISF Data Elements (“10+2”)
04:26 – Filing Deadlines and Flexible Reporting
05:30 – Updates, Withdrawals, and CBP Verification
06:11 – Filing Methods, Bonds & Power of Attorney
07:10 – Exemptions: Bulk & Break Bulk Cargo
07:43 – Final Remarks and Compliance Tips

🔔 Subscribe and turn on notifications for more educational content on U.S. trade law, customs compliance, and federal regulations.

👨‍💼 JSJ International | Trade Education & Compliance

📧 Business inquiries: jaime@jsjinternationalchb.com

metadata.title: The Economics of a Customs Broker
metadata.author: Factory Floor Economics
metadata.shortDescription:
Every truck that crosses from Mexico into the United States needs two signatures: a Mexican agente aduanal and a US customs broker. In fiscal 2025 the US collected $195 billion in customs duties. In February 2026 the Supreme Court struck down most of those tariffs, and the same brokers who filed the entries started filing the refunds. This is the economics of a customs broker: how a shipment really clears two customs systems, who is allowed to do it, what the fees are on both sides of the border, why one wrong code can cost ten times the fee, and how 2026 changed the job on both sides.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Intro: two invisible passengers
1:27 Two signatures: how a load clears
4:07 The gatekeepers: licenses and patentes
6:17 The money: fees and what they protect
9:31 The pressure in 2026
12:37 Who wins
13:42 Final thoughts

SOURCES (checked October 21, 2026)
- US customs duties, FY2025: CRFB analysis of US Treasury data
- Supreme Court IEEPA ruling and Section 122: Bradley; ABA Procurement Lawyer (Fall 2026)
- Section 301 forced labor tariffs and Mexico: Holland & Knight (July 2026)
- CAPE refund process and totals: GHY; C.H. Robinson (Sept 2026); Supply Chain Dive (Oct 2026)
- Licensed customs brokers and license rules: CBP, Becoming a Customs Broker
- US imports: CBP FY2023 Trade Fact Sheet
- Broker exam format and April 2026 pass rate: ST&R; Shipping Solutions; NCBFAA (CBP figures)
- US broker fees: Suaid Global 2026 fee guide (industry estimates); Clearit published pricing
- Merchandise processing fee FY2027: CBP user fee adjustments, via Tradlinx
- Two customs processes at the border: AJOT (Aug 2026)
- Truck e-manifest timing: 19 CFR 123.92
- Mexican customs light and previo: Cargado
- Agentes aduanales and patentes: Estrategia Aduanera; Opportimes (ANAM, CAAAREM); TheLogisticsWorld; Mexico Industry
- Mexican customs operations: ANAM via Ruptura360
- Agente aduanal fees: Camtom via TheLogisticsWorld (Oct 2026); Anexo 4 RMF 2026 via Trade Law College
- Mexico's Customs Law reform 2026: Forvis Mazars; Bloomberg Línea; AJOT
- Mexico's 2026 tariff increase: Expeditors
- Expeditors 2025 results: Q4 2025 earnings release; 2025 Form 10-K

Music and sound design are original, made for this video.

Do you work in customs on either side of the border? Tell me what I got wrong in the comments.

United States carries two invisible passengers.
Neither one is in the cab.
One sits in an office in Nuevo Laredo.
The other sits in an office in Laredo, Texas, maybe a mile away.
Before the truck reaches the bridge,
both of them have already signed off on what is inside it.
They are customs brokers.
In Mexico, agentes aduanales.
And over the last two years, they have worked through one of
the most chaotic stretches of US trade policy in decades.
In fiscal 2025, the United States collected $195 billion in customs duties,
more than two and a half times the year before.
Every one of those dollars was declared on an entry,
the paperwork brokers write for a living.
Then, in February 2026, the Supreme Court struck down most of those tariffs.
And the same people who filed the paperwork to pay
them started filing paperwork to get them back.
More than $136 billion in refunds, so far.
So what does it actually cost to clear a truck?
Who is allowed to do it?
And how does a business that charges a couple of hundred
dollars per shipment end up responsible for millions in taxes?
To answer that, we have to start at the bridge.
Picture a trailer like the ones from the last video.
This one carries finished goods from a factory in Monterrey,
sealed, headed to a customer in Texas.
Here is the first thing most people get wrong.
A cross-border shipment is not one customs process.
It is two.
One under Mexican law, run by Mexico's customs agency, ANAM.
One under US law, run by US Customs and Border Protection.
A US broker cannot file the Mexican paperwork.
A Mexican agent cannot file the American one.
Two licenses, two systems, two signatures.
On the Mexican side, the agente aduanal
prepares the pedimento, the export declaration.
It lists what the goods are, what they are worth,
their tariff classification and the customs regime they move under.
For a factory operating under IMMEX,
Mexico's program for export manufacturers, that regime matters.
It is how the materials entered Mexico without
paying import taxes in the first place.
When the truck reaches the Mexican customs module,
the pedimento goes into the system, and the system answers with a light.
Green, the truck rolls.
Red, the cargo gets a physical inspection.
The selection is random, but weighted by risk.
That is why good agents do a previo, their own inspection
before filing, so a red light finds nothing wrong.
Then the bridge.
On the US side, the carrier must send an electronic manifest before the truck arrives,
30 minutes to 1 hour ahead, depending on the system it uses.
The US broker has usually filed the entry already, so by the time
the truck reaches the booth, CBP knows what it should be carrying.
The US entry answers the same questions in a different language:
a 10-digit tariff code, a value, a country of origin.
For goods made in Mexico, the most valuable line on that entry is often
a single claim: that the goods qualify under USMCA, the trade agreement.
If they qualify, they can skip the newest tariffs entirely.
If they don't, several tariffs can stack on the same box.
After the truck is gone, the work isn't.
The broker files the entry summary,
pays the duties and fees, and keeps the records.
In Mexico, the agent keeps the electronic file of every operation.
One Mexican brokerage describes the job as being a notary of foreign trade.
The truck moves the goods.
The broker moves the legal identity of the goods.
Here is how small this world is.
In the United States, there are about 14,454 active licensed customs brokers.
That counts people, not companies.
For a country that imports more than $3 trillion of goods a year,
that is one licensed broker for more than $200 million of imports.
To get a license, you pass the Customs Broker License Exam.
Eighty questions, four and a half hours, open book, 75% to pass.
It sounds easy.
It isn't.
In April 2026, CBP reported that 22% of test-takers passed.
The book is open, but the book is thousands of pages of
regulations and tariff schedules, and the clock doesn't stop.
A brokerage company doesn't need everyone licensed.
It needs at least one licensed officer or partner.
If it goes more than 120 days without one, the company's license is revoked.
A license can literally walk out the door.
Mexico is even tighter.
Mexico has roughly 800 active agentes aduanales.
An industry count put it at 824 in 2023,
and the main association says it represents more than 800.
That is for 50 customs offices and, in 2024,
about 22 million foreign trade operations.
To get a patente, you must be Mexican by birth,
hold a professional degree, have more than five years of customs experience,
and pass both a knowledge exam and a psychometric exam.
New patentes come out of periodic calls and a selection process.
For decades, a patente was effectively for life,
and whole agencies were built around one person's license.
And it can be taken away.
In April 2025, ANAM cancelled 41 patentes at once,
linking those agents to illegal imports.
So on both sides, the business has the same shape.
A small number of licensed people.
A huge volume of operations.
And a license that is both the moat and the risk.
So how does a broker get paid?
In the US, mostly per entry.
Industry guides put a standard formal entry at $150 to $250.
A complex one, with many lines or other agencies involved, $250 to $400.
Then come security filings, bonds,
amendments and per-line classification charges.
One online broker publishes a flat price of $149.95 for an ocean entry.
Those fees are separate from what the government charges.
The merchandise processing fee is 0.3464% of the value,
with a minimum of $34.58 and a maximum of $670.86 per entry in fiscal 2027.
The broker collects it and passes it to CBP.
It isn't revenue.
In Mexico, there is no official tariff for agents.
Industry estimates run from 3,500 to 8,000 pesos for a standard operation,
roughly $190 to $440, or 0.35% to 0.65% of the cargo value, with minimums.
On top of that come taxes, the customs processing fee,
which for an IMMEX operation is a fixed 462 pesos in 2026,
and the prevalidation charge on each pedimento.
Put the two sides together.
A trailer carrying $60,000 of goods might
pay both brokers $400 to $700 in total.
Around 1% of the cargo, or less.
Now look at what those fees are protecting.
If that trailer's USMCA claim fails, its goods can owe
a 10% Section 301 tariff on top of their normal duty.
Roughly ten times what both brokers charged.
That is the economics of brokerage in one line.
You charge for minutes of work, but you get paid for being right.
The cost side is people, software and liability.
Every entry is touched by classifiers and entry writers,
and US law puts their supervision on the license holder.
Software matters because the fee is per entry and the labor is per minute.
The faster an entry is built correctly, the more margin it leaves.
That is why the big players love this business.
At Expeditors, one of the largest freight forwarders in the US,
customs brokerage and other services brought in $4.27
billion in 2025, up about 13%, and 39% of total revenue.
In the fourth quarter, the company said demand for customs brokerage remained strong,
and that it was adding people particularly in customs brokerage.
For a small broker in Laredo, the math is different.
The clients are factories, carriers and forwarders who cross every day.
Volume is steady, but every client compares price per crossing.
The margin isn't in the basic entry.
It is in everything around it: classification reviews,
USMCA certificates, duty drawback, compliance audits.
And in 2026, refunds.
The last two years tested every broker on
both sides of the border, in three ways.
The first is tariff whiplash.
In 2025, new tariffs arrived by executive order,
under an emergency law called IEEPA.
Each one meant new codes on the entry, new exemptions and new deadlines.
Customs duties in fiscal 2025 hit $195 billion.
On February 20, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled
6 to 3 that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs.
Four days later, a temporary 10% surcharge under a different law,
Section 122, took its place, with USMCA goods exempt.
It expired on July 24.
The same day, new Section 301 tariffs started on imports from 60 economies.
Mexico was assigned 10%, again with USMCA- qualifying goods excluded.
For a broker, every one of those changes is the same question, asked again.
Do these goods qualify, and can you prove it?
The second test is refunds.
CBP built a system called CAPE to return the IEEPA tariffs.
Only the importer, or the licensed broker who
filed the original entries, can submit a claim.
Each claim is a file of up to 9,999 entry numbers.
By mid-September, claims covered more than 27 million entries.
By early October, CAPE had accepted about $136.6
billion in potential and certified refunds.
Think about what that means.
The broker who filed your entries in 2025 is the one holding
the records you need to get your money back in 2026.
The third test is on the Mexican side, and it is personal.
On January 1, 2026, a reform of Mexico's Customs Law took effect.
Patentes are no longer for life.
They now last 20 years, renewable.
Agents must recertify every three years.
They have to verify their clients' identity, tax status and facilities.
Agents who are partners in a customs agency are jointly
liable for the taxes on the operations they handle.
And customs fines in some cases can reach 300% of the commercial value.
Read that from the agent's side.
For a fee of a few thousand pesos, you can end up
answering for the taxes on a shipment worth millions.
At the same time, Mexico raised its own tariffs,
by 5 to 50 percentage points, on 1,463 tariff lines from countries
without a trade agreement, starting January 1, 2026.
More classification work, and more risk in every code.
Put the three together and you get a profession whose workload went up,
whose liability went up, and whose licensed workforce can't grow overnight.
So who makes money in this business now?
Not the cheapest broker.
Cheap brokerage is easy to sell and expensive to buy.
The winners share five things.
Clean data.
They get part lists, codes and origin records
from the factory before the truck is loaded.
USMCA expertise.
Proving origin is now the difference between zero and 10%, or more.
Both sides of the bridge.
They run a Mexican agency and a US brokerage together, or partner closely,
so one file follows the trailer from Nuevo Laredo to Laredo.
Technology.
Entries built in minutes instead of hours,
because the fee is fixed and the labor is not.
And a license held by someone who knows when to say no.
With joint liability, the most valuable thing a broker
can do is refuse a client whose paperwork doesn't add up.
That is why the big forwarders are hiring,
and why a good licensed broker is so hard to replace.
Remember the trailer at the bridge.
A driver, a seal, a pedimento in Nuevo Laredo, an entry in Laredo.
Two licenses, two systems, and two people who never
touch the cargo but answer for every number on it.

The broker's responsibility is all of it.

At Expeditors, one of the largest freight forwarders in the US, customs brokerage and other services brought in $4.27 billion in 2025, up about 13%, and 39% of total revenue. In the fourth quarter, the company said demand for customs brokerage remained strong, and that it was adding people particularly in customs brokerage. For a small broker in Laredo, the math is different. The clients are factories, carriers and forwarders who cross every day. Volume is steady, but every client compares price per crossing. The margin isn't in the basic entry. It is in everything around it: classification reviews, USMCA certificates, duty drawback, compliance audits. And in 2026, refunds. The last two years tested every broker on both sides of the border, in three ways. The first is tariff whiplash. In 2025, new tariffs arrived by executive order, under an emergency law called IEEPA. Each one meant new codes on the entry, new exemptions and new deadlines. Customs duties in fiscal 2025 hit $195 billion. On February 20, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs. Four days later, a temporary 10% surcharge under a different law, Section 122, took its place, with USMCA goods exempt. It expired on July 24. The same day, new Section 301 tariffs started on imports from 60 economies. Mexico was assigned 10%, again with USMCA- qualifying goods excluded. For a broker, every one of those changes is the same question, asked again. Do these goods qualify, and can you prove it? The second test is refunds. CBP built a system called CAPE to return the IEEPA tariffs. Only the importer, or the licensed broker who filed the original entries, can submit a claim. Each claim is a file of up to 9,999 entry numbers. By mid-September, claims covered more than 27 million entries. By early October, CAPE had accepted about $136.6 billion in potential and certified refunds. Think about what that means. The broker who filed your entries in 2025 is the one holding the records you need to get your money back in 2026. The third test is on the Mexican side, and it is personal. On January 1, 2026, a reform of Mexico's Customs Law took effect. Patentes are no longer for life. They now last 20 years, renewable. Agents must recertify every three years. They have to verify their clients' identity, tax status and facilities. Agents who are partners in a customs agency are jointly liable for the taxes on the operations they handle. And customs fines in some cases can reach 300% of the commercial value. Read that from the agent's side. For a fee of a few thousand pesos, you can end up answering for the taxes on a shipment worth millions. At the same time, Mexico raised its own tariffs, by 5 to 50 percentage points, on 1,463 tariff lines from countries without a trade agreement, starting January 1, 2026. More classification work, and more risk in every code. Put the three together and you get a profession whose workload went up, whose liability went up, and whose licensed workforce can't grow overnight. So who makes money in this business now? Not the cheapest broker. Cheap brokerage is easy to sell and expensive to buy. The winners share five things. Clean data. They get part lists, codes and origin records from the factory before the truck is loaded. USMCA expertise. Proving origin is now the difference between zero and 10%, or more. Both sides of the bridge. They run a Mexican agency and a US brokerage together, or partner closely, so one file follows the trailer from Nuevo Laredo to Laredo. Technology. Entries built in minutes instead of hours, because the fee is fixed and the labor is not. And a license held by someone who knows when to say no. With joint liability, the most valuable thing a broker can do is refuse a client whose paperwork doesn't add up. That is why the big forwarders are hiring, and why a good licensed broker is so hard to replace. Remember the trailer at the bridge. A driver, a seal, a pedimento in Nuevo Laredo, an entry in Laredo. Two licenses, two systems, and two people who never touch the cargo but answer for every number on it. The broker's fee is under 1% of the shipment. The broker's responsibility is all of it. If you work in customs, on either side of the border, tell me what I got wrong, or what I missed, in the comments. And subscribe, because next time we go to the ground those factories stand on. Who builds the industrial parks of nearshoring, who rents them, and what a square foot of factory floor really earns. The economics of an industrial park.

metadata.title: Customs Broker Modernization Regulations
metadata.author: CH Powell Company
metadata.shortDescription:
Customs Broker Modernization Regulations 19 CFR 111, effective as of December 19, 2022, introduced several notable changes to the customs brokerage industry, including the elimination of broker districts and district permits and additional responsible supervision and control requirements. Geoff Powell, CH Powell Company President, discusses the key modernizations and their implications for brokers and importers.

#CustomsBrokerage #CBP #Modernization #ExpertsAtYourSide

metadata.title: Duty Drawback Part 1 (Oct. 2017 CBLE Class)
metadata.author: Law Office of Yuri Starikov, LLC
metadata.shortDescription:
Thank you for watching this video segment from Customs Broker License Exam (“CBLE”) Preparation Class preparing examinees to pass October 2017 CBLE.  Focus of this class is on Duty Drawback and its regulatory adaptation to Trade Facilitation and Trade Enforcement Act of 2015 (“TFTEA”).

Drawback is the refund (usually 99%) of the duties, taxes, and fees paid on imported merchandise.  19 C.F.R. § 190.2.  Questions related to drawback are regularly tested on CBLE.

Pursuant to TFTEA, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (“CBP”) promulgated a whole new part under Code of Federal Regulations (“CFR”).  As such, Title 19 has two Parts related to Duty Drawback: original Drawback under Part 191, and Modernized Drawback under Part 190.

The discussion is a part of lecture series designed to prepare for the upcoming April 2021 Customs Broker License Examination. Please visit https://www.lawcustoms.com/live/ for details about CBLE preparation classes.

We also invite you take a look at our recent publication- the 6th Edition of U.S. Customs Broker License Examination Preparation Guide Textbook – which is comprised of two volumes. Please visit https://www.lawcustoms.com/tb/ for details about CBLE preparation textbooks.

metadata.title: ITM How to receive drawback on destroyed merchandise
metadata.author: International Tariff Management
metadata.shortDescription:
Today, we're going to discuss destruction, drawback opportunities for all our importers and exporters out there. Destruction Drawback is the eligibility to claim drawback on items that are destroyed in the United States that have once been imported and duty paid. So for the purposes of drawback, a lot of claimants are aware that you can import a product into the country, pay a duty on it and export it.


But you can also import product into the United States, destroy it in the United States so completely that it has no commercial value. And also claim drawback on those products that are destroyed. There are various reasons that a company would destroy their goods. The number one reason would be that they're defective, that they were imported and they didn't meet specifications. Also, maybe goods had been ruined in some way in the warehouse also for food items that have expired. One may want to destroy them in the United States and take advantage of duty. Drawback or items could be outdated and no longer salable because they're out of fashion or outdated.

metadata.title: Paid an ATM Fee? Visa and Mastercard Will Pay
metadata.author: Receipts
metadata.shortDescription:
The Visa and Mastercard ATM fee settlement (Burke v. Visa) puts $167.5 million toward people who paid a surcharge at a non-bank ATM in the U.S. from Oct. 24, 2007 to Aug. 14, 2026. Claims close Feb. 10, 2027.

Watch next: The Apple iPhone Settlement Has a Catch https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pz15ff94ANc&list=PLPOsKTMuqSXA

0:00 The $3 ATM fee
0:46 Who owns gas station ATMs
1:31 The rule Visa and Mastercard set
2:14 The ATM fee lawsuits
2:50 Round one in court
3:13 Visa v. Osborn at the Supreme Court
4:06 Class actions and bank payouts
4:50 The $197.5M and $167.5M deals
5:31 Who qualifies
6:20 The claim form catch
7:14 The final scoreboard
7:37 How much you'll get

Who's in (per the settlement notice): you used a Visa or Mastercard card to withdraw cash from your own account at a U.S. ATM not owned by a bank or credit union, between Oct. 24, 2007 and Aug. 14, 2026, and paid a surcharge your bank didn't fully reimburse. Opt-out/objection deadline: Dec. 11, 2026. Claim deadline: Feb. 10, 2027 (online or postmarked by mail). Final approval hearing: Feb. 17, 2027. Claim through the official settlement website, nonbankatmsurchargesettlement.com. The per-person amount is not known; it depends on approved fees and costs and on how many valid claims are filed.

Visa and Mastercard deny any wrongdoing, and neither settlement is an admission. The 52 million figure is our own math ($167.5 million / the 2025 average surcharge of $3.22). The $365 million is our sum of the two Visa and Mastercard settlements ($197.5M Mackmin + $167.5M Burke). Not legal advice.

Sources: Burke v. Visa, No. 1:11-cv-01882 (D.D.C.) settlement notice and agreement; National ATM Council v. Visa and Mackmin v. Visa (D.D.C., filed 2011); Osborn v. Visa, 797 F.3d 1057 (D.C. Cir. 2015); Visa Inc. v. Osborn, No. 15-961 (U.S. Supreme Court, dismissed Nov. 17, 2016; SCOTUSblog); Supreme Court order denying review, Apr. 15, 2024; Hagens Berman case page (Mackmin $197.5M, final approval June 20, 2025; ~$67M paid June 2023 from bank settlements); Bankrate 2025 Checking Account and ATM Fee Study (Sept. 10, 2025); Kiplinger, CNBC, Bloomberg Law and ClassAction.org coverage of the Burke settlement.

Video clips and photos are stand-ins, not the people, places or companies involved: Pexels. Thumbnail art is an illustration.

segments.text: hi my name is Chris Roberts I'm a class
action attorney I've been a class action
attorney for over 10 years and today I'm
going to talk about one of the most
common questions I receive and is that
is should I actually submit a claim to
be part of this class action settlement
the answer to that question usually is
yes and here's why typically speaking um
in a what we call a claims made
settlement which most class action
settlements tend to be nowadays you have
to submit a claim to receive any type of
payment if you don't submit a claim and
you don't exclude or opt out from the
class you're still a part of the class
action but you receive no payment and
you give up certain rights to Sue that
company for maybe the same misconduct
that was an issue in the case so in
other words if you don't submit a claim
you get nothing out of it and you have
to ask yourself this question do you
plan to file a suit on your own is it
financially worth it or does the issue
at hand mean enough to you to file suit
if the answer to that question is no
then typically the answer to whether or
not you sub submit a claim is yes
because otherwise you're not going to
receive any money anyway and it's
essentially like found money a lot of
people complain about uh submitting
claims because they think that the
payment might be small um or it's not

usually doesn't take very long to submit
a claim and you might as well get
something out of it in the process
so in short it usually makes sense for

of that class you should never submit a
fake claim just to get money or anything
like that but each case is different so
what you should do is look at the
settlement website um see if you want to
pursue a claim on your own and if you
don't and you have no issues with the
settlement then typically you should
submit a claim thanks so much for
watching
