segments.text: To bring in your customs entries, go to Settings, at the bottom of the sidebar.
Open the Purchasing group, which lists every purchasing setting, then choose Duty Rates.
Then open the Customs entries tab, next to Rates and Jurisdictions.
Your broker files an entry summary for every shipment you import, with the duty charged on each line.
Each row here is one entry, with its date, supplier, purchase orders, value, and duty.
The blue banner totals the IEEPA duty you paid, which may be refundable.
Export worksheet downloads those lines for a refund claim.
First, add the importer numbers your company files under.
Click the menu beside Import entries, then click Importer numbers.
Type a number, and press Enter after each entry in the box.
Then click Save, and the dialog closes with your numbers kept.
An entry filed for another company is then flagged, and is never applied.
To bring an entry in, click the Import entries button.
Choose 7501 PDF for one entry from your broker, or ACE ES-003 report for many at once.
Drop the file here, or click to browse your computer.
The dialog shows the file, and what it detected.
Click Import, at the bottom right of the dialog, to start the import.
The import then runs in the background, and you can follow it in the job tray.
Reading a 7501 takes a few seconds, and you can keep working meanwhile.
When the import finishes, the entry appears in the list, waiting for review.
Its flags show anything worth checking.
Click the entry number to see the details.
The Totals card shows the entered value, the duty, and each fee.
The Checks card compares the entry with your purchase order.
Here the customs value is lower than the order value, so check that with your broker.
Below, each line shows its HTS code, entered value, and the duty charged.
The stack lists every tariff that applied, such as a Section 301 duty on top of the base rate.
Matched SKUs shows the purchase order lines that each entry line covers.
Expand a line to see how each product was matched, and with what confidence.
Under Proposals are the changes this entry supports, and the confident ones are ticked.
Product codes sets each product's HTS code and country of origin.
A product filed under a different code than it carries stays unticked, so you can check it first.
Duty rates adds a dated rate for each tariff on the entry, with the broker entry as its source.
Shipment fills in customs details on the inbound shipment.
Untick anything you don't want to change, then click Apply selected at the bottom.
Nothing changes until you do, and applying takes a few seconds.
The entry is now marked Applied, and its duty rates and product codes are in place.
Your purchase orders now estimate duty with these rates and codes.
Next, link the broker's bill that charged this duty.
Click Link duty bill, at the top of the entry.
Then type part of its invoice number into the search box.
Pick the bill from the list that appears.
Click Link bill to save the link, and the bill joins the entry's links at the top.
Next, open the bill from the entry's links, near the top of the entry page.
It opens on its details, its lines, and how its cost is split today.
Click Edit, at the top right of the bill, to change how it splits.
Then click the Proration Method field, near the top of the form.
Choose By cost category, so each line splits by its own category.
The duty line now shows By customs entry, because a fully matched entry is linked.
Freight and brokerage keep splitting by cost.
Under the lines, the Customs entry card shows the duty split by this entry.
Click Save, at the top right of the bill.
The bill works out each product's share again, which takes a few seconds.
How this bill is split now lists the duty line under By customs entry.

metadata.title: ACE Question/Answer Forum: Session One Introduction
metadata.author: Scarbrough Global
metadata.shortDescription:
This recorded webinar will answer the following questions and give an overview of CBP's new ACE system. Some questions that will be answered include:
- As an importer / exporter, I would like to know exactly what is needed from my company to make transition smooth.  Usually the broker / forwarding agent handles the AES, 3461 & 7501 forms so why would my company need a portal?
- I worked for another company when I set up my first application. Should I use my birthday and this year or just use the date I submitted on the application
- How can importers obtain 7501 & 3461 if paper copies are no longer available.
- Do you happen to know how many PGA's are actively participating in the ACE Certification process?
- Do we need an AES account to ship via Fed Ex or UPS to Canada or Mexico?
- Have you heard anything about the ACE Export Reports "missing" data?  
- Is there a test system where users can practice filing export commodity data?
- Our company imports and exports.  Do we need to complete both application forms (for non-exporter and for exporter)?
- I hear ACE is a hassle and you are constantly having to call CBP to reset your password.  Thoughts?
- Am I absolutely required to apply for an ACE portal?
- Can Scarbrough help us to fill out the ACE application?  
- Will ACE be taking the place of ABI and what are the system requirements for ACE?
- If a company is not a licensed broker, can you hire them to fill out export documents (including AES) on your behalf?
- Who should I contact if I have further questions in the future?
Scarbrough info@scarbrough-intl.com or CBP ACE.Support@CBP.DHS.GOV
- Can a company have more than one ACE Portal account?
- How long will it take for CBP to complete my ACE application?

metadata.title: U.S. Customs (CBP) Entry Summary: General Overview Webcast Preview
metadata.author: Law Office of Yuri Starikov, LLC
metadata.shortDescription:
This webcast gives introduction to the CBP Form 7501, also known as, Entry Summary.  The form is utilized by Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to collect duties and admit merchandise.  In addition to exploring details of the form, the webcast gives preparatory suggestions and analysis of questions from previous U.S. Customs Broker License Examinations.  Supplemental regulatory information, charts, tables and relevant practice quiz questions are also included.

Webcast Runtime: 2 hrs. 50 min.

The webcast comes in the form of on demand HD streaming video presentation. Online internet video podcast is coupled with follow along written material available for download as .pdf file.

Please visit LAWCUSTOMS.COM/STORE

- The problem with manual inbond entry creation
- Extracting data from source documents (BOL, invoice, manifest)

- Auto-populating the NetCHB inbond entry screen

Docxster is a no-code intelligent document processing platform built for customs brokerage, logistics, and freight workflows — with native cross-document validation so entries don't get transmitted with mismatched data.

metadata.title: Essentials of Customs Entry Auditing
metadata.author: Shapiro
metadata.shortDescription:
Description
Jane Taeger, Director of Compliance at Shapiro, a Customhouse broker and freight forwarder, presenting The Essentials of Customs Entry Auditing webinar for the International Compliance Professionals Association (ICPA).

Under Section 484 of the Tariff Act, as amended (19 U.S.C. 1484), the importer of record is legally responsible for using reasonable care to enter, classify and determine the value of imported merchandise and to provide any other information necessary to enable U.S. Customs and Border Protection to properly assess duties, collect accurate statistics, and determine whether other applicable legal requirements, if any, have been met. Included in the reasonable care responsibility is the need to audit your Customs entries. This webinar will educate attendees on entry auditing basics and best practices for setting up an audit program.   Taeger will also walk you through corrective actions and recordkeeping procedures to reduce the likelihood of penalties. 


Who Should Watch?
All importers responsible for regulatory Customs compliance should attend this session, as well as logistics and supply chain executives and personnel.

What You Will Learn:
Why is auditing important?
Reasonable care
Internal controls
How to set up an audit program
What to audit
Recordkeeping

metadata.title: CBP ACH Refund Deadline 2026: Importers Must Enroll by February 6 or Lose Tariff Refunds
metadata.author: Ask The Customs Manager
metadata.shortDescription:
CBP ACH refund deadline 2026 explained for importers. Learn why February 6, 2026 is critical, how to enroll in ACH, and how potential tariff refunds could impact your business. Discover expert customs compliance insights, training, and consultancy to protect your trade operations.

CBP ACH refund deadline 2026 explained — importers must enroll by February 6 or risk losing tariff refunds.
If you import goods into the United States, this regulatory change could directly impact your cash flow, compliance strategy, and ability to recover customs duties.

Starting February 6, 2026, US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) will issue refunds only through ACH (Automated Clearing House) electronic transfers. Paper checks will no longer be sent except in rare waiver cases. This affects all types of customs refunds, including duty overpayments, liquidation adjustments, penalties, and potential tariff reimbursements.

Why this matters now: the Supreme Court is reviewing tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). If those tariffs are ruled invalid, billions in refunds could be issued to importers. Companies that are not enrolled in ACH by the deadline may miss out on these refunds entirely.

In this video, you’ll learn:

What the CBP ACH refund rule means for importers

Why February 6, 2026 is a critical deadline

How to enroll in ACH via the ACE portal

The link between tariffs, Supreme Court decisions, and refunds

Practical compliance steps to protect your business

I never use Import Genius. metadata.title: The $166 Billion Tariff Refund: Who Actually Gets It, Checked
metadata.author: PolitiClash
metadata.shortDescription:
$166 billion in tariff refunds is on the move in America right now — the biggest refund operation Customs has ever run. The checks are real. They are just not addressed to you: the money follows the name on the customs entry, and only about 330,000 importers of record are in the system. This video checks the refund machine against the record — how much was collected, who can claim it, how much has actually been certified — and grades seven claims about your refund check. It is the sequel to the ruling video: the Supreme Court struck down the emergency tariffs in February and said nothing about refunds, so a trade court, Customs, and a claims portal called CAPE decided where the money goes.

THE VERDICTS
• "Everyone who paid higher prices because of the tariffs gets a refund check" — FALSE
• "The refunds are automatic — file nothing, and the money just comes" — FALSE
• "The Supreme Court ordered the government to pay these refunds" — MISLEADING
• "About $166 billion was collected, and about $126 billion has already been certified for payment" — MOSTLY TRUE
• "All the Trump tariffs are being refunded, including the China tariffs" — FALSE
• "Importers have to pass the refund on to the customers who paid the higher prices" — FALSE
• "A $2,000 tariff dividend check is coming to most Americans" — FALSE

THE CALL
PolitiClash predicts the bulk of the $166 billion reaches importers during 2027; the appeal narrows the fight to the hardest entries rather than stopping the money; and the household dividend stays a promise unless a bill actually moves. Confidence: high on the importer money, low on the household check. Both predictions get scored in public when the numbers land.

CHAPTERS
0:00 The $166 Billion Question
1:05 The Pool: $166 Billion, 53 Million Entries
1:41 The Name That Gets Paid: Importer of Record
2:17 The CAPE Claims System: No Filing, No Refund
3:01 Three Phases and the Scoreboard
3:52 The Court Fight: The Universal Order and the Class
4:46 Who Actually Paid: The Pass-Through Gap
5:32 The Other Check: The $2,000 Dividend Promise
6:38 The Fact-Check Desk: Seven Claims Graded
9:51 What Happens Next: The Call
10:42 Next on PolitiClash: The Subpoenas They Promised

SOURCES
U.S. Customs and Border Protection — "IEEPA Duty Refunds" page (cbp.gov): the CAPE system, importer-of-record-only filing, the CAPE Declaration, refunds generally within 60–90 days of acceptance, with interest
CBP declarations filed at the U.S. Court of International Trade (Brandon Lord declarations, Atmus Filtration and Freestyle World cases): about $166 billion collected on about 53 million entries by about 330,000 importers; as of October 2, 2026, about $136.6 billion accepted into CAPE and about $126 billion, interest included, certified and sent to the Treasury for payment; the finally liquidated (Phase 3) pool about $11.4 billion
Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, decided February 20, 2026 (6–3): IEEPA does not authorize the President to impose tariffs; the opinion orders no refunds
U.S. Court of International Trade — universal refund direction, March 4, 2026 (Judge Eaton), appealed by the Justice Department, appeal pending; Freestyle World, Inc. v. CBP, Slip Op. 26-123 (October 8, 2026): nationwide class certified for importers of record who paid the duties February 1, 2025 – February 19, 2026 and did not sue on their own; no classwide payout order yet
The $2,000 dividend: the President's November 9, 2025 post; NEC Director Kevin Hassett, Face the Nation, December 21, 2025; three congressional rebate bills, all in committee, none for the full $2,000; IRS statements debunking claims that $2,000 tariff refund deposits were landing (2026)

PHOTOS AND FOOTAGE
PortMiami and Port of Tacoma aerials; U.S. Capitol; U.S. Treasury Building; Supreme Court building; White House north front (channel asset base for this video, files/assets/video29/stills).

Narration is AI-generated (Solemn Pillar voice) from a human-checked script; every claim was graded against the sources above.

One question before you go. The importer gets the refund — but the shopper paid the higher price. Should the law make importers pass the refund through to the customers who absorbed it — or does the money belong to the name that took the risk? Tell me in the comments. If this check helped, like and subscribe — the receipts keep coming.

#Tariffs #Trade #PolitiClash

What follows is the record: how much was collected, who can claim it, how much has
actually moved — and seven claims about your refund check, graded.
PolitiClash — no side taken.
Start with the size of the pot.
Customs and Border Protection told the trade court, in its own filings, what the
emergency tariffs took in: about $166 billion in duties, paid across roughly 53
million separate import entries, by about 330,000 importers.
Picture it: every container, every pallet, every shipment that crossed an American
dock or border crossing in that year generated paperwork.
And on that paperwork sits one name that matters more than any other name in this
entire story.
That name is the importer of record.
When goods enter the United States, one company is legally on the hook for the
shipment.
It files the entry, it stands behind the paperwork, and it pays the duty.
Sometimes that is a giant retailer importing for its own shelves.
Sometimes it is a small business with one container a year.
Either way, the duty was paid in that name — or by its customs broker, acting for it.
And customs law pays the refund to the name on the entry.
Not to the store that stocked the shelf.
Not to the shopper who paid the higher price at the register.
The name on the entry.
And nobody's refund simply arrives.
Customs built a claims system inside its trade portal.
The name is a mouthful — the Consolidated Administration and Processing of Entries,
mercifully shortened to CAPE.
Customs' own refund page is blunt about how it works: only the importer of record,
or the broker it authorized, may file a claim — a declaration listing every entry
being claimed.
No declaration, no refund.
Once a claim is accepted, Customs says refunds generally go out within 60 to 90
days, with interest.
It is a filing window, not a mailbox.
The system opened in phases.
Phase one, last April, took the simplest entries — about 63 percent of them.
Phase two followed in June.
Phase three opened October 6th, for the hardest cases: entries already finally
settled, where a court has to order the books reopened.
About $11.4 billion sits in that phase alone.
And here is the scoreboard, from Customs' filings as of October 2nd: of the $166
billion collected, about $136.6 billion has been accepted into the claims pipeline
— and about $126 billion, interest included, has been certified and sent to
the Treasury for payment.
Now do the subtraction the posts never do: roughly $29 billion of that pool had not
even entered the pipeline yet.
Why phases and courts at all?
Because the Supreme Court's ruling said nothing about refunds, a second court
built the machine.
On March 4th, the Court of International Trade ordered Customs to refund the
struck-down duties — for everyone, not just the companies that sued.
The Justice Department has appealed that universal order, and the appeal is still
pending.
In October, the trade court also certified a nationwide class of importers — the case
is called Freestyle World — covering importers who paid the duties between
February 1st, 2025, and February 19th, 2026, and did not sue on their own.
No final classwide payout order has landed.
Translation: the money is moving, but the biggest legal fight over who must be paid
is still in front of judges.
Now the part that stings.
Who actually felt those tariffs?
The importer wrote the check to Customs — but a year of higher shelf prices says
much of the cost rolled downhill, to stores, and then to shoppers.
The refund, however, does not roll back uphill.
It stops at the name on the entry.
Nothing in the court's orders, and nothing on Customs' refund page, requires an
importer to hand any of it back to the customers who absorbed the higher prices.
A company may choose to — some may, for goodwill.
The law simply pays the name.
If you paid more for a phone, a couch, or a pair of shoes this year, that
overpayment is not a claim.
It never becomes one.
So where did 'a check is coming to you' come from?
Partly from a promise.
In November of last year, President Trump posted that tariff revenue would pay, in
his words, a dividend of at least $2,000 a person — most Americans included, high
earners excluded.
His case, in its strongest form: the tariffs took in enormous money, and
sending some of it back to households is only fair.
His economic adviser later said a proposal would go to Congress.
Here is the record since: no administration bill was ever formally
sent.
Three rebate bills from members of Congress — none of them for the full
$2,000 — sit in committee.
None has passed either chamber.
And this summer, the IRS publicly debunked viral claims that $2,000 tariff refund
deposits were already landing.
A proposal is not a program.
There is no application, no schedule, and no check.
Time for the Fact-Check Desk.
Seven claims about the tariff refund checks, checked against the court's
orders, Customs' own filings, and Customs' own refund page.
Claim one: everyone who paid higher prices because of the tariffs gets a refund
check.
False.
The refund follows the customs entry, not the price tag.
The only names in the system are about 330,000 importers of record — the
companies that filed the entries and paid the duties.
Claim two: the refunds are automatic — file nothing, and the money just comes.
False.
Customs' own page: only the importer of record, or its authorized broker, can file
a claim — a declaration inside the CAPE system, listing the entries.
No filing, no refund.
And even after a claim is accepted, Customs says payment generally takes 60 to
90 days.
Claim three: the Supreme Court ordered the government to pay these refunds.
Misleading.
Read the ruling — it is the video linked at the end of this one.
The justices struck down the tariffs and said nothing about refunds at all.
The refund orders came from the Court of International Trade, starting March 4th —
and the government is appealing the biggest one.
Claim four: about $166 billion was collected, and about $126 billion has
already been certified for payment.
Mostly true.
Both numbers come from Customs' own court filings — $126 billion, interest included,
certified and sent to the Treasury as of October 2nd.
Two honest caveats: certified for payment is not the same as received.
And roughly $29 billion of the pool was not yet even in the pipeline.
Claim five: all of the Trump tariffs are being refunded, including the China
tariffs.
False.
This process covers only the struck-down emergency tariffs — the ones collected
under the emergency law.
The separate national-security and China tariffs, imposed under different laws,
were never struck down.
They remain in force, and they are not in this refund system at all.
Claim six: importers have to pass the refund on to the customers who paid the
higher prices.
False.
The refund belongs to the importer of record — full stop.
No court order, and no Customs rule, requires a cent of it to be passed
through.
Whether any of it reaches shoppers is each company's choice, not its obligation.
Claim seven: a $2,000 tariff dividend check is coming to most Americans.
False — as a program, it does not exist.
It began as a presidential post in November 2025.
A year later, there is no law, no passed bill, no application, and no payment
schedule — and the tax agency has debunked claims that deposits are landing.
If Congress ever passes a rebate, that will be a new story, and I will check it
the same way.
So what happens next?
Here is the call.
The importer refunds keep flowing: the pipeline is built, $126 billion is already
certified, and the trade court's machinery grinds on even while the appeal runs.
PolitiClash predicts the bulk of the $166 billion reaches importers during 2027; the
appeal narrows the fight to the hardest entries rather than stopping the money;
and the household dividend stays a promise unless a bill actually moves — watch the
committees, not the posts.
The honest confidence: high on the importer money, because it is already
moving; low on the household check, because a year of record says proposals
are not payments.
Both predictions get scored in public when the numbers land.
Next on PolitiClash: the subpoenas they promised.
The incoming chairs said it on the record — investigations, testimony, and one very
reluctant witness whose name keeps coming up.
Next time, I check what a subpoena can actually force — and what happens when the
man in the middle says no.
One question before you go.
The importer gets the refund — but the shopper paid the higher price.
Should the law make importers pass the refund through to the customers who
absorbed it — or does the money belong to the name that took the risk?
Tell me in the comments.
If this check helped, like and subscribe — the receipts keep coming.

metadata.title: CBP Refund Portal is LIVE - Claim Your 2025 Tariff Money Now!
metadata.author: NextGen CPA
metadata.shortDescription:
The CBP refund portal is LIVE as of April 20, 2026. At the same time, a major court ruling on May 8th just declared the new Section 122 tariffs unlawful. Here is how to claim your 2025 cash and protect your 2026 imports.

👉 In this follow-up video, we break down two massive shifts in the trade landscape. First, we cover the launch of the CBP CAPE platform as of April 20, 2026. This is the official system for claiming your 2025 IEEPA refunds. We explain the "Phase 1" eligibility rules, specifically why your liquidation date must be after January 30, 2026, and why an ACH-enabled ACE account is mandatory for payment.
Second, we analyze the May 8, 2026, Court of International Trade (CIT) ruling that declared the new Section 122 surcharges unlawful (ultra vires). While the injunction currently only protects the plaintiffs, we discuss the critical CPA-led strategy of filing Post-Summary Corrections now to preserve your right to future refunds. Finally, we look at the upcoming July 24 deadline and the administration’s expected pivot to Section 301 investigations, helping you project your 2026 cash flow through the next wave of trade policy.

🔗 Resources & Links
• Official CBP CAPE Refund Portal: [https://cbp.gov/trade/programs-administration/trade-remedies/ieepa-duty-refunds]
• Step-by-Step CAPE Filing Guide (PDF): [https://www.cbp.gov/sites/default/files/2026-04/trade_information_notice_cape_508c.pdf] 

📥 Timestamps 
0:00 - Breaking Tariff News: Refunds & New Rulings 
0:38 - CBP CAPE Portal: How to Claim 2025 Refunds 
0:50 - Phase 1 Eligibility: The Jan 30th Liquidation Rule 
1:23 - ACE Portal Setup: ACH is Required 
1:35 - Section 122 Struck Down: The May 8th CIT Ruling 
2:22 - Legal Strategy: Filing Protests to Protect Your Cash 
2:39 - July 24 Deadline & The Section 301 Pivot 
3:13 - Summary Checklist

📌 Subscribe and turn on the bell 🔔to build profitably, stay compliant, and make confident financial decisions. 

#TariffRefund #tariffupdate  #SmallBusiness #CBP #Section122 #Section301 #TradeWar #SCOTUS #NextGenCPA

segments.text: Two big updates since my last video on
the Supreme Court's tariff ruling.
First, the refund window for your 2025
e-pa payments is officially open as of
April 20th.
But second, and more urgently, the
replacement tariffs we've been paying
since February were just struck down in
court a few days ago.
Today, we are doing a deep dive into the
new Cape platform you need to use to get
your money back. And why a recent ruling
from the Court of International Trade
means the current 10% surcharge is on
life support.
If you're a small business owner or an
importer, the next 90 days are critical
for your cash flow.
Let's start with the money you've
already paid. On April 20th, 2026, US
Customs and Border Protection or CBP
launched the Cape platform. Now, this is
the only way to claim your e-pa refunds.
Here is what you need to know about
phase one.
First, the window. It currently only
covers unliquidated entries or those
liquidated within the last 80 days.
Essentially, if your goods entered
starting around January 30th, 2026,
you are in the front of the line.
Second, the no mistakes rule. You file a
Cape declaration in the ACE portal.
But be warned, once you submit, you
cannot amend it.
If you miss a 7501 form, you have to
start a new declaration, which can push
you to the back of the queue.
Lastly, timeline. CBP is saying 60 to 90
days for the cash to hit your account,
but you must have an ACH account set up
in ACE. No paper checks are being issued
for these.
While you're filing for those old
refunds, the new 10% surcharge just hit
a massive legal wall.
On May 8th, 2026, the Court of
International Trade ruled that the
Section 122 tariffs, the ones the
administration pivoted to in February,
are unlawful. Why did they lose?
The court said Section 122 can only be
used for large and serious balance of
payments deficits.
The government tried to use trade
deficits as a reason, but the court said
that's not what the law meant back in
The catch for small businesses.
The court did not issue a nationwide
injunction.
Right now, the relief only applies to
the specific plaintiffs in the case,
which includes the state of Washington
and a few private importers.
The strategy?
Unless you are a plaintiff, you still
have to pay the 10% for now.
However, you should be filing post
summary corrections or formal protests
on every entry.
If this ruling goes nationwide later
this summer, you need that paper trail
to claim your second round of refunds.
What happens in July?
Even if Section 122 is struck down, it
was already set to expire on July 24th,
2026 with the 150-day limit.
The administration is already moving to
Section 301 investigations.
They are currently holding hearings to
replace these expiring tariffs with a
more permanent wave three in August.
The CPA tip?
For your 2026 budget, keep that 10 to
15% duty buffer in your models.
The legal justification is changing, but
the cost to your business likely isn't
going away.
To wrap up, here is your checklist.
First, audit your ACE portal. Make sure
your ACH info is current so CAPE can pay
you. Second, file your phase one
declaration for those late January /
early February entries.
Third, talk to your broker about filing
protests on your current Section 122
entries to preserve your rights after
the May 8th ruling.
I've put links to the CBP CAPE guide and
the court ruling in the description
below. If you found this helpful, hit
subscribe. I'll be tracking the Section
301 hearings as we head into July.

metadata.title: Who Gets the $166 Billion Tariff Refund? (Not You)
metadata.author: Who Pays For It
metadata.shortDescription:
The Supreme Court struck down the emergency tariffs, and the government started paying back about $166 billion. But the refund goes to whoever's name was on the import paperwork, not to the people who paid higher prices at the register. So who actually paid for these tariffs, and who's getting the money back?

In this video:
• Why Customs bills the "importer of record," not the factory or the shopper
• What the Supreme Court decided, and what it left open
• What the New York Fed study measured (and what it didn't)
• Why the same refund can be fair for one company and a windfall for another
• The fight still going on: the class action and the appeal

Chapters
0:00 The invoice
0:53 Who writes the check
2:00 The ruling
3:47 Who actually paid?
5:37 Whose name is on the check
8:03 The fight that's still open
9:36 So, who pays?

• CBP, IEEPA FAQ: https://www.cbp.gov/trade/programs-administration/trade-remedies/IEEPA-FAQ
• Supreme Court of the United States, Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump (Feb. 20, 2026): https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/slipopinion/25

• Federal Reserve Bank of New York, "How Fast Do Tariffs Pass Through into Consumer Prices?" (Oct. 6, 2026): https://libertystreeteconomics.newyorkfed.org/2026/10/how-fast-do-tariffs-pass-through-into-consumer-prices/

metadata.title: Who Actually Gets The $126 Billion Tariff Refund?
metadata.author: Casually Capital
metadata.shortDescription:
The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs on February 20, 2026, and billions in refunds are now going out. But there's a catch: the refund goes to the importer of record, the business named on the customs paperwork, not to the shoppers who may have paid higher prices.
In this video: what the court decided, how Customs' CAPE refund portal works, how much has been certified so far, why a secondary market for refund claims appeared, and what the New York Fed found about who bore the cost of the 2025 tariffs.

KEY FACTS (dates shown, figures change)
• Feb 20, 2026: Supreme Court rules 6-3 that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs
• Mar 4, 2026: the Court of International Trade rules that all importers of record are entitled to the benefit of the decision
• Apr 20, 2026: CBP's CAPE portal begins accepting refund claims
• Oct 2, 2026: about $136.6B accepted for processing and about $126B (duties plus interest) certified to the Treasury for payment, out of roughly $166B in IEEPA duties collected (per CBP's court filing, as reported by law firms)
• NY Fed (Feb 2026): nearly 90% of the economic burden of the 2025 tariffs fell on U.S. firms and consumers
• Refund-claim trading: reportedly about 20 cents on the dollar before the ruling and up to about 60 cents after (Sidley, April 2026, citing press reports). These are past prices, not current ones.
• The $1,000,000 / $300,000 refund-claim example in the video is a hypothetical illustration, not a real deal.
• "Certified to the Treasury" is not the same as "paid." Check the latest CBP and Court of International Trade filings for updates.


SOURCES
• Norton Rose Fulbright: https://www.nortonrosefulbright.com/en/knowledge/publications/20f2de87/potential-refunds-us-supreme-court-overturns-ieepa-tariffs
• Stinson: https://www.stinson.com/newsroom-publications-supreme-court-invalidates-ieepa-tariffs-recent-developments-accelerate-refund-process
• Davis Wright Tremaine (CIT class certification, Oct 2026): https://www.dwt.com/insights/2026/10/cit-certifies-ieepa-duty-refund-importer-class
• Great Lakes Customs Law (CAPE status, Oct 2026): https://greatlakescustomslaw.com/ieepa-tariff-refunds/
• Supply Chain Dive (refunds paid as of July 31): https://www.supplychaindive.com/news/cbp-has-paid-100b-in-ieepa-tariff-refunds/827257/
• Sidley (refund-claim market): https://www.sidley.com/en/insights/newsupdates/2026/04/ieepa-tariff-refund-claims-key-considerations-for-lenders-borrowers-and-claims-purchasers
• Fortune (refund-claim buyers): https://fortune.com/2026/03/07/winners-supreme-court-tariff-ruling-hedge-funds-creating-100-billion-secondary-market-refunds-brandon-howard-lutnick/
• New York Fed, Liberty Street Economics: https://libertystreeteconomics.newyorkfed.org/2026/02/who-is-paying-for-the-2025-u-s-tariffs/


DISCLAIMER
This video is for educational and informational purposes only. It is not financial, investment, legal, tax or customs advice. Buying or selling refund claims is complex and risky, and importers should consult a licensed customs attorney or broker. Figures can change. Do your own research. Any action you take is at your own risk.

#TariffRefunds #IEEPA #SupremeCourt #Tariffs #TradeWar #USEconomy #Importers #Customs #HedgeFunds #FinanceNews #Economics #BusinessNews #SupplyChain #Inflation #CasuallyKapital"

metadata.author: CBC News

metadata.title: Who Actually Gets the $166B Tariff Refund?
metadata.author: Frontier Report
metadata.shortDescription:
$166 billion in tariff money has to go somewhere — and everyone is asking the same question: who actually gets paid?In this video we break down the $166B tariff refund story: where the money came from, who is legally first in line to claim it, and why most people who paid the tariffs may never see a single dollar of it.We look at:
• How the tariff refund process actually works
• Which importers, businesses and consumers have a real claim
• Why the biggest recipients are usually not the people who paid
• What this means for prices, and who ends up holding the billIf you want the news behind the headline — no noise, no spin, just the money trail — you're in the right place.👉 Subscribe to Frontier Report for daily breakdowns of the stories that move money.
💬 Tell us in the comments: do you think the refund should go to importers or straight back to consumers?Frontier Report — follow the money, not the narrative.Sources & further reading are linked in the pinned comment.#FrontierReport #TariffRefund #TrumpTariffs #166B #USPolitics #TradeWar #Tariffs #USEconomy #BreakingNews #SupremeCourt

That is how much the government
collected under tariffs the Supreme
Court said were illegal. And now it is
being paid back.
So here is the question, paid back to
whom?
If you bought a jacket, a toaster, a car
part, or a bag of coffee in the last two
years, you probably paid a little extra.
Some of that extra was tariffs. But when
the refund checks go out, they do not go
to you. They go to the companies that
paid the tariff at the border, the
importers.
This week, a new investigation found
that at least nine companies are using
part of their refunds to pay bonuses.
Meanwhile, other companies say they will
use their refunds to cut prices. And
consumers are suing dozens of companies,
arguing that nobody should get paid
twice for the same tariff.
So tonight, one question,
who actually gets the money? Here is
what we are going to do. We will walk
through how the refund system works and
who is allowed to claim. We will look at
who bore the cost. We will line up what
companies say, what consumers say, and
what economists say.
And we will test the biggest question,
whether any of this will lower the
prices you pay against what we can
actually verify.
Because the honest answer is more
complicated than either side suggests.
Welcome to Frontier Report. If you want
to know where the money is really going,
stay with me. Let's start with the
basics.
Here is the story in plain language. In
2025, President Trump imposed sweeping
tariffs using an emergency law called
IEPA.
In February 2026, the Supreme Court said
that law did not give the president the
power to impose tariffs. That raised an
obvious problem. The government had
already collected about $166 billion.
The court did not say who gets the money
back or how.
That job fell to the Court of
International Trade, which ruled in
March that importers who paid the
tariffs are entitled to refunds.
In April, Customs and Border Protection
launched an online system called CAP.
Refunds began flowing in May.
But look at who qualifies, only the
importer of record, the company or its
customs broker that paid the duty to the
government. If you are a shopper, you
are not on that list. You paid a tariff
indirectly through a price. There's no
form for you to fill out. That is why
there are now more lawsuits than most
people can count aimed at the companies
that received the money.
And on November 10th, lawyers for a
nationwide class of importers asked the
court to order refunds for every
importer in the class. So here is the
situation.
A refund system that works for
businesses, a rule that excludes
consumers,
and a fight over what companies owe the
people who covered the cost.
To see how we got here, we need the
timeline. The Supreme Court rules that
IETA does not authorize the tariffs. The
ruling opens the door to refunds, but
does not say how they should work.
The administration replaces some of the
tariffs with a new global duty under a
different law that tells you the
administration was never planning to
give up tariffs. It was changing the
legal tool.
The Court of International Trade rules
that importers who paid the illegal
tariffs are entitled to refunds.
At that point, more than 2,000 companies
had already sued. Many more had not.
The government prepares to issue
refunds. By mid-April, tens of thousands
of importers have registered for the
electronic payment system. And Customs
says they are eligible for well over
$100 billion,
including interest. The CAP portal
opens. Importers and customs brokers
file lists of the shipments they paid
duties on. Customs says valid refunds
should arrive within 60 to 90 days.
The first refunds reach businesses.
Money moves quickly.
By the time of a court filing in late
summer, the government had refunded more
than $100 billion,
or roughly 60% of what it owed
importers. Consumers start suing.
Plaintiff's firms file class actions
against retailers and brands, arguing
they passed tariff costs to shoppers and
now want to keep the government's
refund, too.
The Center for American Progress
publishes a report calling the refunds a
windfall for corporate America. It notes
that several companies, including Ross
Stores, Polaris, and Carter's, had
reported that refunds boosted their
profits.
The Court of International Trade
certifies a nationwide class of
importers. It covers companies that paid
the tariffs
between February 1st, 2025, and February
19th, 2026. Class counsel files a motion
asking the court to order refunds for
the class.
A ProPublica analysis reports at least
nine companies have disclosed they are
using refunds for bonuses, including the
owner of TJ Maxx and the toolmaker
Stanley Black and Decker. Other
retailers say they will use their
refunds to lower prices. That is the
timeline.
Now let's be precise about how the
system decides who is paid. There is one
rule that drives everything else. A
tariff refund goes to whoever paid the
duty to the government. That is the
importer of record. It can also be a
customs broker who paid on the
importer's behalf.
Let's walk through the people in the
chain. A big retailer, a manufacturer,
or a small business that brought goods
into the country. If it paid the tariff
at the border, it can claim
about 330,000 importers paid these
duties. A broker who paid duties on an
importer's behalf can also claim
companies like FedEx, UPS, and DHL often
paid tariffs at the border and then
build the customer at delivery. Those
carriers can claim refunds, and the
question is what they do next. FedEx
said it would issue refunds to the
shippers and consumers who originally
bore those charges.
A report this fall put that figure at
$800 million.
DHL also said it is refunding consumers
as it receives money. If they did not
import the goods themselves, they are
not on the list. Reporting says
downstream distributors, retailers, and
consumers are not entitled to claim from
the government, not eligible to file a
claim.
As one summary put it, you can only get
money if someone chooses to give it to
you or a court forces them to. Now think
about what that means. The refund system
is a refund of the tax to whoever sent
the payment. It is not a refund to
whoever bore the cost. Those are two
very different things because a tariff
is paid at the border but often felt at
the register.
So how big is the gap? Here is where we
have to be careful.
Research from the New York Federal
Reserve cited in the Center for American
Progress report estimated that about 26%
of the 2025 tariff increase was passed
through to consumers in the form of
higher prices.
Other studies reach different numbers.
The Yale Budget Lab put the cost at
roughly $900 per household per year, and
the Tax Foundation estimated about
$1,000 per household in 2025. Those
figures do not match because if they
measure different things and use
different methods. The safe summary is
this. Consumers paid some of the cost,
companies and workers paid some, nobody
can say precisely how much for any
single product.
Now let's look at where the money
stands. Let's keep the numbers honest.
About $166 billion collected under the
struck-down tariffs. That is what
customs officials estimate importers
paid.
It is a total, not what is left to pay.
Reporting this fall put the figure above
$100 billion.
A court filing in late summer said the
government had refunded more than $100
billion, or about 60% of what it owed.
Some trackers put the total near $126
billion by early October, but those
figures come from secondary sources, so
treat the exact number with care.
Roughly $40 to $60 billion,
depending on the date and the source
plus interest. That is not an official
figure. Why does it matter? Because the
class action filed this month is aimed
at importers who have not been paid yet,
including many smaller businesses.
If the court orders refunds for the
class, customs would have a legal basis
to pay them. The government has argued
that customs needs a court order before
it can pay importers who did not sue. A
judge has said everyone who paid is
owed. We covered that fight in detail in
an earlier video.
For tonight, the key point is that the
legal battle is about which importers
get paid. It is not about whether
consumers do.
There are two more facts worth keeping.
First, interest.
The government must pay refunds with
interest, and the Center for American
Progress says it compounds daily. That
means delay is costly. Second, the debt.
The same report notes that refunds in
some months exceeded tariff collections,
which adds to borrowing. So the cost of
the refund is not only a transfer from
the government to companies, it is also
a cost to taxpayers.
Now let's hear from the people with a
stake in the answer. The argument goes
like this. The company paid the tariff.
The law says refunds go to the importer
of record. Nothing requires it to give
the money to anyone else. Costco, for
example, has said it plans to return
refunds to members through lower prices
and better values, and it has asked the
court to dismiss a lawsuit arguing it
should do more. Several major retailers
have made public promises. Reports list
Burlington Stores, Target, Walmart,
Costco, ELF Beauty, and Tractor Supply
as saying they will use their refunds to
reduce prices. What supports this
version? The law is on their side so
far. No statute requires an importer to
pass a refund to customers. What is
missing? A way to verify the promises.
Shoppers who paid inflated prices last
year are not necessarily the ones who
benefit from price cuts this year, and
there's little way to check how much of
a cut is real. The argument goes like
this. Shoppers covered part of the
tariff through higher prices.
If the company now collects a refund, it
gets paid twice. One lawsuit against
Stanley Black & Decker puts it directly.
Unless the court stops it, the company
stands to recover the same tariff
payments twice, once from consumers and
again from the government. Plaintiffs
have sued Amazon, Walmart, Target,
Costco, Nike, Lululemon, Ford, Toyota,
and many others. Counts differ. One
tracker lists at least 21 consumer class
actions. A Legal News report says more
than 100 putative class actions have
been filed in more than 30 federal
districts.
What supports this version?
The moral logic is simple, and some of
the filings are detailed. Several
businesses have also acknowledged that
costs were passed on.
What is missing?
A win.
As of the reporting we found, there were
no settlements, and companies like
Costco argue that consumer protection
laws do not require refunds when a price
goes up. They say the answer depends on
how much was actually passed through,
and that is hard to know.
Goldman Sachs economists wrote in
February that they would not expect
companies to cut prices as fast as they
raised them. UBS's chief economist said
he would not bet on refunds reaching
consumers.
A Decato Institute analyst put it
simply. Companies will pass refunds
along only if they choose to or if a
court forces them.
What supports this version? How price
changes tend to work. Prices usually
rise quickly and fall slowly. What is
missing?
Product-by-product data.
Nobody outside the companies knows
exactly how much of a given price was a
tariff. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent
has argued that responsibility for any
transfer of wealth from consumers to
companies lies with those who challenge
the tariffs in court, not with the
administration that imposed them. That
is his argument as reported, critics
dispute it. The administration has also
been fighting in court to narrow who is
paid, as we covered earlier. What
supports this version? The legal reality
that the court, not Congress or the
White House, set the refund rules. What
is missing? Any plan for consumers.
The administration has not proposed a
mechanism to send money to shoppers. So
here's the fair summary. Companies say
the law lets them keep the money.
Consumers say that is a double recovery.
Economists say consumers are unlikely to
see much.
And the government says the courts
caused this. Now let's look at the
sharpest new fight, which is what
companies are doing with the money. This
is where the story has moved in the last
few days.
ProPublica analyzed thousands of
securities filings and earnings calls.
It found at least nine companies that
disclosed using their refunds for
bonuses rather than paying consumers
back.
One of them, Stanley Black & Decker, is
getting at least $298 million in
refunds. The owner of TJ Maxx is also on
the list. Securities experts who
reviewed the disclosures said the
windfall boosted profits, which feed
into formulas that help set bonus pay
for executives and other employees.
Now we need to be fair here. That is not
illegal as far as the reporting
indicates.
Customs rules only say refunds go to
importers of record with no restrictions
on how the money is spent. A refund of a
tax you paid is ordinary income to a
company. And bonuses are not the whole
picture. Other companies have said they
will use refunds to lower prices.
Burlington Stores, Target, Walmart,
Costco, ELF, Beauty and Tractor Supply
are among those named. There's also a
third group, companies that have been
vague. Reporting notes, dozens of public
companies have not said how they will
spend the money. And some businesses
used refunds as a financial lifeline.
Small importers often absorbed tariff
costs and did not raise prices. One
small business owner told a news outlet
she paid $34,000 in tariffs and absorbed
much of the cost rather than raise
customer prices. For that kind of
business, the refund is simply getting
its own money back. So it is not
accurate to say all refunds are
windfalls. It is more accurate to say
the same refund can mean very different
things depending on who receives it. A
company that passed on the whole tariff
and keeps the refund looks like a
windfall. A small firm that ate the cost
looks like a repayment.
That is the difficulty at the center of
this story. The government pays one rule
to the importer, but the economic
reality has many layers.
Now let's deal with the question that is
probably on your mind. Here is the
question everyone asks. If companies get
billions back, will prices come down?
Let's be careful. The honest answer is
that we do not know and the evidence so
far does not support a confident claim
in either direction.
Here is what we can say. Walmart,
Costco, Target, Kroger, and others have
talked about using refunds to lower
prices or invest in value. But those are
statements.
Costco, for example, books refunds only
when cash arrives and shoppers have
little way to check how much of any
future price cut is tied to refunds.
Goldman Sachs economists said prices
were unlikely to fall as quickly as they
rose. That was a forecast made in
February before most refunds had been
paid. A refund is a single payment. A
price cut is a recurring cost. Companies
facing other pressures, such as new
tariffs under different laws, may prefer
to use a one-time windfall to protect
margins. Remember, the administration
replaced some of the struck-down tariffs
with other duties, and other tariffs
such as steel and aluminum remain in
place. So even if companies wanted to
cut prices, many still face import
costs. So what should viewers take from
that? Do not assume refunds will show up
as lower prices on the shelf. Some may
in some stores, on some products,
but no one has shown that this will
happen broadly and there is no mechanism
that forces it.
There's also a second point. Even if
prices do fall at a retailer, the people
who benefit are future customers. They
are not necessarily the shoppers who
paid the extra last year. That is the
fairness problem in one sentence. The
refund is paid for the past. A price cut
helps the future.
Now let's look at the politics. This
fight has become a political one, too.
Earlier this year, 26 Senate Democrats
announced a bill called the Tariff
Refund Act.
It would require customs to pay refunds
with priority for small businesses. That
is a bill about speed and fairness in
the existing system.
It does not send checks to households.
Other Democrats went further. Some
governors argued that families were owed
money, with one estimate in the
neighborhood of $1,700 per household.
That figure assumes tariffs were fully
passed on, which is a claim many
economists dispute.
On the other side, the administration
has argued that the court rulings, not
its policies, created the refund bill.
And the president himself has promised a
different kind of payout, floating
checks for Americans funded by tariff
revenue. That idea became harder to
defend once the court struck down the
largest tariffs, and the government had
to hand back more than $100 billion.
Politically, the story is awkward for
both sides.
For Republicans, it is a reminder that
the tariffs were ruled unlawful and that
large companies are collecting the
proceeds. For Democrats, it raises a
question they have not fully answered.
If you believe consumers were hurt, how
do you get money to them when the legal
system only recognizes the importer?
And for everyone, it shows how a legal
ruling can create a very different
result than a political promise. Now
let's answer the question in the title.
Let's test the question directly, not
directly. There is no claim process for
shoppers, and customs rules pay only
importers of record.
Yes.
More than $100 billion has already gone
to them, and a nationwide class is
asking the court to order the rest for
importers who have not been paid. Some
do. FedEx, DHL, and others have said
they will refund customers who paid
duties at delivery. That is a real route
for some consumers, but it only applies
to shipments where the carrier collected
the tariff. Possibly. There are dozens,
and by one count over 100 class actions
pending.
But there are no known settlements yet,
and defendants are arguing that the law
does not require them to share. Some
retailers say so. The evidence is not
yet there, and economists expect slow
change. So here is the honest answer.
The refund goes to importers. Whether it
reaches the people who paid the cost
depends on three things, what each
company chooses to do, what courts
decide in the consumer lawsuits, and
whether Congress writes a rule. Right
now, the default is that the money stays
with the companies. There is a caution
for viewers here. Be skeptical of any
headline that says consumers will get
refund checks. As of today, that is not
what the system does. And be equally
careful with the opposite claim that
every dollar is a corporate windfall.
Some small businesses absorb the costs
and are being repaid.
Now let's map the roads ahead. I will
not predict. But here are the roads. The
consumer lawsuits fail or stall. Refunds
become ordinary corporate income. Some
companies use them for price cuts, some
for profits and bonuses, most remain
vague. What makes it plausible?
Customs rules place no limits on how
refunds are spent. Defendants say
consumer protection laws do not require
refunds.
What makes it hard? Public pressure and
the growing number of lawsuits.
One or more consumer class actions win
or settle, and companies that sold
directly to shoppers must share part of
the refunds.
What makes it plausible? The double
recovery argument is easy to understand
and plaintiffs have filed in many
courts. What makes it hard? Proving how
much of any price came from tariffs and
which customers paid it.
Lawmakers pass a rule that requires
companies to pass through some refunds
or creates a fund for consumers and
small businesses. What makes it
plausible? The topic is politically
popular and the new Congress arrives in
January.
What makes it hard? Any such law faces a
president who could veto it and a
business lobby that would fight it. So
which is most likely? The evidence
points towards scenario one as the
default with scenario two as the main
wildcard.
A broad law looks the least likely in
the near term.
The next few months of court rulings
will tell us a lot. Five signals will
tell you which road we are on.
Signal one, the first ruling on the
consumer class actions.
A motion to dismiss decision in the
Costco case or any other would show how
courts view double recovery. Signal two,
the class motion for importers.
The government's response is due
December 9th and the court will decide
how far the refunds extend.
Signal three, the earnings reports.
Watch how companies describe refunds in
their filings. Profit, bonuses, price
cuts, or something else.
Signal four, the price tags. If refunds
are really funding price cuts, you
should see them in specific products and
the companies should be able to say
which. Signal five, Congress. Watch for
hearings and bills in the new session,
especially those aimed at consumers and
small businesses.
One more point.
In a story about money, it is easy for
claims to be bigger than the facts. We
will keep doing what we did tonight. We
will separate what a company promised
from what it did and what was claimed
from what was verified.
So let's bring it home. $166 billion
collected, more than $100 billion
already paid back, a rule that pays
importers, not shoppers, companies using
the money in very different ways,
consumers in court,
and a government that says the courts
caused this.
Who actually gets the refund? Right now,
importers do. Whether anyone else does
is still being decided.
And the answer will not come from a
press release. It will come from the
courts, from earnings reports, and from
what actually happens at the checkout.
So here is my question for you in the
comments.
If a company charged you extra
because of a tariff and then got that
tariff refunded, do you think it should
have to pay you back?
Tell me why.
I read the replies. If this breakdown
helps you cut through the noise, hit
like, subscribe, and turn on
notifications so you catch the next
update the moment it drops,
because when the next ruling comes, we
will be here. I will see you in the next
one.

But look at who qualifies, only the importer of record, the company or its customs broker that paid the duty to the government. If you are a shopper, you are not on that list. You paid a tariff indirectly through a price. There's no form for you to fill out. That is why there are now more lawsuits than most people can count aimed at the companies that received the money. And on November 10th, lawyers for a nationwide class of importers asked the court to order refunds for every importer in the class. So here is the situation. A refund system that works for businesses, a rule that excludes consumers, and a fight over what companies owe the people who covered the cost. To see how we got here, we need the timeline. The Supreme Court rules that IETA does not authorize the tariffs. The ruling opens the door to refunds, but does not say how they should work. The administration replaces some of the tariffs with a new global duty under a different law that tells you the administration was never planning to give up tariffs. It was changing the legal tool. The Court of International Trade rules that importers who paid the illegal tariffs are entitled to refunds. At that point, more than 2,000 companies had already sued. Many more had not. The government prepares to issue refunds. By mid-April, tens of thousands of importers have registered for the electronic payment system. And Customs says they are eligible for well over $100 billion, including interest. The CAP portal opens. Importers and customs brokers file lists of the shipments they paid duties on. Customs says valid refunds should arrive within 60 to 90 days. The first refunds reach businesses. Money moves quickly. By the time of a court filing in late summer, the government had refunded more than $100 billion, or roughly 60% of what it owed importers. Consumers start suing. Plaintiff's firms file class actions against retailers and brands, arguing they passed tariff costs to shoppers and now want to keep the government's refund, too. The Center for American Progress publishes a report calling the refunds a windfall for corporate America. It notes that several companies, including Ross Stores, Polaris, and Carter's, had reported that refunds boosted their profits. The Court of International Trade certifies a nationwide class of importers. It covers companies that paid the tariffs between February 1st, 2025, and February 19th, 2026. Class counsel files a motion asking the court to order refunds for the class. A ProPublica analysis reports at least nine companies have disclosed they are using refunds for bonuses, including the owner of TJ Maxx and the toolmaker Stanley Black and Decker. Other retailers say they will use their refunds to lower prices. That is the timeline. Now let's be precise about how the system decides who is paid. There is one rule that drives everything else. A tariff refund goes to whoever paid the duty to the government. That is the importer of record. It can also be a customs broker who paid on the importer's behalf. Let's walk through the people in the chain. A big retailer, a manufacturer, or a small business that brought goods into the country. If it paid the tariff at the border, it can claim about 330,000 importers paid these duties. A broker who paid duties on an importer's behalf can also claim companies like FedEx, UPS, and DHL often paid tariffs at the border and then build the customer at delivery. Those carriers can claim refunds, and the question is what they do next. FedEx said it would issue refunds to the shippers and consumers who originally bore those charges. A report this fall put that figure at $800 million. DHL also said it is refunding consumers as it receives money. If they did not import the goods themselves, they are not on the list. Reporting says downstream distributors, retailers, and consumers are not entitled to claim from the government, not eligible to file a claim. As one summary put it, you can only get money if someone chooses to give it to you or a court forces them to. Now think about what that means. The refund system is a refund of the tax to whoever sent the payment. It is not a refund to whoever bore the cost. Those are two very different things because a tariff is paid at the border but often felt at the register. So how big is the gap? Here is where we have to be careful. Research from the New York Federal Reserve cited in the Center for American Progress report estimated that about 26% of the 2025 tariff increase was passed through to consumers in the form of higher prices. Other studies reach different numbers. The Yale Budget Lab put the cost at roughly $900 per household per year, and the Tax Foundation estimated about $1,000 per household in 2025. Those figures do not match because if they measure different things and use different methods. The safe summary is this. Consumers paid some of the cost, companies and workers paid some, nobody can say precisely how much for any single product. Now let's look at where the money stands. Let's keep the numbers honest. About $166 billion collected under the struck-down tariffs. That is what customs officials estimate importers paid. It is a total, not what is left to pay. Reporting this fall put the figure above $100 billion. A court filing in late summer said the government had refunded more than $100 billion, or about 60% of what it owed. Some trackers put the total near $126 billion by early October, but those figures come from secondary sources, so treat the exact number with care. Roughly $40 to $60 billion, depending on the date and the source plus interest. That is not an official figure. Why does it matter? Because the class action filed this month is aimed at importers who have not been paid yet, including many smaller businesses. If the court orders refunds for the class, customs would have a legal basis to pay them. The government has argued that customs needs a court order before it can pay importers who did not sue. A judge has said everyone who paid is owed. We covered that fight in detail in an earlier video. For tonight, the key point is that the legal battle is about which importers get paid. It is not about whether consumers do. There are two more facts worth keeping. First, interest. The government must pay refunds with interest, and the Center for American Progress says it compounds daily. That means delay is costly. Second, the debt. The same report notes that refunds in some months exceeded tariff collections, which adds to borrowing. So the cost of the refund is not only a transfer from the government to companies, it is also a cost to taxpayers. Now let's hear from the people with a stake in the answer. The argument goes like this. The company paid the tariff. The law says refunds go to the importer of record. Nothing requires it to give the money to anyone else. Costco, for example, has said it plans to return refunds to members through lower prices and better values, and it has asked the court to dismiss a lawsuit arguing it should do more. Several major retailers have made public promises. Reports list Burlington Stores, Target, Walmart, Costco, ELF Beauty, and Tractor Supply as saying they will use their refunds to reduce prices. What supports this version? The law is on their side so far. No statute requires an importer to pass a refund to customers. What is missing? A way to verify the promises. Shoppers who paid inflated prices last year are not necessarily the ones who benefit from price cuts this year, and there's little way to check how much of a cut is real. The argument goes like this. Shoppers covered part of the tariff through higher prices. If the company now collects a refund, it gets paid twice. One lawsuit against Stanley Black & Decker puts it directly. Unless the court stops it, the company stands to recover the same tariff payments twice, once from consumers and again from the government. Plaintiffs have sued Amazon, Walmart, Target, Costco, Nike, Lululemon, Ford, Toyota, and many others. Counts differ. One tracker lists at least 21 consumer class actions. A Legal News report says more than 100 putative class actions have been filed in more than 30 federal districts. What supports this version? The moral logic is simple, and some of the filings are detailed. Several businesses have also acknowledged that costs were passed on. What is missing? A win. As of the reporting we found, there were no settlements, and companies like Costco argue that consumer protection laws do not require refunds when a price goes up. They say the answer depends on how much was actually passed through, and that is hard to know. Goldman Sachs economists wrote in February that they would not expect companies to cut prices as fast as they raised them. UBS's chief economist said he would not bet on refunds reaching consumers. A Decato Institute analyst put it simply. Companies will pass refunds along only if they choose to or if a court forces them. What supports this version? How price changes tend to work. Prices usually rise quickly and fall slowly. What is missing? Product-by-product data. Nobody outside the companies knows exactly how much of a given price was a tariff. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has argued that responsibility for any transfer of wealth from consumers to companies lies with those who challenge the tariffs in court, not with the administration that imposed them. That is his argument as reported, critics dispute it. The administration has also been fighting in court to narrow who is paid, as we covered earlier. What supports this version? The legal reality that the court, not Congress or the White House, set the refund rules. What is missing? Any plan for consumers. The administration has not proposed a mechanism to send money to shoppers. So here's the fair summary. Companies say the law lets them keep the money. Consumers say that is a double recovery. Economists say consumers are unlikely to see much. And the government says the courts caused this. Now let's look at the sharpest new fight, which is what companies are doing with the money. This is where the story has moved in the last few days. ProPublica analyzed thousands of securities filings and earnings calls. It found at least nine companies that disclosed using their refunds for bonuses rather than paying consumers back. One of them, Stanley Black & Decker, is getting at least $298 million in refunds. The owner of TJ Maxx is also on the list. Securities experts who reviewed the disclosures said the windfall boosted profits, which feed into formulas that help set bonus pay for executives and other employees. Now we need to be fair here. That is not illegal as far as the reporting indicates. Customs rules only say refunds go to importers of record with no restrictions on how the money is spent. A refund of a tax you paid is ordinary income to a company. And bonuses are not the whole picture. Other companies have said they will use refunds to lower prices. Burlington Stores, Target, Walmart, Costco, ELF, Beauty and Tractor Supply are among those named. There's also a third group, companies that have been vague. Reporting notes, dozens of public companies have not said how they will spend the money. And some businesses used refunds as a financial lifeline. Small importers often absorbed tariff costs and did not raise prices. One small business owner told a news outlet she paid $34,000 in tariffs and absorbed much of the cost rather than raise customer prices. For that kind of business, the refund is simply getting its own money back. So it is not accurate to say all refunds are windfalls. It is more accurate to say the same refund can mean very different things depending on who receives it. A company that passed on the whole tariff and keeps the refund looks like a windfall. A small firm that ate the cost looks like a repayment. That is the difficulty at the center of this story. The government pays one rule to the importer, but the economic reality has many layers. Now let's deal with the question that is probably on your mind. Here is the question everyone asks. If companies get billions back, will prices come down? Let's be careful. The honest answer is that we do not know and the evidence so far does not support a confident claim in either direction. Here is what we can say. Walmart, Costco, Target, Kroger, and others have talked about using refunds to lower prices or invest in value. But those are statements. Costco, for example, books refunds only when cash arrives and shoppers have little way to check how much of any future price cut is tied to refunds. Goldman Sachs economists said prices were unlikely to fall as quickly as they rose. That was a forecast made in February before most refunds had been paid. A refund is a single payment. A price cut is a recurring cost. Companies facing other pressures, such as new tariffs under different laws, may prefer to use a one-time windfall to protect margins. Remember, the administration replaced some of the struck-down tariffs with other duties, and other tariffs such as steel and aluminum remain in place. So even if companies wanted to cut prices, many still face import costs. So what should viewers take from that? Do not assume refunds will show up as lower prices on the shelf. Some may in some stores, on some products, but no one has shown that this will happen broadly and there is no mechanism that forces it. There's also a second point. Even if prices do fall at a retailer, the people who benefit are future customers. They are not necessarily the shoppers who paid the extra last year. That is the fairness problem in one sentence. The refund is paid for the past. A price cut helps the future. Now let's look at the politics. This fight has become a political one, too. Earlier this year, 26 Senate Democrats announced a bill called the Tariff Refund Act. It would require customs to pay refunds with priority for small businesses. That is a bill about speed and fairness in the existing system. It does not send checks to households. Other Democrats went further. Some governors argued that families were owed money, with one estimate in the neighborhood of $1,700 per household. That figure assumes tariffs were fully passed on, which is a claim many economists dispute. On the other side, the administration has argued that the court rulings, not its policies, created the refund bill. And the president himself has promised a different kind of payout, floating checks for Americans funded by tariff revenue. That idea became harder to defend once the court struck down the largest tariffs, and the government had to hand back more than $100 billion. Politically, the story is awkward for both sides. For Republicans, it is a reminder that the tariffs were ruled unlawful and that large companies are collecting the proceeds. For Democrats, it raises a question they have not fully answered. If you believe consumers were hurt, how do you get money to them when the legal system only recognizes the importer? And for everyone, it shows how a legal ruling can create a very different result than a political promise. Now let's answer the question in the title. Let's test the question directly, not directly. There is no claim process for shoppers, and customs rules pay only importers of record. Yes. More than $100 billion has already gone to them, and a nationwide class is asking the court to order the rest for importers who have not been paid. Some do. FedEx, DHL, and others have said they will refund customers who paid duties at delivery. That is a real route for some consumers, but it only applies to shipments where the carrier collected the tariff. Possibly. There are dozens, and by one count over 100 class actions pending. But there are no known settlements yet, and defendants are arguing that the law does not require them to share. Some retailers say so. The evidence is not yet there, and economists expect slow change. So here is the honest answer. The refund goes to importers. Whether it reaches the people who paid the cost depends on three things, what each company chooses to do, what courts decide in the consumer lawsuits, and whether Congress writes a rule. Right now, the default is that the money stays with the companies. There is a caution for viewers here. Be skeptical of any headline that says consumers will get refund checks. As of today, that is not what the system does. And be equally careful with the opposite claim that every dollar is a corporate windfall. Some small businesses absorb the costs and are being repaid. Now let's map the roads ahead. I will not predict. But here are the roads. The consumer lawsuits fail or stall. Refunds become ordinary corporate income. Some companies use them for price cuts, some for profits and bonuses, most remain vague. What makes it plausible? Customs rules place no limits on how refunds are spent. Defendants say consumer protection laws do not require refunds. What makes it hard? Public pressure and the growing number of lawsuits. One or more consumer class actions win or settle, and companies that sold directly to shoppers must share part of the refunds. What makes it plausible? The double recovery argument is easy to understand and plaintiffs have filed in many courts. What makes it hard? Proving how much of any price came from tariffs and which customers paid it. Lawmakers pass a rule that requires companies to pass through some refunds or creates a fund for consumers and small businesses. What makes it plausible? The topic is politically popular and the new Congress arrives in January. What makes it hard? Any such law faces a president who could veto it and a business lobby that would fight it. So which is most likely? The evidence points towards scenario one as the default with scenario two as the main wildcard. A broad law looks the least likely in the near term. The next few months of court rulings will tell us a lot. Five signals will tell you which road we are on. Signal one, the first ruling on the consumer class actions. A motion to dismiss decision in the Costco case or any other would show how courts view double recovery. Signal two, the class motion for importers. The government's response is due December 9th and the court will decide how far the refunds extend. Signal three, the earnings reports. Watch how companies describe refunds in their filings. Profit, bonuses, price cuts, or something else. Signal four, the price tags. If refunds are really funding price cuts, you should see them in specific products and the companies should be able to say which. Signal five, Congress. Watch for hearings and bills in the new session, especially those aimed at consumers and small businesses. One more point. In a story about money, it is easy for claims to be bigger than the facts. We will keep doing what we did tonight. We will separate what a company promised from what it did and what was claimed from what was verified. So let's bring it home. $166 billion collected, more than $100 billion already paid back, a rule that pays importers, not shoppers, companies using the money in very different ways, consumers in court, and a government that says the courts caused this. Who actually gets the refund? Right now, importers do. Whether anyone else does is still being decided. And the answer will not come from a press release. It will come from the courts, from earnings reports, and from what actually happens at the checkout. So here is my question for you in the comments. If a company charged you extra because of a tariff and then got that tariff refunded, do you think it should have to pay you back? Tell me why. I read the replies. If this breakdown helps you cut through the noise, hit like, subscribe, and turn on notifications so you catch the next update the moment it drops, because when the next ruling comes, we will be here. I will see you in the next one.

metadata.title: IEEPA Tariff Refund Opportunities: What Businesses Need to Know
metadata.author: Lutz
metadata.shortDescription:
Over the last year and a half, many businesses have grappled with new tariffs imposed by the federal government under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). Recent court rulings have created potential refund opportunities for certain importers, and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has begun processing refund claims.

Join us for a webinar as Dave McGuire, Shareholder and Co-Founder of McGuire Sponsel, discusses the latest developments. We’ll cover what companies should be doing now, common challenges to be aware of, and why timing may play an important role in maximizing available opportunities.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: 
Which Tariffs Are Eligible for Refunds
How the Refund Process Works
Important Deadlines & Timing Considerations
Why Involving Your CPA Is Important

metadata.title: IEEPA Tariff Refunds: What Phase 1 Means for Importers and How to Prepare Without Triggering Risk
metadata.author: Grassi
metadata.shortDescription:
As U.S. Customs and Border Protection continues to roll out the IEEPA tariff refund process, importers are facing critical questions around eligibility, timing, compliance, and enforcement risk. With Phase 1 underway and heightened scrutiny from Customs, understanding how to prepare and how to avoid missteps is essential.

Join Grassi Partner, Michael Violano, and Nunzio DeFilippis, Co‑CEO of CargoTrans, for a timely discussion on the practical realities of the IEEPA tariff refund landscape and what importers should be doing now.

Viewers will learn: 
- What Phase 1 eligibility means for importers and which entries may qualify
- How the 45‑day CBP review and liquidation timeline works
- Compliance pitfalls that can delay or disqualify refund claims
- Why ACH readiness is critical to the timely receipt of refunds
- What CBP is scrutinizing most closely during the refund process

This session will translate recent CBP guidance into clear, actionable next steps for Manufacturing & Distribution companies navigating tariff refunds and ongoing compliance risk

metadata.title: Update on new “Forced Labor” Tariffs and other Tariff-Related Developments
metadata.author: International Housewares Association
metadata.shortDescription:
Get the details on USTR’s proposed “Forced Labor” tariffs for 60 economies and other tariff investigations and legal actions.

IHA’s Washington, DC-based government affairs representatives Craig Brightup and Rafe Morrissey will examine USTR’s proposed Sec. 301 tariffs for 60 economies’ alleged failure to enforce laws prohibiting forced labor imports.  The discussion will also cover USTR’s other sweeping Sec. 301 investigations of 16 economies for excess manufacturing capacity, and legal actions concerning IEEPA refunds and the temporary Sec. 122 tariffs that replaced the IEEPA tariffs.
