metadata.title: U.S. Customs (CBP) Bonds Webcast Preview
metadata.author: Law Office of Yuri Starikov, LLC
metadata.shortDescription:
This webcast is about security procedures that CBP (Customs and Border Protection) requires of importers prior to release certain merchandise. As one of CBP's goals is securing the revenue of the United States, customs bond is an instrument which holds importer responsible if things do not go as planned. How much and what type of bond is required is subject to this discussion. Questions of bonds appear with regular frequency on the U.S. Customs Broker License Examination.

Webcast Runtime: 3 hrs. 58 min.

The webcast comes in the form of on demand HD streaming video presentation. Online internet video podcast is coupled with follow along written material available for download as .pdf file.

Please visit LAWCUSTOMS.COM/STORE

segments.text: A U.S. Customs Import Bond is known by a
variety of names including; Importer Bond,
Customs Bond, C1 Bond, and an Activity
Code One Bond. Despite its many names,
they are all talking about the same
piece of the importing process. Now we
know what to call it,
but what exactly is a U.S. Customs
Import Bond? A U.S. Customs Bond is a
three party contract between a bond
principal, a Treasury listed surety, and U.S.
Customs and Border Protection, also known
as CBP. In the case of a U.S. Customs
Bond, the bond principal is usually a
person or company that imports goods
into the United States. Having a bond on
file is a mandatory requirement of the
importing process and goods will not be
cleared at their port of entry without
one. U.S. Customs and Border Protection is
the government agency that controls,
regulates, and facilitates the movement
of goods into and out of the United
States. A U.S. Customs Bond is a type of
surety bond so it must be written by an
insurance company. Here at TRG we are an
insurance agency that works directly
with the insurance company to provide
these bonds directly to the importer.
Now what does the U.S. Customs bond do?
Although it is a type of surety bond, a
Customs Bond does not function like a
typical insurance product. A Customs Bond
does not protect the bond principle nor
does it protect the goods they import.
Instead it protects the government's
revenue stream. A Customs Bond is a
financial guarantee that CBP will be
paid any and all duties, taxes, and fees
determined to be due during the process
of importing. If the principle of the
bond is unable or unwilling to pay these
duties, taxes, and fees the bond ensures
the surety that wrote the bond will pay
up to the bond amount to CBP on behalf
of the principle. However, in the case of
a surety payout, the importer is not
absolved of their obligation. In fact, the
importer is still liable for the damages to
the surety as well as any remaining
obligation to Customs. There are two ways
of securing a Customs Bond for your
business; as a Single Entry Bond or as a
Continuous Bond. To learn the differences,
check out our videos specifically
covering the details of the two. Like
what you learned? Subscribe to our
channel for more tips and insights into
the international trade world.
[Music]

metadata.author: Freight & Trade
metadata.shortDescription:
What Is a Customs Bond? A Beginner’s Guide to Importing into the U.S.

If you're importing commercial goods into the United States, you may have heard the term customs bond but wondered what it actually means.

What is a customs bond? Why is one required? Who obtains it? And does having a customs bond mean your customs duties have already been paid?

In this beginner-friendly video, we explain customs bonds in simple terms and show how they fit into the U.S. import and customs clearance process.

In this video, you'll learn:

What a customs bond is
Why CBP may require a customs bond
Whether every import shipment requires a bond
Who obtains a customs bond
The role of the customs broker
The difference between a Single Transaction Bond and a Continuous Bond
How the bond amount is determined
The difference between the bond amount and the bond premium
Why a customs bond does not pay your customs duties
What can happen if an importer fails to meet certain obligations
How a customs bond fits into the overall import process
Common mistakes beginners should avoid

We also walk through a simple example of a commercial shipment entering the United States and explain how the importer, customs broker, CBP, and surety fit into the process.

If you're new to importing, freight forwarding, customs clearance, logistics, or international trade, this video will help you understand one of the important pieces of the U.S. import process.

👍 If you found this video helpful, please like the video.

🔔 Subscribe to Freight and Trade for more simple explanations of freight forwarding, international shipping, importing, exporting, customs, shipping documents, logistics, and global trade.

📺 Don't forget to watch our other videos about:

Customs Brokers
Freight Releases
Delivery Orders
Arrival Notices
Bills of Lading
Commercial Invoices
Packing Lists
Certificates of Origin
HS Codes
Other important shipping topics

Each video is designed to help you build your freight and trade knowledge step by step.

Thanks for watching, and remember:

Keep learning. Keep shipping. And keep your documents in order.

EDUCATIONAL DISCLAIMER:

This video is for general educational purposes only and is not legal, customs, tax, or professional import advice. Customs bond requirements, entry requirements, bond amounts, duties, fees, and procedures may vary depending on the merchandise, entry type, importer, and specific circumstances. Always verify current requirements with U.S. Customs and Border Protection, your customs broker, surety, or another qualified professional.

metadata.shortDescription:
In this webinar, Travis Smith explains how to manage the open liability on your U.S. Customs bond by explaining how liability stacks and how that impacts the underwriting on your U.S. Customs bond. Some topics that will be covered include:

- How Does the Exposure on Your Bond Stay Open
- Understanding How Bond Liability Stacks
- Anticipated Impact of CAPE on Bond Sufficiency

metadata.shortDescription:
If your company sources imported goods through an intermediary, you might be voluntarily paying extra taxes on another company's profit margin. This video introduces the First Sale for Export Rule, a strategy that helps multinational brands save millions in import duties annually. Learn how to structure your international trade operations to legally reduce these customs duty costs and improve your tax compliance.

First Sale Rule explained — learn how importers legally reduce customs duties and stop paying taxes on middleman markups.

If your company imports goods through a trading company, sourcing agent, or foreign vendor, you may be paying import duty on profit margins that are not part of the manufacturing cost. In this video, we break down one of the most powerful — yet underused — customs valuation strategies in global trade: the First Sale for Export rule.

Using a real multi-tier supply chain example, you’ll discover how importers legally declare the factory price instead of the higher reseller invoice value — potentially reducing duty liability by 20–40% depending on tariff rates. Major multinational brands use this strategy every year to optimize landed costs while remaining fully compliant with customs regulations.

You will learn:

✔ How the First Sale rule works in international trade
✔ Why importers unknowingly pay duty on vendor profit margins
✔ The three strict legal tests customs authorities require
✔ Documentation and audit risks you must prepare for
✔ How blind trusts and third-party compliance auditors protect supplier confidentiality
✔ When First Sale valuation is legally defensible — and when it is not

Because customs authorities closely audit First Sale claims, proper compliance, documentation, and trade expertise are critical. A structured valuation strategy must align with customs law, export controls, and global compliance frameworks to avoid penalties.

If you want expert support implementing duty-saving strategies, customs valuation optimization, or supply-chain compliance, explore professional guidance and training from Customs Manager:

Customs Manager provides consultancy, customs training, trade intelligence, and compliance solutions helping businesses navigate EU, UK, and U.S. customs regulations while identifying lawful duty-saving opportunities.

📩 Join the Trade Intelligence newsletter for regulatory updates, cost-saving insights, and compliance guidance from industry experts.

Whether you are an importer, compliance manager, logistics professional, or global sourcing leader, understanding customs valuation strategies like First Sale can significantly improve margins while maintaining audit-ready compliance.

Subscribe for practical customs compliance strategies, export control insights, sanctions updates, and global trade intelligence designed for real-world supply chains.

through a trading company, a middleman,
or a foreign vendor rather than buying
directly from the factory, you are
voluntarily paying the government extra
taxes on another company's profit
margin.
Welcome back.
Today, we are looking at one of the most
lucrative, legally approved cost-saving
strategies in global trade.
It is called the first sale for export
rule. And it literally saves
multinational brands millions of dollars
in import duties every single year.
To understand how powerful this is, you
need to look at a standard multi-tiered
supply chain.
Imagine you are an importer.
You place an order with a trading
company in Hong Kong for a container of
jackets.
You agree to pay the trading company $10
per jacket.
The trading company then goes to a
manufacturing factory in Vietnam and
buys those exact jackets for $7 each.
The factory ships the goods, they arrive
at your border, and your broker declares
the value at $10.
You pay your import duty on that $10
price.
But think about what just happened.
$3 of that invoice is simply the trading
company's profit margin.
Under standard logic, you are paying a
customs tax on a markup.
The first sale for export rule allows
you to bypass this.
If you meet strict legal requirements,
customs authorities will actually allow
you to declare the $7 factory price at
the border, completely legally, even
though you paid the trading company $10.
You instantly reduce your tax liability
However, because this strategy takes
massive amounts of revenue away from the
government, customs heavily audits it.
You cannot just guess the factory price
and put it on your declaration.
You have to prove it with absolute
certainty.
To successfully execute a first sale
strategy, your transaction must meet
three non-negotiable legal tests.
First, there must be two distinct
simultaneous sales.
A sale from the factory to the
middleman, and a sale from the middleman
to you.
Second, the goods must be clearly
destined for your specific country at
the exact moment the factory sold them
to the middleman.
They cannot go into a general warehouse
inventory overseas to be sold later.
You prove this by showing that the
factory printed your country-specific
safety labels, language tags, or your
corporate logo on the products during
manufacturing.
Third, and this is the hardest part, you
must provide a complete, unbroken paper
trail.
You need the original factory invoice,
the factory's purchase order, and the
actual bank transfer showing the
middleman paying the factory the $7.
This creates a massive commercial
conflict. Your middleman does not want
to give you the factory invoice because
then you will see exactly how much
profit they are making off of you, and
you might try to cut them out of the
deal completely.
So, how do major brands solve this
problem?
They use a blind trust or a third-party
trade compliance auditor.
The middleman hands the highly
confidential factory pricing data
directly to the independent auditor.
You never see the factory's invoice,
protecting the vendor's commercial
secrets.
The auditor packages all the
documentation into a secure legal file
and submits it directly to customs.
Customs gets the proof they need, the
vendor keeps their margin secret, and
your company saves millions in import
duties.
If you have a multi-tiered supply chain
and you are paying high duty rates, the
first sale rule is the most valuable
tool in your compliance arsenal.
Are you currently buying through a

Drop a comment below and let's discuss

Thanks for watching.
Protect your margins, optimize your

video.

metadata.title: A Quick Guide to Customs Valuation Methods to Determine the Value of Goods | Customs-Declarations.uk
metadata.author: CustomsDeclarationsUK
metadata.shortDescription:
Customs valuation is the process of determining the value of goods or commodities for Government taxation purposes.  The customs value serves as the foundation for the following activities:

computing the customs duty, imposed as a percentage of the total worth of the products and is known as 'ad valorem' duty
calculating the VAT on imported items
compiling trade statistics and reports
The UK and the European Union use the internationally recognised notion of 'customs value' developed by the World Trade Organization (WTO).

There are six methods to determine the value of goods:
Method 1: Transaction Value
Method 2: Transaction Value of identical goods
Method 3: Transaction Value of similar goods
Method 4: Deductive Method
Method 5: Computed Method
Method 6: Fall-back Method


For more information please visit our website:
https://www.customs-declarations.uk/

metadata.title: Customs Valuation Explained – How Customs Calculate Import Duty
metadata.author: Customs Directory
metadata.shortDescription:
Understanding customs valuation is essential for anyone involved in international trade. In this video, we explain how customs authorities determine the value of imported goods and why it matters for duty and VAT calculations.

Customs valuation directly affects the amount of import duty you pay, so getting it wrong can lead to delays, penalties, or additional costs. We cover the main valuation method used worldwide under the WTO Customs Valuation Agreement and explain what costs must be included in the customs value.

In this video you will learn:

What customs valuation is

Why customs value is important for duty and VAT

The transaction value method

Additional costs that must be added (freight, insurance, assists, royalties, etc.)

Common mistakes businesses make when declaring customs value

Practical tips to stay compliant with customs regulations

If you are an importer, exporter, customs agent, freight forwarder, or trade professional, this guide will help you understand how customs value is calculated and how to avoid costly errors.

If you are looking for customs agents, customs training providers, or customs software, visit:
🌐 https://www.customsdirectory.com

Subscribe for more videos on customs compliance, HS classification, rules of origin, and import/export procedures.

segments.text: So, if you're in the world of
international trade, you know customs
valuation is one of those things that's
just absolutely critical to get right.
But man, can it feel complicated? Today,
we're going to break it all down and
make it simple. All right, picture this.
You're importing something. You've got
an invoice. You know you have to pay
duties. But the real question, the one
that everything hinges on, is what value
are customs officials actually going to
accept? Answering that one correctly is
job number one for any importer.
You see, when customs figure out your
final bill, they're really looking at
three key things. What your goods are,
where they came from, and the big one,
what they're worth. And while they all
matter, today we're going to focus on
the absolute foundation of it all, the
customs value.
Okay, so here's our game plan. First,
we'll talk about why this is such a huge
deal. Then, we'll get into the global
rules that keep things from turning into
total chaos. We'll spend a good chunk of
time on the main method everyone uses,
and then cover the backup plans. And
finally, we'll look at the stakes. What
happens if you get this wrong? So, why
is this such a high-stakes game? Well,
it all comes down to one really simple,
but really powerful concept. And here it
is. Most duties are ad valorem. That's
just a fancy Latin term that means
according to the value. So, if your duty
rate is, say, 10%, it's 10% of the
customs value. Get the value wrong, and
you get the tax wrong. Simple as that.
And believe me, customs authorities are
paying very close attention to this
number.
Now, you can just imagine the total
chaos if every single country made up
its own rules for this, right? Well, for
a long time, that's pretty much what
happened. But thankfully, the world
finally got its act together to create
one single system for everyone.
Yeah, before 1981, it was a mess. You
had all these different competing
systems that just created massive
headaches for traders. Then came the
GATT valuation code, and for the first
time we had a fair and consistent set of
rules.
Fast forward to 1995, and this code
becomes a mandatory part of the World
Trade Organization. That means pretty
much every country has to play by the
exact same rulebook.
And that rulebook is built on three
really powerful ideas. First, fairness.
No more customs officers just making up
a value on the spot. Second, uniformity.
The rules are the same whether you're
importing into the UK or Japan.
And third, neutrality. The value has to
be based on what actually happened in
the real world, not some made-up number.
So, all those principles led to one main
method. You can think of it as the
superhighway of customs valuation. It's
the route that absolutely everyone is
supposed to take whenever possible.
And when I say it's the main highway, I
am not kidding. A staggering 95% of all
global imports are valued using this one
single method. So, look, if you only
remember one thing from all this, make
it this one.
And here it is. It's called the
transaction value. And the key phrase,
the one to burn into your memory, is
price actually paid or payable. This
isn't some theoretical price or what
your competitor paid. Nope. It is the
price from the one specific sale that
caused those goods to be shipped to you.
But it's not always as easy as just
grabbing the final number on the
invoice. The whole system works on a
pretty simple formula. You take that
price you paid, you add a few specific
things the law says you have to, and
then you subtract a few things the law
says you can. What's left is your
customs value. So, let's start with what
gets added on. Think of these as costs
that are part of the real value of
getting the goods to the border, even if
they're not on the main invoice. We're
talking about things like packing costs,
selling commissions. Oh, and one that
trips up a lot of people is something
called an assist. So, here's how an
assist works. Let's say you, the
importer, give something to your
supplier for free to help them make the
goods. Like in this example, you provide
the denim fabric and the design
sketches. Well, the value of that free
fabric and design work has to be added
back into the customs value. Why?
Because it was a real cost of making
those jackets, so it has to be accounted
for.
Okay, now on the flip side, there are
things you can actually deduct if they
happen to be bundled into your invoice
price. The logic here is pretty simple.
We're trying to strip out any costs that
happen after the goods are already
imported. For example, any trucking
costs inside the destination country.
That's not part of the import value.
Same goes for any charges to assemble
the product after it's already arrived.
And this brings up a great question I
hear all the time. What about discounts?
Well, as long as it's a real legitimate
discount that's part of the deal, like
this early order special for Christmas
cards, then the customs value is based
on that final lower price you actually
paid. It all comes back to that idea of
commercial reality. But, what happens
when that main highway, the transaction
value method, is blocked? What if you
can't use it? Well, the rules provide a
very clear set of detours you have to
follow. For instance, you can't use
transaction value if there wasn't even a
sale to begin with. You know, like free
samples or goods sent on consignment.
You also can't use it if the price was
messed with because the buyer and seller
are related companies. In those cases,
that highway is closed and you need to
find a different path. And those paths
have to be taken in a very strict order,
often called the valuation waterfall.
You always have to start at the top,
with method one. If for some reason you
can't use it, you must move to method
two, which is the value of identical
goods. Can't use that? Then you go to
method three, similar goods, and so on,
right down the line. You can't just pick
and choose your favorite method. It's a
rigid hierarchy designed to get as close
as possible to a real fair value.
Now, those first two detours, methods
two and three, are all about looking at
other shipments. But, the difference is
really key. Identical means just that,
the same in every single way, down to
the quality and reputation. Similar is a
little looser. It means the goods aren't
exactly alike, but they have similar
features, can do the same job, and you
could basically swap one for the other
in the marketplace.
Okay, we've gone through the rules, the
main highway, the detours, but let's
circle all the way back to our first
question. Why does any of this really
matter? Why is it so incredibly
important to get it right?
Because getting it wrong has serious,
serious consequences. We're talking
about customs audits that can go back
years, and suddenly hit you with a
massive, unexpected duty bill. On top of
that, you could be facing huge fines and
penalties. Your shipments could get
stuck at the port, or worse, even
seized. And in the most extreme cases of
deliberately undervaluing goods, it can
even lead to criminal charges.
So, the takeaway here is crystal clear.
This isn't just about filling out a box
on a form. It's about having a
rock-solid, legally defensible value for
every single thing you import. The
system is fair, but the responsibility
is all on you, the importer.
So, the final question you've got to ask
yourself is this: When that audit comes,
are you ready?

Today, we’ll be discussing Customs Value—a critical factor in the import process that
determines the duties and taxes you’ll pay on your goods. Ensuring your goods
are valued correctly not only avoids penalties but also ensures compliance with U.S. Customs
and Border Protection, or CBP, regulations. In simple terms, Customs Value is the price
of your goods as determined by specific rules set by CBP. The most common method used is
the transaction value, which is based on the price paid or payable for the goods when sold
for export to the United States. This value includes additional costs such as packing,
royalties, or licensing fees that the buyer is responsible for paying.

metadata.shortDescription:
Flexport Customs: Mastering the First Sale Rule
Flexport Webinar
August 2024

Are you looking to optimize your import costs and enhance your customs compliance strategies? Join us for an insightful webinar where we'll dive into the First Sale Rule and reveal how it could be a game-changer for your business.

In this webinar, you will:
- Understand the Basics: Get a clear explanation of the First Sale Rule and how it impacts customs valuation and duty calculations.
- Learn the Benefits: Discover how leveraging First Sale can lead to significant cost savings and improved profitability for your business.
- Navigate Compliance: Gain insights into the requirements and documentation needed to qualify for the First Sale Rule, and learn how to avoid common pitfalls.
- Get Expert Advice: Participate in a Q&A session with our customs and trade experts to address your specific questions and challenges.

Speakers:
- Tom Gould | Senior Advisor, Global Customs & Trade, Flexport
- Anna Zajac | Senior Trade Advisory Manager, Flexport

metadata.title: Customs 101: Methods of valuation for import duty
metadata.author: Chartered Inst. of Export & International Trade
metadata.shortDescription:
This 1-hour webinar introduces methods for establishing the value on which customs duty is calculated. It will help importers to better understand their costs and potential savings.

Customs duty is often charged as a percentage of the value of your goods - which is often called ‘ad valorem duty’. The amount of duty an importer must pay depends on the customs value of their goods. 

The webinar was delivered by Steve Cock from the UK Customs Academy and KGH Customs Services. 

It covered:

- Overview of WTO valuation rules and EU legislation
- Methods of valuation
- Evidence to support the valuation
- What to do when you dispute a valuation

The UK Customs Academy is an essential resource for industry professionals that not only offers leading-edge training and education, but a unique range of individual and business membership benefits to support the profession, providing invaluable business resources, advice on industry best practice, and a virtual community for industry professionals.

The UK Customs Academy has been developed at the request of HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) to support the development of a robust and sustainable customs intermediaries sector of the future, through investing in quality training and learning, up-skilling more people and making learning opportunities more flexible and accessible to all.

www.ukcustomsacademy.co.uk

metadata.title: How U.S. Companies Are Mitigating Trump Tariffs With Foreign Trade Zones
metadata.author: CNBC
metadata.shortDescription:
A foreign trade zone is a physical site located near a U.S. port of entry where goods can be stored, assembled, modified, or repackaged duty free. Fees are collected only after a product leaves the zone and enters U.S. commerce. Companies that have operated inside Foreign Trade Zones include Ford, GM and Chrysler as well as General Electric, Intel and Sony. Since tariffs were announced interest in foreign trade zones has surged. But a rule change by the Trump administration has drastically changed the way FTZs operate. CNBC traveled to Virginia and New York to find out companies use foreign trade zones to mitigate custom duties and tariffs and how the change to FTZ operations will impact businesses.

hooks. I mean, in the first five days,

Foreign trade zones fall under strict U.S.
Customs and Border Protection supervision.
Customs, for example, has overall responsibility for the
movement of goods in and out of the zone.
FTZs were created by Congress during the Great Depression to
encourage international trade and boosts exports.

duty-free. Duties are collected after a product leaves the zone and

shippers to bonded warehouses.

The bonded is what shelters you from the Trump tariffs right now.

said good, and then they can pay it based on where that tariff is when
they withdraw it from that bonded area.

When the president announced first a 10% across the board tariff.
We talked to our factories.
We got a little bit of a cost concession,
but then it went to 20% and then it went to 125%.
We had four shipments that had left China in that period.
We did have to pay an additional 10% on two of the shipments,
and the fourth shipment would have been 125%.
So, we decided to put that container into a bonded warehouse.
What's interesting with both of these,
a lot of people may think, "How is this possibly legal?" But
this is federally regulated.
Correct, yes. Customs has a very close eye on all of our activities
for the bonded. They're the ones that dictate,
you know, what we can bond.
They check on the space to ensure we're operating accurately and

But costs can be significant.

So every time you withdraw, you have to pay a fee.
So, if I've got a container full of goods,

Obviously adds some additional costs.

markings: the yellow and white lines you see on the roads.
Our product goes down on every road,
every highway, and those roads need to be striped.
So, the material is important or people die.
Launched in 2016, the company has about 100 clients.
Regent's annual revenue is roughly $10 million to $50 million.
Helen Torkos runs the family business,

Our guys take the material and they put it into each individual hopper.
Once that material is mixed, that formula now,

How many of your components can truly be made here in America?
65%. So, our product is basically like baking a cake.

metadata.author: Greater Cincinnati Foreign Trade Zones
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, we break down everything you need to know about FTZs in clear, simple terms. Whether you're new to the concept or looking for a refresher, this explainer covers the essentials.

In this video, you'll learn:
• What a Foreign Trade Zone (FTZ) is
• How FTZs work
• The financial and operational benefits
• Who can use an FTZ
• Why companies leverage FTZ programs

Foreign Trade Zones can help businesses reduce duties, improve cash flow, and streamline international trade operations. Watch to understand how the program works and whether it might apply to you.

If you found this helpful, like the video and subscribe for more clear, business-focused explainers.

#FTZ #ForeignTradeZone #InternationalTrade #SupplyChain #Logistics

segments.text: Does your company import a high volume of goods?
Are duty payments affecting your cash flow?
Would streamlined customs procedures help you stay competitive?
For many companies, utilizing a foreign trade zone offers
greater control over when and how duties are paid,
and that may be the competitive advantage your business needs.
Foreign trade zones or FTZs are designated
areas within the United States considered outside of U.S.
customs territory.
Think of them as duty free zones for businesses.
Secure spaces where imported goods can be stored, manufactured,
assembled, reexported, scrapped, and more,
all with reduced or deferred customs duties.
Here in Greater Cincinnati and Northern Kentucky, we're home to FTZs
46 and 47, governed by the Greater Cincinnati and Northern Kentucky
Foreign Trade Zone Boards.
Our region sits at the heart of North America's commerce corridor.
We're home to Cincinnati Northern Kentucky International Airport,
one of the largest cargo airports in North America and the world.
The ports of Cincinnati
and Northern Kentucky move an estimated 48 million tons of cargo each year,
and with access to major interstates and rail lines
reaching over half the US population within a day's drive.
Businesses here can reach more customers faster.
Together, this powerful combination makes FTZs 46
and 47, a premier hub for logistics, manufacturing and global trade.
If your company imports a high volume of goods,
especially from countries without U.S.
free trade agreements, the benefits of an FTZ may be a strong fit.
Once approved and activated, your business could gain
deferred, reduced, or even eliminated duties.
The ability to pay entry transaction fees weekly instead of per entry.
Direct import delivery to FTZs.
Zone to zone transfers.
Unlimited storage time for goods.
Elimination of tariffs on exports
and added benefits for scrap and waste.
Together, these advantages mean lower costs,
streamlined customs and stronger competitiveness.
And remember the greater Cincinnati Northern Kentucky FTZ team is always here
to guide and connect
you with experts, making your application process smooth and successful.

videos.full_text: Does your company import a high volume of goods? Are duty payments affecting your cash flow? Would streamlined customs procedures help you stay competitive? For many companies, utilizing a foreign trade zone offers greater control over when and how duties are paid, and that may be the competitive advantage your business needs. Foreign trade zones or FTZs are designated areas within the United States considered outside of U.S. customs territory. Think of them as duty free zones for businesses. Secure spaces where imported goods can be stored, manufactured, assembled, reexported, scrapped, and more, all with reduced or deferred customs duties. Here in Greater Cincinnati and Northern Kentucky, we're home to FTZs 46 and 47, governed by the Greater Cincinnati and Northern Kentucky Foreign Trade Zone Boards. Our region sits at the heart of North America's commerce corridor. We're home to Cincinnati Northern Kentucky International Airport, one of the largest cargo airports in North America and the world. The ports of Cincinnati and Northern Kentucky move an estimated 48 million tons of cargo each year, and with access to major interstates and rail lines reaching over half the US population within a day's drive. Businesses here can reach more customers faster. Together, this powerful combination makes FTZs 46 and 47, a premier hub for logistics, manufacturing and global trade. If your company imports a high volume of goods, especially from countries without U.S. free trade agreements, the benefits of an FTZ may be a strong fit. Once approved and activated, your business could gain deferred, reduced, or even eliminated duties. The ability to pay entry transaction fees weekly instead of per entry. Direct import delivery to FTZs. Zone to zone transfers. Unlimited storage time for goods. Elimination of tariffs on exports and added benefits for scrap and waste. Together, these advantages mean lower costs, streamlined customs and stronger competitiveness. And remember the greater Cincinnati Northern Kentucky FTZ team is always here to guide and connect you with experts, making your application process smooth and successful.

metadata.title: What Is Free Trade Warehousing Zone (FTWZ)? How It Solves Customs Duty & Cash Flow Problems in India
metadata.author: OSV FTWZ

In Episode 1, we broke down the complete import-export supply chain and exposed the six major problems businesses face every day — upfront customs duty, demurrage charges, documentation delays, compliance barriers, lack of visibility, and restricted operational flexibility.

We ended that video with a simple statement: every one of those problems has a solution.

In this episode, we reveal that solution.

The Free Trade Warehousing Zone (FTWZ) is one of the most powerful yet least understood trade structures available in India today. Used by global manufacturers, importers, exporters, distributors, and traders, an FTWZ can transform the way inventory, cash flow, customs duty, and international trade operations are managed.

In this video, we explain exactly what an FTWZ is, how it works, how it compares to a traditional import setup, and which businesses can benefit the most from the model.

→ FTWZ vs Traditional Import Setup
→ How foreign companies can operate without an Indian entity
→ Which businesses benefit most from an FTWZ
→ How OSV FTWZ supports global trade operations

metadata.title: What is an FTZ?
metadata.author: LionSky
metadata.shortDescription:
Put simply, Foreign Trade Zones (aka FTZs) are designated areas within the United States that are considered outside of U.S. Customs but operate under the oversight and supervision of US Customs and Border Protection (or CBP). The programs was created for exporters so that they won’t have to pay tariffs on imported raw materials if they export their final products. However, even if the final customer is in the U.S., some or all of the tariffs may still be avoidable, and at a minimum, applicable tariffs won’t have to be paid until a sale has been made which is good for a company’s cash flow. In other words, the government pretends that your imported items haven’t entered the country until after you have added value and declared the sale in the U.S. Or, if you export your final product the government pretends it never entered the country at all, enabling you to avoid paying the tariffs altogether.
So why would the government create this loophole for manufacturers? Because it’s good for the country. Manufacturers don’t have to offshore to avoid tariffs, and increases in U.S. exports bring new money into the economy creating high paying jobs for Americans. According to its 2014 Annual Report to Congress, the Foreign-Trade Zones Board noted that there are more than 175 active FTZ programs across the United States, employing 420,000 people at more than 2,700 businesses, and importing over $798 billion dollars in shipments. So who uses FTZs? The companies that love FTZs exhibit, store, assemble, manufacture, produce, and process items that require the use of something imported where there is an associated tariff. It is common to find FTZ users in oil refining, pharmaceuticals, automotive, electronics, and machinery and equipment. That said, it’s important to note that companies large and small, in a variety of common and niche industries may find significant savings and efficiencies in using a foreign trade zone. The City of Albuquerque allows businesses in Bernalillo and Valencia counties, and in Rio Rancho, Bernalillo, Moriarty and Santa Fe to apply to be included in the Foreign Trade Zone #110. Originally, the decades-old foreign trade zone policy only allowed businesses to apply within a 62-acre parcel located at the Albuquerque International Sunport. Now the ABQ FTZ stretched along the vibrant and efficient transportation hub making for easy access to the entire country.

metadata.title: Introduction to Foreign Trade Zones
metadata.author: International Trade Administration
metadata.shortDescription:
This video introduces the Foreign Trade Zones program. It covers basic information such as what an FTZ is, what benefits it has to offer and how to decide if the FTZ program is right for your business. For more: https://www.trade.gov/foreign-trade-zones-board

November 21, 2019

segments.text: Could your company benefit from delayed
or reduced duty payments?
Could streamlined customs procedures help your
bottom line?
Have you heard of the Foreign Trade Zones program?
No? Then keep watching!
Foreign Trade Zones, or FTZs, are special areas
in the United States that allow companies
to reduce import duties and other costs.
While most FTZs are located near ports of entry, you don't have
to relocate your facility to a special location
to use the FTZ program.
With FTZs located in all 50 states and Puerto Rico,
we can bring FTZs to you.
But what exactly can you do in an FTZ?
FTZ approval can allow for a range
of activities involving imported goods such as warehousing,
manufacturing, and more.
What are the benefits
of conducting your business in an FTZ?
There are plenty of benefits!
First, when you bring components into your FTZ, you don't have
to pay U.S. customs duties on imported goods
that are later exported.
FTZ approval can also allow streamlined customs procedures.
With FTZ approval, the goods that you sell
in the U.S. may also benefit from deferred duty payments and,
for goods manufactured in an FTZ,
possibly lower duties rates.
What else do I need to know to decide
if the FTZ program is right for me?
You will work with the closest local FTZ-sponsoring
"grantee" organization to apply for FTZ approval
at your company's warehouse or manufacturing facility.
Once approved, your facility will need authorization
by CBP before you can begin receiving merchandise.
FTZ benefits and costs will vary by company.
You can talk to your local FTZ sponsoring grantee about how
to estimate the costs of being designated an FTZ.
FTZs encourage domestic manufacturing
by helping companies in the U.S. compete more effectively
in the global marketplace.
Not only do they save you money, but they also help to create
and maintain local employment.
By keeping your business and investment in the United States,
you are helping to promote U.S economic growth.
If you have any questions or would like more information,
please contact your closest FTZ-sponsoring grantee
or the U.S. Department
of Commerce's Foreign Trade Zones Office
at 202-482-2862, or at ftz@trade.gov.

metadata.title: The Blue Cross Antitrust Class Action Settlement: Show Me the Money
metadata.author: Horty Springer & Mattern, P.C.
metadata.shortDescription: "Blue Cross Blue Shield recently agreed to settle antitrust claims after more than a decade of litigation. The deadline to submit a claim for a share of the Blue Cross Blue Shield Proposed Net Settlement Fund is quickly approaching. Tune in for an informative how-to so that you don't miss out the opportunity to receive a piece of the settlement fund. For more information, the Facilities Claim form, and to access the portal to submit the Facilities Claim form, please visit https://www.bcbsprovidersettlement.com/."

The Supreme Court just voided $166 billion in IEEPA tariffs, triggering the biggest customs refund event in U.S. history—but there's a brutal catch for Amazon sellers. metadata.title: Step-by-Step: Build a CBP Compliance Manual That Protects You from Fines & Audits
metadata.author: JSJ INTERNATIONAL LCB
metadata.shortDescription:
Want to avoid costly CBP audits, penalties, or shipment delays? The key is having a well-structured Customs Compliance Manual.

In this step-by-step video, I’ll walk you through how to build your own CBP compliance manual — one that actually protects your business, satisfies auditors, and keeps you in full compliance with U.S. Customs laws.

You’ll learn:
 • What sections your manual must include
 • Best practices for importers and customs brokers
 • How to document policies, procedures, recordkeeping, and training

This guide is perfect for importers, logistics teams, compliance managers, and trade consultants.

Don’t just copy a template — build a real compliance system that works.

Subscribe for weekly tutorials on U.S. customs law and trade compliance.

Chapters below:

00:00 Introduction
01:12 Why & What is a CBP Compliance Manual matters
01:37 Core sections of a strong compliance manual
02:20 Required procedures: entries, classification, valuation
02:55 Recordkeeping & document retention (19 CFR Part 163)
04:12 Internal controls and personnel training
04:29 Common Mistakes
05:01 Case example and common compliance gaps
05:42 Final tips to strengthen, Reduce Audit Risk in your import compliance
06:30 Closing Thank you 


#CBPCompliance #CustomsManual #ImportCompliance #TradeAudit #19CFR163 #ComplianceManual #JSJInternational #USCustomsLaw

metadata.shortDescription:
This episode details recordkeeping requirements under 19 CFR Part 163, the benefits and conditions of a prior disclosure for mitigating penalties, and the varying levels of penalties for false statements or omissions based on culpability under 19 USC. §1592.

Full transcript & study notes: https://voraprep.com/audio/cble-cble3-concept-cble-cble3-lesson-002
Practice questions & study guides: https://voraprep.com/cble

segments.text: Hey, welcome to Vore Prep Audio. Glad
you could tune in. Today we're covering
a topic that can feel scary on the exam
and definitely is in real life. That
topic is record keeping, penalties, and
something called a prior disclosure.
You'll see questions that lay out a
messy situation. For example, an
importer, let's call them Global
Garments, gets audited by Customs and
Border Protection or CBP. It turns out
they've been missing key paperwork for
years. Worse, they knowingly fudge the
country of origin on some entries to get
around quotas. Now, you're their broker.
What do you do? This is a classic exam
scenario. It tests three things at once,
the rules, the consequences, and the
escape hatch. Think of it like this.
Your import records are like library
books you've checked out. The
government, the librarian in this case,
says you have to hold on to them for a
set period. You also have to be able to
show them if asked. If you can't, that's
a problem. Now, imagine you realize you
accidentally damaged a book. Say you
made a mistake on an entry. You have a
choice. You can wait for the librarian
to find it and they'll send you a big
bill. That's the penalty. Or you can go
to them before they notice. You explain
what happened and offer to pay for the
repair. That's a prior disclosure. Your
bill will be a whole lot smaller. That's
the basic relationship here. So let's
start with the first part, keeping the
books. This is covered in 19 CFR part
163. The rule is pretty simple. If
you're involved in importing or customs
business, you have to keep records. And
that definitely includes you as a
broker. The ones the exam loves to focus
on are called the A 1 list. It sounds
technical, but it's just the stuff you'd
expect. It includes commercial invoices,
packing lists, bills of lading, and
entry summaries. Basically, it's all the
documents that prove what you imported,
where it came from, and what you paid.
It 's the paper trail that justifies
everything you told CBP. And how long do
you to hang on to all this? The magic
number to burn into your brain is five
years. Five years from the date of
entry. There are a few exceptions for
things like drawback, but for general
purposes, it's five years. And CBP
doesn't care if you keep it in a file
cabinet or on a hard drive. Paper or
electronic is fine. The only rule is
that if they ask for it, you have to be
able to produce it. You must do so
within a reasonable time, which is
usually 30 calendar days. So just having
the record isn't enough. You have to be
able to find it. Now, what happens when
things go wrong? Let's say it's not just
missing records. Let's say your client,
Global Garments, made false statements
like that country of origin issue. This
is where 19 USC Section 1592 comes in.
This law is all about penalties. The
size of the penalty depends entirely on
the level of culpability. It's about
what you knew and when you knew it.
There are three levels. The lowest is
negligence. This is when you just failed
to exercise reasonable care. It could be
an honest mistake or a clerical error
someone should have caught but didn't.
It's not great, but it's understandable.
The penalty here can be up to two times
the revenue CBP lost because of the
mistake. The next step up is gross
negligence. This is worse. This is when
you acted with reckless disregard for
the rules or you knew there was a high
chance you were doing something wrong
and just didn't care. Maybe you used a
classification you knew was probably
wrong without bothering to check. Here,
the penalty can jump to four times the
lost revenue. And then there's the top
tier, fraud. This is when you made a
false statement knowingly with the
intent to deceive CBP. You knew the
rules and you broke them on purpose to
gain an advantage. For our friends at
Global Garments who knowingly
misrepresented the country of origin to
avoid quotas, this sounds like fraud.
And the penalty for fraud is massive. It
can be up to the entire domestic value
of the merchandise itself, not the lost
duties, the value of the goods. Ouch.
So, you see the problem. The client has
made a fraudulent statement. They're
facing a potentially company-ending
penalty. This is where you, the savvy
broker, bring up the prior disclosure.
It's their best option. A prior
disclosure is basically a voluntary
confession to CBP. To work, it has to be
three things, voluntary, timely, and
complete. Voluntary means you do it on
your own, not because you got a notice
that CBP is starting an investigation.
Timely means you do it before they start
that investigation. If you get that
formal notice, the window has closed for
that specific issue. And complete means
you lay it all out. You explain the
violation, identify all the entries
involved, and you tender the duties you
should have paid in the first place. If
you do all that, the benefits are huge.
For a negligence or gross negligence
case, the penalty is drastically
reduced. You'll have to pay the duties
you originally owed plus the interest on
that amount. For a fraud case, the
penalty is usually reduced to one times
the lost duties. Compared to losing the
entire value of the merchandise, that is
a fantastic deal. It's the system's way
of encouraging people to come clean and
fix their own mistakes. If you don't
file a disclosure and CBP finds the
issue, the process starts. They don't
just send a bill. First, they'll send a
pre-penalty notice. This is your chance
to respond and argue your case. If
they're not convinced, then comes the
actual penalty notice. Even then, you
have options to petition for relief, but
you're already on the defensive and it's
a much tougher road. Let's apply this to
our global garment scenario. What's our
advice? First, on the record keeping,
they failed. Not keeping invoices for
five years is a clear violation of Part
163. Second, on the country of origin,
they knowingly made a false statement.
That's potential fraud under Section
1592. The penalty could be the domestic
value of all those goods. So, our
recommendation has to be file a prior
disclosure immediately before CBP
formally starts digging into it. They
need to identify every false entry,
calculate the duties they should have
paid, and tell CBP everything. It's
their only path to drastically reducing
that penalty. On the exam, watch out for
the timing. They'll try to trick you
with a scenario where CBP has already
sent a notice of investigation. In that
case, is a prior disclosure an option?
No, it's too late for that specific
issue. Also, really pay attention to the
words they use to describe the
violation. Clerical error points to
negligence. Reckless disregard or knew
it was probably wrong points to gross
negligence. And intentionally or
knowingly is your big red flag for
fraud. Here's a quick check. An importer
discovers they've been misclassifying a
product for four and a half years
because they misunderstood a rule. It
led to them underpaying duties. CBP
hasn't called them. What should they do?
They should file a prior disclosure.
It's voluntary, it's timely, and it will
limit their penalty to just the lost
duties plus interest. Way better than
waiting for CBP to find it. Another one.
A broker keeps electronic records for
clients for four years, then archives
them offline. CBP asks for a record
that's four years and three months old.
Is the broker compliant? Nope. The rule
is five years. Even if they can
eventually find the record, the fact
that it wasn't readily accessible for
the full five-year period is a violation
of the record-keeping rules. So, the key
takeaways are these. Remember the
five-year rule for records from the date
of entry. Know the difference between
negligence, gross negligence, and fraud.
It all comes down to intent. And
understand that a prior disclosure is
your most powerful tool for fixing a
mistake, but it only works if you use it
before CBP comes knocking. Vora Prep is
a full exam prep app, lessons, practice
questions, and an AI tutor in one place.
Get started at voraprep.com.

They're facing a potentially company-ending penalty. This is where you, the savvy broker, bring up the prior disclosure. It's their best option. A prior disclosure is basically a voluntary confession to CBP. To work, it has to be three things, voluntary, timely, and complete. Voluntary means you do it on your own, not because you got a notice that CBP is starting an investigation. Timely means you do it before they start that investigation. If you get that formal notice, the window has closed for that specific issue. And complete means you lay it all out. You explain the violation, identify all the entries involved, and you tender the duties you should have paid in the first place. If you do all that, the benefits are huge. For a negligence or gross negligence case, the penalty is drastically reduced. You'll have to pay the duties you originally owed plus the interest on that amount. For a fraud case, the penalty is usually reduced to one times the lost duties. Compared to losing the entire value of the merchandise, that is a fantastic deal. It's the system's way of encouraging people to come clean and fix their own mistakes. If you don't file a disclosure and CBP finds the issue, the process starts. They don't just send a bill. First, they'll send a pre-penalty notice. This is your chance to respond and argue your case. If they're not convinced, then comes the actual penalty notice. Even then, you have options to petition for relief, but you're already on the defensive and it's a much tougher road. Let's apply this to our global garment scenario. What's our advice? First, on the record keeping, they failed. Not keeping invoices for five years is a clear violation of Part 163. Second, on the country of origin, they knowingly made a false statement. That's potential fraud under Section 1592. The penalty could be the domestic value of all those goods. So, our recommendation has to be file a prior disclosure immediately before CBP formally starts digging into it. They need to identify every false entry, calculate the duties they should have paid, and tell CBP everything. It's their only path to drastically reducing that penalty. On the exam, watch out for the timing. They'll try to trick you with a scenario where CBP has already sent a notice of investigation. In that case, is a prior disclosure an option? No, it's too late for that specific issue. Also, really pay attention to the words they use to describe the violation. Clerical error points to negligence. Reckless disregard or knew it was probably wrong points to gross negligence. And intentionally or knowingly is your big red flag for fraud. Here's a quick check. An importer discovers they've been misclassifying a product for four and a half years because they misunderstood a rule. It led to them underpaying duties. CBP hasn't called them. What should they do? They should file a prior disclosure. It's voluntary, it's timely, and it will limit their penalty to just the lost duties plus interest. Way better than waiting for CBP to find it. Another one. A broker keeps electronic records for clients for four years, then archives them offline. CBP asks for a record that's four years and three months old. Is the broker compliant? Nope. The rule is five years. Even if they can eventually find the record, the fact that it wasn't readily accessible for the full five-year period is a violation of the record-keeping rules. So, the key takeaways are these. Remember the five-year rule for records from the date of entry. Know the difference between negligence, gross negligence, and fraud. It all comes down to intent. And understand that a prior disclosure is your most powerful tool for fixing a mistake, but it only works if you use it before CBP comes knocking. Vora Prep is a full exam prep app, lessons, practice questions, and an AI tutor in one place. Get started at voraprep.com.

metadata.title: Customs Ready vs. Audit Ready: There’s a BIG Difference
metadata.author: Simply Trade Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
CBP enforcement is a growing priority, and importers need to be prepared before Customs starts asking questions. In this Simply Trade clip, former CBP auditor Kathleen August explains why she now tells companies to focus on becoming Customs Ready, not simply audit ready. With hundreds of thousands of importers of record, CBP can’t audit everyone—but audits aren't the only way Customs can scrutinize an importer.

Kathleen discusses CF28s, CBP enforcement, import compliance, and supply-chain scrutiny, including how Customs inquiries can extend beyond a single entry line. For importers and trade compliance professionals, the takeaway is important: prepare your organization to respond to Customs questions before they arrive. Being Customs Ready means recognizing that today's enforcement environment requires preparation beyond the possibility of a traditional audit.

[TIMESTAMPS / CHAPTERS]

00:00 - Why Importers Need to Be Customs Ready
00:07 - CBP Is in Enforcement Mode
00:20 - Can Customs Audit Every Importer?
00:36 - Why CBP Targets Importers
00:42 - CF28s and Customs Questions
00:53 - Increased Supply Chain Scrutiny
01:05 - Audit Ready vs. Customs Ready

RESOURCES & TRADE COMPLIANCE COURSES:

• Global Training Center
• Importing into the United States Course
• Customs Broker Exam Prep Course

CONNECT & SUBSCRIBE:

Subscribe to Simply Trade for conversations with trade professionals covering customs compliance, imports, exports, tariffs, supply chains, and the issues shaping international trade.

• Simply Trade on YouTube
• Simply Trade on LinkedIn
• Global Training Center
• Trade Geeks Community

#CustomsCompliance #TradeCompliance #CBP #ImportCompliance #SimplyTrade

metadata.title: Steps to Submitting an Allegation - Enforce and Protect Act (EAPA) | Office of Trade | CBP
metadata.author: U.S. Customs and Border Protection
metadata.shortDescription:
EAPA establishes procedures for an “ interested party” to submit an allegation that an importer is evading its payment of antidumping and countervailing (AD/CVD) duties.  AD and CVD duties are intended to offset the value of dumping and/or subsidization, thereby leveling the playing field for domestic industries injured by such unfairly traded imports.

An EAPA allegation is defined as “a filing with CBP under § 165.11 by an interested party that alleges an act of evasion by an importer of AD/CVD orders.” (See:19 USC § 1517(b)(1); and 19 C.F.R. §165.15(b)). 

For more information visit:
https://www.cbp.gov/trade/trade-enforcement/tftea/eapa

Facebook ➤ https://facebook.com/CBPgov

segments.text: Welcome to U.S. Customs and Border Protection
Office of Trade Learning Series.
In this video, we will learn how to file an Enforce and Protect Act, or EAPA
allegation for evasion of Antidumping and Countervailing Duties, or AD/CVD.
Trade & business associations, importers, manufacturers, producers, and foreign
exporters of covered merchandise can file EAPA allegations
to provide CBP with the information necessary to investigate suspected
evasions of AD/CVD.
Which are tariffs imposed onto unfairly traded goods.
These allegations help CBP enforce trade laws and prevent unfairly
traded goods from harming the U.S. economy and American jobs.
An EAPA allegation is defined as a filing with CBP
under 19 CFR § 165.11 by an interested party
alleging an act of evasion by an importer of AD/CVD orders.
To file a new EAPA allegation.
You need to access the Trade Violations Reporting tool
or TVR tool at eallegations.cbp.gov
From the homepage, select the Report Evasion Violations button.
New users must enter their first name, last name, email address, a password
and password confirmation and read and accept the Privacy Policy.
You will receive an email to verify your account.
After logging in, you will access the EAPA Portal main menu.
To submit an EAPA allegation select the Start button within the
Submit EAPA allegation box.
The first section of the initial allegation is Personal Details
For the Filer Category field
Select either Interested Party, US Government Entity, or Other.
Interested parties are defined in 19 CFR § 165.1 and must be
Importers of covered merchandise, trade or business associations,
domestic manufacturers and producers,
foreign manufacturers, producers or exporters of covered merchandise.
If you choose to select Other, you will be redirected to submit
an e-allegation instead of an EAPA allegation
In the interested party field use the dropdown arrow and select the
appropriate category.
In the “Are You a Small Business?” field select Yes or No.
For more information, click the link to the “Small business Administration”
In the "Are You a Lawyer or Agent Representing an Interested Party?"
field select Yes or No.
If you select No for Lawyer or Agent
review all information and ensure the fields are complete.
Be sure to include the allegers business or company name.
If you select Yes
fill out your information in the new section.
After you've entered the required information select the continue button
to confirm the mailing address and move to the next section
Allegation Details
Here you will enter the AD Number or CVD Number
and thoroughly explain the covered merchandise
and the evasion scheme and the product description fields.
You are also required to select at least one type of Evasion Violation.
You can use the right or left facing arrows to move the violation type
or types into the corresponding column.
When complete, select the Continue button.
You must provide the name, address, and email for the violating importer.
Next is the Attach Documents section.
Select the Upload Files button
In this section, drag and drop or upload any documents supporting the allegation
of the evasion.
This could include trade data specific to the importer, market research,

videos.full_text: Welcome to U.S. Customs and Border Protection Office of Trade Learning Series. In this video, we will learn how to file an Enforce and Protect Act, or EAPA allegation for evasion of Antidumping and Countervailing Duties, or AD/CVD. Trade & business associations, importers, manufacturers, producers, and foreign exporters of covered merchandise can file EAPA allegations to provide CBP with the information necessary to investigate suspected evasions of AD/CVD. Which are tariffs imposed onto unfairly traded goods. These allegations help CBP enforce trade laws and prevent unfairly traded goods from harming the U.S. economy and American jobs. An EAPA allegation is defined as a filing with CBP under 19 CFR § 165.11 by an interested party alleging an act of evasion by an importer of AD/CVD orders. To file a new EAPA allegation. You need to access the Trade Violations Reporting tool or TVR tool at eallegations.cbp.gov From the homepage, select the Report Evasion Violations button. New users must enter their first name, last name, email address, a password and password confirmation and read and accept the Privacy Policy. You will receive an email to verify your account. After logging in, you will access the EAPA Portal main menu. To submit an EAPA allegation select the Start button within the Submit EAPA allegation box. The first section of the initial allegation is Personal Details For the Filer Category field Select either Interested Party, US Government Entity, or Other. Interested parties are defined in 19 CFR § 165.1 and must be Importers of covered merchandise, trade or business associations, domestic manufacturers and producers, foreign manufacturers, producers or exporters of covered merchandise. If you choose to select Other, you will be redirected to submit an e-allegation instead of an EAPA allegation In the interested party field use the dropdown arrow and select the appropriate category. In the “Are You a Small Business?” field select Yes or No. For more information, click the link to the “Small business Administration” In the "Are You a Lawyer or Agent Representing an Interested Party?" field select Yes or No. If you select No for Lawyer or Agent review all information and ensure the fields are complete. Be sure to include the allegers business or company name. If you select Yes fill out your information in the new section. After you've entered the required information select the continue button to confirm the mailing address and move to the next section Allegation Details Here you will enter the AD Number or CVD Number and thoroughly explain the covered merchandise and the evasion scheme and the product description fields. You are also required to select at least one type of Evasion Violation. You can use the right or left facing arrows to move the violation type or types into the corresponding column. When complete, select the Continue button. You must provide the name, address, and email for the violating importer. Next is the Attach Documents section. Select the Upload Files button In this section, drag and drop or upload any documents supporting the allegation of the evasion. This could include trade data specific to the importer, market research, customs data, first hand accounts of the evasion scheme, emails. and any other current information. It is important to include as much information as possible pertaining to the evasion scheme. The Upload Files dialog box will appear. Select the Confidentiality Status of the documents uploaded. Please note that if you file a document containing confidential information, you must file a public version of that document as well. Files uploaded successfully will display a success message. metadata.title: US Imports The New CTPAT Rule for Foreign Importers of Record
metadata.author: Ask The Customs Manager
metadata.shortDescription:
Foreign companies importing goods into the United States will face new Importer of Record requirements from 5 January 2027.

On 6 November 2026, US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) published an interim final rule introducing CTPAT-related requirements for foreign Importers of Record (IORs), alongside new verification responsibilities for licensed customs brokers.

In this update, we explain:

When a foreign IOR must use a CTPAT-validated customs broker

How CBP distinguishes a US IOR from a foreign IOR

What happens when a foreign principal is not the owner or purchaser of the goods

The new verification and five-year recordkeeping responsibilities for customs brokers

The key dates businesses and brokers should prepare for

Key dates

Rule effective: 5 January 2027

Customs broker full compliance deadline: 6 May 2027

Deadline for comments on the interim final rule: 5 January 2027

Official sources

Federal Register — Heightened Requirements for Foreign Importers of Record: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-11-06/pdf/2026-22735.pdf

CBP — CTPAT programme: https://www.cbp.gov/border-security/ports-entry/cargo-security/ctpat

CBP — Delayed compliance information for customs brokers: https://www.cbp.gov/trade/strengthening-customs-enforcement/delayed-compliance

Please note: CTPAT eligibility is not currently available to every foreign IOR. CBP's rule identifies Canadian foreign IORs as currently eligible to apply for validation in this category. Businesses should confirm their position with CBP and their customs broker.

Need support with customs procedures, regulatory changes or trade compliance? Contact Customs Manager to discuss expert support and available services.

Explore the Customs Manager website and its free trial options: https://www.customsmanager.info/

program known as CTPAT.
many non-US companies, the practical
question is no longer simply how to
appoint a US customs [music] broker.

validated and whether the company itself
qualifies as a US or foreign importer of
record.

On 6 November 2026, [music] US Customs
and Border Protection published an
interim final rule titled Heightened
Requirements for Foreign Importers of
Record. [music] The rule introduces new
conditions for foreign IORs making
entries for consumption in the United
States.
The central requirement is
straightforward. [music]
A foreign IOR must either be validated
under the CTPAT program [music] or
designate a licensed customs broker that
is also CTPAT validated to make the
entry.
A foreign IOR that is CTPAT validated
may make the entry itself where it has
the right to do so or appoint a licensed
customs broker.
That broker does not necessarily have to
be CTPAT validated.
But if the foreign IOR is not CTPAT
[music] validated, an ordinary customs
broker license alone will no longer be
sufficient. [music] The broker making
the entry must also hold CTPAT
validation.
Two, who counts as a foreign importer of
record?
This is one of the most important parts
of the rule.
CBP has introduced specific [music]
criteria for deciding whether an
importer qualifies as a US IOR.
An individual must be a US citizen or
lawful permanent resident.
A company must be organized under US law
[music] and located in the United
States.
It must also meet one of two
or asset tests.
The first is that at least 51 % of its
beneficial owners are U.S. citizens or
lawful permanent residence who control
the company.
The alternative is that the company
directly owns a significant amount of
unencumbered real property in the United
States.
CBP may also consider the company's
actual U.S. presence, business
operations, [music]
assets, and financial position when
verifying its status.
If an importer does not meet the U.S.
IOR criteria, it is treated as a foreign
IOR under the new rules. [music] So
simply having a U.S. address, a U.S.
registration number, or a U.S. mailing
address does not automatically make a
foreign-owned business a U.S. [music]
IOR.
Three. What does this mean for non-U.S.
companies?
For a foreign company that is not CTPAT
validated, the practical route is to
appoint a CTPAT validated licensed
customs broker. [music] There is an
important detail here.
If the foreign company is the owner or
purchaser of the goods, the CTPAT
validated broker can make the entry on
its behalf.
However, where the foreign principal is
not the owner or purchaser, [music] the
designated CTPAT validated broker must
act as the importer of record for that
entry. [music] Using a CTPAT validated
broker does not make the foreign company
a CTPAT participant.
The broker's validation and the
company's own status are separate
matters.
There is also [music] a limitation on
the self-validation route.
CBP's rule states that at present
[music] only Canadian foreign IORs are
eligible to apply for CTPAT validation
in that [music] capacity.
Companies established in other countries
should therefore assess their broker
[music] arrangements rather than assume
that they can solve the issue by
applying for CTPAT membership.
Four. What changes for customs brokers?
[music]
The rule also creates new
responsibilities for licensed licensed
brokers.
Before declaring a client as a US IOR, a
broker must verify that the client meets
the relevant criteria.
That means requesting and reviewing
supporting records.
or permanent residence evidence,
corporate documents, financial records,
purchase receipts, or documents of
title.
The broker must retain the verification
records for five years.
The rule also requires a power of
attorney when a broker transacts customs
[music] business for a client, including
when the broker acts as the IOR for an
entry.
An inaccurate declaration of US IOR
status may lead CBP to require live
entry or discontinue immediate delivery
privileges.
Brokers may also face enforcement action
where the relevant legal requirements
are breached.
Five. Key dates and practical steps. The
interim final rule took effect on 5th
[music] January 2027.
Customs brokers are expected to meet the
new verification requirements in full by
6th May 2027.
Brokers [music] could request delayed
compliance before 5th January subject to
CBP's conditions.
For foreign companies, the preparation
should start with three questions.
First, does your business [music] meet
the new definition of a US IOR or will
it be treated as a foreign IOR?
Second, if it is a foreign IOR, is it
CTPAT validated and eligible to hold
that status?
If not, is the customs broker handling
your US entries both [music] licensed
and CTPAT validated?
Third, do your contracts, powers of
attorney, and entry arrangements clearly
identify who will [music] act as the
IOR?
Do not wait until the next shipment
[music] is ready to address these
questions.
The new CBP rule does not [music]
prevent foreign companies from importing
into the United States.
It changes the conditions under which
they can make entry and places
additional responsibilities on customs
brokers. [music]
For non-US businesses, checking the IOR
classification and confirming the CTPAT
status of the broker should [music] now
be part of US import planning.
For the full regulatory text, consult
CBP's interim final rule, Heightened
Requirements for Foreign Importers of
Record, published in the Federal
Register on 6 November 2026.
Thank you for watching Ask the Customs
Manager.

metadata.author: Ask The Customs Manager

In this detailed breakdown, we explain what Returned Goods Relief (RGR) is, how it works in practice, and why many businesses miss the requirements and end up paying unnecessary import duty on returned international shipments. You’ll learn how to correctly document re-imports, the role of original export declarations and MRN numbers, and real-world compliance tips to make RGR work for your cross-border operations.

metadata.author: Shipping Solutions
metadata.shortDescription:
If you've sold a piece of equipment to a customer internationally and it needs to be returned for repair, this video is for you. We explain the steps you need to take to import and re-export goods that need repair. 

*************
Free on-demand webinar, What You Need to Know About Exporting Samples and Repaired Goods: https://www.shippingsolutionssoftware.com/exporting-samples-and-repaired-goods

Download free PDFs of export documents here: https://www.shippingsolutionssoftware.com/free-downloadable-export-forms

The Beginner's Guide to Export Forms: 
https://www.shippingsolutionssoftware.com/whitepaper-beginners-guide-to-export-forms

Find 100s of articles about various aspects of exporting on Passages: The International Trade Blog:
https://www.shippingsolutionssoftware.com/blog

Request a free Shipping Solutions demo here: https://www.shippingsolutionssoftware.com/demo-request

**************
Follow these steps if your customer needs to return your product for repair:
Step 1
The first step is for your customer to check with their own customs authority. Every country has different procedures and documentation requirements for repairs. Some countries may require the goods to be registered with customs before sending them to the U.S. This ensures they won’t be charged full duty upon return.

Step 2
Contact your customs broker. Discuss the import process for repairs with your broker. They can advise on using a Temporary Importation Bond, or TIB, or if they are eligible for import using the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the U.S. number found in Heading 9802. They'll also provide instructions for completing the necessary paperwork.

Step 3
Review HTSUS Chapter 98. This chapter details situations where imports might be duty-free, but specific conditions apply. 

Step 4
Prepare commercial documents for import. You (or your broker) will likely be able to enter the goods duty-free if they haven't been improved. Here's what you need to do:

Step 5
Repair and return the equipment. Once the repairs are complete, you'll need to prepare documents for sending the equipment back. These typically include a customs invoice, packing list and potentially an EEI filing.

Congratulations! You've successfully navigated the repair process and returned the equipment to your customer quickly and efficiently. For more details on this process, look for a link below.

Follow these steps if your customer needs to return your product for repair:
Step 1 The first step is for your customer
to check with their own customs authority. Every country has different procedures and documentation
requirements for repairs. Some countries may require the goods to be registered with customs
before sending them to the U.S. This ensures they won’t be charged full duty upon return.
Step 2 Contact your
customs broker. Discuss the import process for repairs with your broker. They can advise on
using a Temporary Importation Bond, or TIB, or if they are eligible for import using the Harmonized
Tariff Schedule of the U.S. number found in Heading 9802. They'll also provide instructions
for completing the necessary paperwork. Remember: When you're listed as the importer
(even for repairs), you become subject to U.S. Customs and Border Protection regulations.
Step 3 Review HTSUS Chapter 98. This
chapter details situations where imports might be duty-free, but specific conditions apply. Some of
the requirements that must be met include: The goods haven't been improved or
advanced in value while abroad. The goods weren't exported with a drawback.
The goods are being returned within three years of export under the designated HTSUS code.
There are some additional considerations for foreign-made goods:
If the equipment is foreign-made and meets the above conditions,
you'll need proof of export within the last three years (for example, entry documents,
an export invoice or AES filing records). If the goods have been abroad for more than
three years, they might be subject to duty based on the HTSUS classification, unless they meet
specific exceptions. Step 4
Prepare commercial documents for import. You (or your broker) will likely be able
to enter the goods duty-free if they haven't been improved. Here's what you need to do:
Issue a Materials Return Authorization, or MRA, instructing the customer to prepare a
customs invoice stating "the goods are of U.S. origin, being returned for repair,
have not been advanced in value or improved in condition." (Modify this for foreign-made goods.)
Ask the customer to include two HTSUS numbers on the invoice:
9801.00.1055 (for U.S. or foreign returned goods) and
The specific HTSUS number for the item being returned
Then instruct the customer to complete the Shipper's Declaration as per CBP
regulations. As the importer, you'll need to submit either the Importer's
Declaration or Manufacturer's Affidavit to your broker to avoid duty payments.
Step 5 Repair and return the equipment.
Once the repairs are complete, you'll need to prepare documents for sending the equipment back.
These typically include a customs invoice, packing list and potentially an EEI filing.
Congratulations! You've successfully navigated the repair process and returned the equipment to
your customer quickly and efficiently. For more details on this process, look for a link below.
