segments.text: If you import components and export finished goods,
you might be leaving real money on the table. U.S. duty drawback can refund
up to 99% of the duties, taxes and fees you paid on import—if you know how to claim it.
I’m Kari Crane, editor of Shipping Solutions International Trade Blog Passages.
Before we dive in, make sure you subscribe to our channel! We publish Basics of Exporting
and Importing videos twice a week to help you simplify international trade.
Duty drawback is a refund of certain import duties, internal revenue taxes, and fees
after you export or destroy the imported item, a substituted equivalent, or a product made from
it. It’s one of the most complex programs U.S. Customs and Border Protection administers because
it touches both imports and exports—but it can be worth significant savings for frequent traders.
CBP allows several types of drawback. Here’s a quick tour:
You import parts, use those exact items to make a product in the U.S.,
and then export or destroy it. You can claim up to 99% of the duties you paid on the imports.
You use imported articles—or other articles of the same kind and quality—to manufacture items
that are later exported or destroyed before use. You may claim drawback if
the imported and substituted merchandise share the same 8-digit HTS classification,
and the imported merchandise’s HTS code is not described as “other.”
You import merchandise and later export or destroy it without
using it. Up to 99% of duties are recoverable. You export or destroy goods that were defective,
didn’t match specs or samples, arrived without the consignee’s consent, or were nonconforming
at import. Up to 99% of duties can be recovered. Any of the following may file a drawback claim:
The president or vice president of the firm An authorized employee with the authority
to bind the company An employee or customs
broker with a valid power of attorney An individual acting on their own behalf
Here’s how filing works. You need to submit a drawback entry with all the supporting documents
within three years from the date you exported or destroyed the merchandise. File electronically
in CBP’s Automated Commercial Environment, or ACE, and expect processing times to vary.
CBP expects a solid audit trail. Depending on your claim type, gather:
Drawback entries Certificates of
delivery and certificates of manufacture Notices of intent to export, destroy or return
Exporter certifications on bills of lading or evidence of exportation
Once CBP determines your claim is complete and compliant, they verify
and refund the drawback to the exporter or destroyer, unless rights were transferred.
Shipping Solutions export documentation and compliance software helps with many
of the key things you need to get right when claiming duty drawback:
It centralizes export documentation—your commercial invoice, packing list and
certificates—so your evidence of export is complete and consistent.
It ensures and documents proper HTS classification.
You can file your export information through AES directly from Shipping Solutions.
Click here to learn more about Shipping Solutions export software, or watch this
video to learn more about all the documents you need to include with your exports—for claiming
duty drawback and for export compliance. Thanks for watching and I’ll see you back here soon.

metadata.title: What is Duty Drawback?
metadata.author: CITTA Brokerage
metadata.shortDescription: This video provides a basic overview of how duty drawback works. It also introduces how CITTA Brokerage helps our clients by simplifying the complexities of duty drawback and maximizing the money that they put back into their business.

segments.text: Hi everyone, I'm Don McCormick, Chief Storyteller here at CITTA Brokerage,
a customs brokerage specializing in duty drawback. And today I'm speaking with CITTA Brokerage CEO,
Scott Sorensen. Hi, Scott. Hi, Don.
Thanks for joining us today. Absolutely, I'm excited.
So, for people who don't know a whole lot about duty drawback,
can you give us a high-level overview? Yeah, absolutely. So, duty drawback is
a refund of duties that are paid on products imported to the United States. So about 50% of
products that come into the United States pay some type of duty or tariff on those
items when they are imported. And we've seen a real increase in those duties over the last
five or six years with what are called the 301 tariffs that have been put in place on China.
Products come into the United States, oftentimes they pay a duty or a tariff.
And when those products later leave the United States, they can qualify for what is called a
duty drawback or a refund on the duties that are paid up to 99 % of the duties that are paid when
they leave the United States. And that applies to all duties,
not just the 301 tariffs, correct? Well, there are some duties that will
be put on products when they come in. Anti-dumping and countervailing duties don't qualify for duty
drawback, but that's something that we work with our clients to better understand. Like, are these
duties that do qualify for drawbacks? But yes, 301 duties, in general, do qualify for drawbacks.
So, it depends on how they're classified, really.
Correct. So, there's a lot
of products coming in the United States, a lot of products going out. What kind of companies
does CITTA Brokerage typically work with? Great question. So, we work with companies
across a variety of industries. And I would classify it as anything from car parts and to
clothing and apparel to makeup to medical devices, healthcare. I mean, any industry that is importing
products that are later leaving the United States, we work with those companies across industries.
Another way of classifying who we're working with is we're working with companies that bring
products into the United States to manufacture other products that they are later exporting.
We're also working with clients that are just bringing products in and later reselling them.
Those are identified as unused goods or unused merchandise that comes in the United States
and then leaves. So, you could classify it as manufacturing companies, as well as wholesalers
or distributors that bring products in that they don't touch and resell internationally.
Okay, that's a fairly wide variety of different types of industries that you're working in. So,
what makes filing claims and doing all the paperwork and all this stuff
related to duty drawbacks so challenging? Yeah, I think there are a number of things
that make it challenging. One thing that happens with duty drawback is with the new changes to
drawback regulations the TFTEA regulations is what we call it. It allows you to go back in
time five years to file drawbacks for duties that were paid going back as far as five years. So,
one of the first challenges that we find working with clients is just collecting the documents
needed to recoup the maximum amount possible and that would be going back the full five years.
So, I think that one piece is the record keeping and gathering the necessary documents.
So, they could see almost an immediate return on investment by recouping the money they've left
on the table for the last five years, right? Exactly. Yeah. And that's money that is just
going uncaptured. So, US Customs and the US Treasury don't report a lot on how much is
being left on the table. But the last report that they issued about six years ago showed
that about $3 billion a year was eligible for duty drawback and less than a billion dollars
is actually being captured in duty drawbacks. And so essentially what that's saying is that
there are a lot of importers and exporters that just aren't capturing these funds that
are available. Sometimes that's because it's complicated and sometimes it's just
because they're not aware that those funds are available for them to collect. And that's
where we step in and try to help educate them on the process. And since all we do is file
duty drawback, we try to make it as simple as possible to move through these complexities.
So, some have an awareness. Some may have tried to navigate that on their own. And I'm guessing
that unsuccessful claims those that don't go through have a negative ROI in terms
of the resources that were spent. So, how does CITTA ensure that the juice truly is worth the
squeeze that when you file a claim, it's going to get processed and going to get approved?
So, a couple of things. Even before we process the claim, we spend time working with our
clients to understand at a high level, okay, what documentation do you have and what's available and
what is the feasibility of filing a claim? And there are times when they may not have
the information that they need, or it's just too difficult to collect,
going back historically. And with those clients, we'll talk to them about, going forward, let's
make sure you are capturing these funds. So, these are the documents that you should be collecting
on a regular basis and working with your customs brokerage or with your freight forwarders or other
partners to collect these necessary documents, even though going back, historically, you may
not be able to recoup the full amount, going forward, we want to make sure that you are.
So, I think that's the first piece that we do to try to make sure that we're not bringing
someone on board and trying to file claims if it s a wild goose chase, so to speak,
to collect the documents that they need. The next piece that you talked about is once we've
filed the claim, how do we make sure that it goes through? There are a couple of things that we like
to do there. One is, again, making sure that we've got the correct documentation because US Customs
is going to go through a pretty thorough process what's called a full desk review to analyze
claims on a frequent basis. And so, one thing we want to do
is make sure that we have all the backup that we need before submitting a claim.
And then when Customs does come back and say, before we pay out this duty drawback,
we need verification or this audit or full desk review on this claims file. One thing that we
do at CITTA is we maintain that interaction and that relationship with Customs. So, our clients
are not going back and sitting at the table or across the table from Customs on their own.
We're sitting right beside them. And we're working with Customs to make sure that they have all the
information that they need to approve the claim. So, let's talk more about ROI. I'm sure that each
company is different. Each type of duty drawback claims filing is different. But as a rule, how do
you ensure that your clients see a positive ROI? Yeah, so some of that comes back to the analysis
upfront that we will perform in determining, okay, does it make sense to go backwards in
time versus just going from this point forward? Some of it is that initial analysis that we just
talked about. The other side of it is we really like to view this as a partnership with our
clients where we're getting paid together at the same time from the US Treasury.
What we try to do is set it up so the payment terms are aligned, where we're not saying we need
this upfront fee or these additional expenses that you're incurring. Yes, there will be some
time required for it. But again, from a payment standpoint, we try to create a partnership with
our clients in such a way that we're getting paid at the same time and that we minimize
any cash outflows that they may see. I want to touch on something that you mentioned
earlier. You talked about interfacing with your clients existing brokers. So, you're not in
competition with those other brokers. You're just providing a very targeted service when it comes to
duty drawback. Is that how I understand that? That's exactly right. We're not coming in and
trying to start with filing duty drawback and then later moving up to do your classification work and
to clear items and products that you're bringing into the United States. So, we have a great
relationship with other customs brokers that may not be experts and may not be specializing in duty
drawback the way that we are. We work well with those other customs brokers that have an existing
relationship with these clients to collect docs and make sure that their clients our collective
clients are maximizing their drawback potential. Well, that sounds like a really strong and
valuable partnership, not only with your clients, but also with the other
brokerages that they work with. Thanks so much for speaking with us today, Scott.
Thank you, Don. It's great to talk and we're eager to get the message out that
we're here to help our clients by simplifying the complexities of duty drawback and maximizing
the money that they put back into their business. And to our audience, thank you so much for joining
us today. If you are an importer or exporter of record, see what CITTA Brokerage can do for you
by visiting CittaBrokerage.com. And while you're there, you can even use an online calculator to
get an estimate of refund duties that may come to you. Thanks very much, everyone. Again,
Scott, thanks so much. Thank you, Don.

And that's money that is just going uncaptured. So, US Customs and the US Treasury don't report a lot on how much is being left on the table. But the last report that they issued about six years ago showed that about $3 billion a year was eligible for duty drawback and less than a billion dollars is actually being captured in duty drawbacks. And so essentially what that's saying is that there are a lot of importers and exporters that just aren't capturing these funds that are available. Sometimes that's because it's complicated and sometimes it's just because they're not aware that those funds are available for them to collect. And that's where we step in and try to help educate them on the process. And since all we do is file duty drawback, we try to make it as simple as possible to move through these complexities. So, some have an awareness. Some may have tried to navigate that on their own. And I'm guessing that unsuccessful claims those that don't go through have a negative ROI in terms of the resources that were spent. So, how does CITTA ensure that the juice truly is worth the squeeze that when you file a claim, it's going to get processed and going to get approved? So, a couple of things. Even before we process the claim, we spend time working with our clients to understand at a high level, okay, what documentation do you have and what's available and what is the feasibility of filing a claim? And there are times when they may not have the information that they need, or it's just too difficult to collect, going back historically. And with those clients, we'll talk to them about, going forward, let's make sure you are capturing these funds. So, these are the documents that you should be collecting on a regular basis and working with your customs brokerage or with your freight forwarders or other partners to collect these necessary documents, even though going back, historically, you may not be able to recoup the full amount, going forward, we want to make sure that you are. So, I think that's the first piece that we do to try to make sure that we're not bringing someone on board and trying to file claims if it s a wild goose chase, so to speak, to collect the documents that they need. The next piece that you talked about is once we've filed the claim, how do we make sure that it goes through? There are a couple of things that we like to do there. One is, again, making sure that we've got the correct documentation because US Customs is going to go through a pretty thorough process what's called a full desk review to analyze claims on a frequent basis. And so, one thing we want to do is make sure that we have all the backup that we need before submitting a claim. And then when Customs does come back and say, before we pay out this duty drawback, we need verification or this audit or full desk review on this claims file. One thing that we do at CITTA is we maintain that interaction and that relationship with Customs. So, our clients are not going back and sitting at the table or across the table from Customs on their own. We're sitting right beside them. And we're working with Customs to make sure that they have all the information that they need to approve the claim. So, let's talk more about ROI. I'm sure that each company is different. Each type of duty drawback claims filing is different. But as a rule, how do you ensure that your clients see a positive ROI? Yeah, so some of that comes back to the analysis upfront that we will perform in determining, okay, does it make sense to go backwards in time versus just going from this point forward? Some of it is that initial analysis that we just talked about. The other side of it is we really like to view this as a partnership with our clients where we're getting paid together at the same time from the US Treasury. What we try to do is set it up so the payment terms are aligned, where we're not saying we need this upfront fee or these additional expenses that you're incurring. Yes, there will be some time required for it. But again, from a payment standpoint, we try to create a partnership with our clients in such a way that we're getting paid at the same time and that we minimize any cash outflows that they may see. I want to touch on something that you mentioned earlier. You talked about interfacing with your clients existing brokers. So, you're not in competition with those other brokers. You're just providing a very targeted service when it comes to duty drawback. Is that how I understand that? That's exactly right. We're not coming in and trying to start with filing duty drawback and then later moving up to do your classification work and to clear items and products that you're bringing into the United States. So, we have a great relationship with other customs brokers that may not be experts and may not be specializing in duty drawback the way that we are. We work well with those other customs brokers that have an existing relationship with these clients to collect docs and make sure that their clients our collective clients are maximizing their drawback potential. Well, that sounds like a really strong and valuable partnership, not only with your clients, but also with the other brokerages that they work with. Thanks so much for speaking with us today, Scott. Thank you, Don. It's great to talk and we're eager to get the message out that we're here to help our clients by simplifying the complexities of duty drawback and maximizing the money that they put back into their business. And to our audience, thank you so much for joining us today. If you are an importer or exporter of record, see what CITTA Brokerage can do for you by visiting CittaBrokerage.com. And while you're there, you can even use an online calculator to get an estimate of refund duties that may come to you. Thanks very much, everyone. Again, Scott, thanks so much. Thank you, Don.

metadata.title: CBP Form 7501 Entry Summary Explained, Block by Block — and What Changed in 2026
metadata.author: CustomsPrep — Customs Broker License Exam
metadata.shortDescription:
CBP Form 7501, the entry summary, explained block by block — using the 7501 CBP printed on the April 2026 Customs Broker License Exam, and the renumbering in CBP's February 2026 revision of the form.

WHAT CHANGED IN 02/26
Blocks 1–20: unchanged.
New: 21 Country of Melt and Pour, 22 Primary Country of Smelt, 23 Secondary Country of Smelt, 24 Country of Cast (Section 232 steel and aluminum).
Everything after them moved up by four:
  Location of goods: 21 → 25
  Importer number: 23 → 27
  Importer of record: 26 → 30
  Line number: 27 → 31
  HTSUS number: 29 → 33
  Entered value: 32 → 36
  Duty and IR tax: 34 → 38
  Total entered value: 35 → 39
  Broker/importer file no.: 43 → 47

THE EXAM QUESTION (April 2026, Q18): which of blocks 6, 8, 9 or 10 is wrong? Block 6 — port code 0900. In Schedule D, 09 is the Buffalo district; the port is 0901, Buffalo–Niagara Falls.

The April 2026 paper and its exhibits, with CBP's answer key:
https://customsprep.com/past-exams/april-2026?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=form-7501
Every past exam:
https://customsprep.com/past-exams?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=form-7501
Next sitting: October 28, 2026.

SOURCES
CBP Form 7501 (02/26) and instructions: https://www.cbp.gov/sites/default/files/2026-02/cbp_form_7501.pdf
CBP Form 7501 (2/18): https://www.cbp.gov/sites/default/files/assets/documents/2018-Feb/CBP%20Form%207501.pdf
Schedule D, customs district and port codes (U.S. Census Bureau)
HTSUS 2026 Basic Edition (USITC); April 2026 CBLE and answer key (CBP)
CBP forms, past exams and answer keys are works of the U.S. government in the public domain (17 U.S.C. §105).

metadata.title: What Is a Customs Entry  A Beginner’s Guide to U S  Imports
metadata.author: Freight & Trade
metadata.shortDescription:
What Is a Customs Entry? A Beginner’s Guide to U.S. Imports

When goods arrive in the United States from another country, they usually cannot simply leave the port or airport and continue to their final destination.

A customs entry is an important part of the U.S. import process.

But what exactly is a customs entry? Who files it? What information does it contain? And what happens after it is submitted to U.S. Customs and Border Protection?

In this beginner-friendly video, we explain the customs entry process in simple terms and show how it connects the Importer of Record, customs broker, shipping documents, CBP review, and cargo release.

In this video, you'll learn:

✅ What a customs entry is

✅ Why a customs entry is required

✅ Who files a customs entry

✅ The role of the Importer of Record

✅ The role of a customs broker

✅ What information is included in a customs entry

✅ How the commercial invoice and packing list support the entry

✅ Why the correct value, classification, and country of origin matter

✅ What happens after the entry is filed

✅ How Customs may review or examine a shipment

✅ How a customs entry connects to cargo release

✅ Common mistakes beginners should avoid

We also walk through a simple example of imported merchandise arriving at a U.S. port and show how the process works from cargo arrival → customs entry → CBP review → cargo release.

If you're new to importing, freight forwarding, customs, logistics, or international shipping, this video will help you understand one of the fundamental steps in the U.S. import process.

Related Freight and Trade Topics

Continue learning with our videos about:

• Importer of Record

• Customs Bonds

• Customs Brokers

• Freight Releases

• Delivery Orders

• Arrival Notices

• Bills of Lading

• Commercial Invoices

• Packing Lists

• Certificates of Origin

• HS Codes

• Shipping Documents

👍 If you found this video helpful, please give it a like.

🔔 Subscribe to Freight and Trade for more simple explanations of freight forwarding, international shipping, importing, exporting, logistics, customs, shipping documents, and global trade.

📺 And don't forget to watch our other videos to continue building your freight and trade knowledge step by step.

Thanks for watching!

Keep learning. Keep shipping. And keep your documents in order.

Educational Disclaimer

This video is for general educational purposes only and is not legal, customs, tax, or professional import advice. U.S. customs requirements can vary depending on the merchandise, shipment, entry type, and other circumstances. Always verify current requirements with U.S. Customs and Border Protection, your customs broker, or another qualified professional.

Hashtags

#CustomsEntry #USCustoms #ImporterOfRecord #CustomsClearance #FreightAndTrade #CustomsBroker #ImportExport #FreightForwarding #InternationalShipping #Logistics

segments.text: When goods arrive in the United States
from another country, they don't simply
leave the port or airport and go
straight to the customer. There is an
important customs process that has to
happen first. One of the most important
parts of that process is called a
customs entry. But what exactly is a
customs entry? Who files it? What
information does it contain? And how
does it help get your cargo released? In
this video, I'll explain the customs
entry process in simple terms. What is a
customs entry? A beginner's guide to US
imports. Hello everyone and welcome back
to Freight and Trade. If you're
interested in freight forwarding,
international shipping, importing,
exporting, logistics, customs, and
global trade, you're in the right place.
Let's get started. So, what is a customs
entry? In simple terms, a customs entry
is the information submitted to US
Customs and Border Protection about
imported merchandise. It tells customs
important details about the shipment.
For example, what the goods are, who is
importing them, how much they are worth,
where they were made, and how they
should be classified for customs
purposes. Customs uses this information
to determine whether the shipment meets
US import requirements and what duties,
taxes, and fees may apply. Think of the
customs entry as the official
information package that tells customs
what is entering the country. Now, who
actually files the customs entry? In
many cases, the importer of record uses
a licensed customs broker to prepare and
submit the entry information to customs.
But there is an important point to
understand. The customs broker may file
the entry, but the importer of record
remains responsible for the accuracy of
the information and compliance with
applicable customs requirements. This is
why choosing a qualified customs broker
and providing accurate information is so
important. The broker is helping with
the customs process, but the importer
still has responsibilities.
So, what kind of information goes into a
customs entry? There are several
important pieces.
First, there is a description of the
merchandise. Next, the quantity and
value of the goods are important. The
country where the goods were
manufactured or produced is also
important. The merchandise must also be
classified using the appropriate
harmonized tariff schedule or HTS
classification.
Other information can include the
importer, exporter, port of entry,
transportation information, and
information needed to calculate duties
and other applicable charges. The exact
requirements can vary depending on the
type of shipment and merchandise.
The information in a customs entry
usually comes from the documents and
information provided by the parties
involved in the shipment. For example,
the commercial invoice provides
important information about the seller,
buyer, merchandise, quantity, and value.
The packing list can provide details
about the packages and how the goods are
packed. The bill of lading or air
waybill provides transportation
information, and additional documents
may be required depending on the type of
merchandise. This is why accurate
shipping documentation is so important.
If the information on the documents is
incorrect, it can create problems during
the customs process.
Once the entry information is submitted,
customs reviews the information.
Depending on the shipment, customs may
release the cargo without further
examination, but customs can also
request additional information, hold the
shipment, or examine the merchandise.
If everything is in order and the
applicable requirements are satisfied,
the shipment can move forward toward
release and delivery. The customs entry
is therefore an important step between
the arrival of your cargo and getting
that cargo legally released into the
United States. Let's look at a simple
example.
Imagine a company in the United States
purchases 500 electronic accessories
from a supplier overseas.
The shipment arrives at a US port.
Before the merchandise can move through
the normal import process, the required
customs information has to be submitted.
The importer of record provides the
necessary information and may authorize
a customs broker to file the entry. The
entry identifies the merchandise, its
value, classification, country of
origin, and other required information.
Customs reviews the entry. If everything
is acceptable and the applicable

metadata.title: Who Can Import Into America? The January 5 Rule Rewriting the Answer
metadata.author: How Stuff Moves
metadata.shortDescription:
On January 5, 2027, roughly a third of the foreign companies that import goods into the United States will lose the way they have been doing it. Not because of a tariff. Not because of a ban. Because of a checkbox.

Every container that enters America has a name on its customs paperwork — a legal role called the importer of record. Until now, a foreign company could hold that role by filling out a single form. Starting January 5, U.S. Customs and Border Protection's interim final rule, "Heightened Requirements for Foreign Importers of Record," asks a question no one at the border used to ask: are you actually American enough to import? A procurement professional explains what the importer of record is, the new Part 110 test — 51 percent U.S. beneficial ownership or U.S. real property — the two doors left open (CTPAT validation, or a CTPAT-validated broker), the 32 percent of foreign importers who must change, and what the new checkbox on every entry means for buyers, brokers, and cargo already on the water.

In this video:
- The importer of record: who CBP holds legally responsible, and why the broker does not take the liability
- The old system: one form, one number, and 1.16 billion dollars in lost revenue with a 3.1 percent recovery rate
- The new test: Part 110, the 51 percent ownership test, the real-property route, and why receivables do not count
- The two doors: CTPAT validation (0.4 percent of foreign importers, Canadians only for now) or a validated broker (21 percent of brokers)
- The checkbox: live entry, penalties up to the domestic value of the goods, and brokers as gatekeepers
- What it means for buyers: DDP shipments, confirming the importer of record in writing, and the May 6 broker deadline

Chapters:
00:00 Hook
00:50 What an importer of record is
02:18 The old system
04:07 The new test
06:29 The two doors
09:04 The checkbox
11:30 What it means for buyers
13:36 What happens next
15:01 Close

Sources: CBP interim final rule "Heightened Requirements for Foreign Importers of Record," CBP Dec. 26-19, 91 FR 69977 (Nov 6, 2026), docket USCBP-2026-1387, effective Jan 5, 2027; Troutman Pepper Locke (JD Supra); Diaz Trade Law; Docket. The False Claims Act exposure and the expected legal challenge are presented as trade counsel's analysis, not as CBP statements. No CBP forms or Federal Register text are reproduced in the video; the checkbox and the test are summarized in original graphics.

How Stuff Moves explains the hidden systems behind global trade, shipping, and supply chains — from someone who has spent their career inside them. New videos regularly.

Are you actually American enough to import? This is how the role works, why the government just rewrote it, and what happens to the cargo of anyone who is not ready. Every commercial shipment that enters the United States needs an importer of record, the one party that US Customs and Border Protection holds legally responsible for that shipment. segments.text: What to do if you've received a U.S Customs and Border Protection (CBP) seizure notice.
Whether it's money, personal effects, or a commercial shipment of cargo, it's a terrible
day when U.S Customs and Border Protection takes something of yours at the border. Normally, one
thinks of CBP seizing property upon importation, but it's important to remember that even if
you are leaving the country, especially when transiting by airplane, that the agency can take
and will take U.S currency when over ten thousand dollars and no advance declaration has been made.
While you may be unsure as to whether or not you will see your merchandise or money again,
CBP's intention to never return it to you becomes clear once you receive the seizure notice.
A seizure notice advises the person or company whose merchandise or money has been confiscated
that U.S customs intends to keep it and sets worth its reasons for having decided this way.
CBP sends this notification so that an interested party can try and recover the
merchandise through a government administrative process. Depending on the reasons for the seizure,
the chances on merchandise being released can vary. When a seizure notice has been received,
it is important that a response to the letter is provided so that there is documented evidence that
an attempt to clear the name of the interested party of the allegations that led to the seizure
in the first place has been made. Without doing so, the history of any alleged violations and
no attempt to dispute them remains attached to the electronic record of that person or company
effectively leaving them with a red flag hanging over their identity. U.S custom seizures can occur
for reasons such as no apparent authorization to import goods with a particular trademark,
an import of a knockoff or counterfeit goods (I.E no actual authorization to import) an allegation
of smuggling money to another country, heading outbound. Have questions about a seizure notice?
Give our office a call today at 917-546-6997 and we will be happy to speak with you.

Duty drawback refers to the refund or rebate an importer can receive on certain duties, taxes, and fees imposed on imported goods when those goods are subsequently exported or used in the production of exported goods. ISF compliance, which involves providing specific information about the imported cargo to US Customs and Border Protection (CBP), is essential for eligibility in duty drawback programs. Failure to comply with ISF requirements can result in the loss of duty drawback claims and penalties from CBP. Proper ISF compliance streamlines the process of claiming import reimbursement by accurately reporting the necessary data. Working with experienced customs brokers can greatly assist importers in navigating ISF compliance and duty drawback programs.

metadata.title: CBP Ruling HQ 350722 & Guardrails for AI in Trade Compliance
metadata.author: KYG Trade
metadata.shortDescription:
CBP HQ 350722, 350722, Richard Wortman, Todd R. Smith, Anand Raghavendran, Guardrails for AI, AI Enterprise Adoption Checklist, CAPE, IEPPA refunds

This "Guardrails" webinar includes trade attorney Richard Wortman's content concerning CPB Ruling HQ 350722.

(It is not the comprehensive "Guardrails" content.)

0:00 — Topic Summary and Introduction of Experts
5:40 — The Key Facts of Ruling 350722
9:22 — Explanation Of What Ruling 350722 Held
16:16 — Using Docusign For Powers Of Attorney (POA) Agreements
17:26 — Which Roles Require a POA?
19:05 — Does an Importer Need a Licensed Customs Broker on Its Staff?
21:10 — Using AI To Extract Information and the Importance of Human Oversight
28:38 — What Qualifies as Customs Business?
35:09 — Unprecedented Trade Remedies
36:50 — IEEPA Refunds & CAPE
49:30 — Questions
52:25 — Enterprise AI Adoption Guardrails

The beginning of the webinar is a Current Events discussion of Ruling HQ 350722 and CAPE/IEPPA refunds and the implications and impact.

PLUS: A sneak peak at Guardrails for AI in Trade Compliance.

How tool design, workflow integration, and user interface language can create—or mitigate—regulatory risk.
Practical guardrails and internal controls that support a “trust but verify” approach to AI driven compliance.
Key questions to ask technology vendors to assess whether their AI solutions align with CBP expectations.
How to future proof your compliance program as regulators increase scrutiny of AI in global trade operations.

metadata.shortDescription: In this episode of Freight Expectations, Scarbrough's Adam Hill and Caleb Hall discuss the benefits and capabilities of CBP's ACE Portal.

segments.text: Welcome to another edition of Freight
Expectations. Joining me today, Adam
Hill, president and CEO of Scar Bro
Global, and Caleb Paul, director of US
Customs Brokerage. Adam, Caleb, thank
you for joining me today. I'm excited to

>> Worth 1% as well as it should. And it

>> February 6, so a little less than two
weeks ago.
>> Um, so that is a huge change. Um,

gotten into the ACE portal before.

how does that relationship work back and

metadata.title: Is Your Importer of Record Status at Risk - Validating Your CBP Records   Understanding Form 5106
metadata.author: GHY International
metadata.shortDescription:
Is your Importer of Record status at risk? Since September 18, 2026, CBP may immediately void new or existing IOR numbers when the identity information on CBP Form 5106 is inaccurate or incomplete. Earlier this year, CBP also deactivated approximately 5.3 million inactive IOR numbers. Your importer number is not just a number. It represents your company's identity within CBP.

In this webinar, Corie Koropatnicki, LCB, CCS, Director, US Client Services at GHY International, walks importers through how to validate the information CBP holds about them and protect their importer identity before CBP checks it.

What we cover:

01. Why now: CBP's inactivity deactivations and enhanced CBP Form 5106 enforcement

02. What CBP sees: your importer identity profile, the importer self-check, and where to review your record in the ACE Portal

03. Why verification matters: why your broker is asking for identity, authority, and POA details, plus a red flag traffic-light check

04. How to protect your identity: seven practical controls and a 10-minute importer health check

metadata.title: Demystifying the Customs Power of Attorney: Key Role in International Trade!
metadata.author: Scarlett Jones
metadata.shortDescription:
ISF Template | 562-453-7357 | isf@isftemplate.com | www.isftemplate.com

This video discusses the importance of a Customs Power of Attorney (POA) in the customs brokerage field. A Customs POA is a legal document that grants a customs broker the authority to act on behalf of an importer or exporter in customs matters. It allows the broker to handle tasks such as customs clearance, compliance with regulations, and obtaining customs bonds. Without a POA, the broker would not have the legal authority to perform these tasks. The document is essential in securing and obtaining customs bonds and plays a crucial role in filing the Importer Security Filing (ISF) as well. Compliance with customs regulations is crucial in international trade, and the POA establishes the legal responsibility between the broker and the client for accurate and complete information. Overall, the Customs Power of Attorney is a vital document for customs brokerage and facilitates smooth trade operations.
 #usimportbond
 #isfcustomsbroker
 #uscustomsclearing
 #isfentry

Video Disclaimer Here: This video is designed for education and is unaffiliated with US government bodies.

00:28 Customs Power of Attorney (POA) is a legal document granting authority to act on behalf of another party in customs matters.
00:55 Needed for customs clearance, compliance with regulations, and handling tasks like import declarations, duty payments, permits, and communication with officials.
1:26 Crucial for securing customs bond in international trade, required by customs authorities for importing goods.
1:56 Plays a vital role in filing Importer Security Filing (ISF) and ensures compliance with customs regulations to avoid delays, penalties, and goods seizure.

metadata.author: ISF Solution

ISF Solution | (832-904-9333) 
clearance@isfsolution.com | www.isfsolution.com

Understanding the relationship between customs power of attorney (POA) and Importer Security Filing (ISF) is crucial for importers navigating U.S. customs regulations and appointing representatives to act on their behalf. A customs power of attorney grants authorized individuals or entities the legal authority to conduct customs-related activities, including ISF submissions, on behalf of the importer. Importers must carefully select and authorize customs brokers or agents to ensure compliance with ISF requirements and customs regulations. Collaboration with experienced customs brokers familiar with ISF protocols and possessing a valid customs power of attorney is essential for seamless ISF submissions and customs clearance processes. Importers must maintain open communication with their appointed representatives to facilitate efficient ISF filings and address any compliance issues promptly. By leveraging customs power of attorney effectively, importers can streamline ISF submissions, enhance compliance, and expedite customs clearance for their shipments. #usimportbond #isfcustomsbroker #uscustomsclearing #isfentry

metadata.title: How to Use the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States
metadata.author: Shipping Solutions
metadata.shortDescription:
As an exporter, you’re probably familiar with Schedule B codes, but you may not be as familiar with the role of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule, or HTS, codes. This video explains HTSUS basics, including what it is, when it should be used and why Schedule B codes are a better option for companies that ONLY export.

***************************
► Easily classify your products with Product Classification Software: https://www.shippingsolutionssoftware.com/international-trade-compliance-product-classification
► Search for HTSUS numbers: 
https://hts.usitc.gov/
► Visit the Census Bureau website to see which HTS codes you can’t use for export purposes: https://www.census.gov/foreign-trade/aes/documentlibrary/concordance/hts-not-for-aes.html
► Free guide, Classifying Your Products for International Trade:
https://www.shippingsolutionssoftware.com/whitepaper-classifying-your-products
► Find 100s of articles about various aspects of exporting, including dozens explaining product classification, on Passages: The International Trade Blog:
https://www.shippingsolutionssoftware.com/blog

***************************
The Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States, known as HTSUS or simply HTS, is used by U.S. Customs and Border Protection to classify imported goods and determine duty rates. Goods are classified based on their material composition, product name and intended function. The HTS is a 10-digit code designed so that each article falls into only one category. 

It is divided into chapters, each of which has a 2-digit number. Each product category within the various chapters is designated by 4, 6, 8 or 10 digits. The 4-digit categories are called headings. The 6-, 8- and 10-digit classifications are called subheadings.

The HTS uses the same structure of the Harmonized System, or HS, administered by the World Customs Organization, which is a universal classification tool used across the globe. There are 6 digits in an HS code. Many governments add additional digits to the HS number to further distinguish products in certain categories. These additional digits are typically different in every country—that’s where HTS codes come in. An HTS code takes the same form as an HS code for the first 6 digits and then has 4 differing last digits.

Schedule B and HTS codes are separate entities that are used for exporting and importing respectively. Schedule B codes are a 10-digit subset of HTS codes for U.S. EXPORTERS. They are maintained by the U.S. Census Bureau and a way for the U.S. government to monitor U.S. exports.
As with HTS codes, the first 6 digits of a Schedule B code should be the same as an HS number, but the last 4 digits may differ from the HTS code.

If you’re doing both importing and exporting, you are required to use HTS codes for your imports, so you might as well use those codes for your exports as well. But do know that there are some HTS codes that cannot be used for export. Look for a link below to the Census Bureau website to see which HTS codes this applies to.
If you’re only exporting, using the Schedule B code is the easiest way to go. It isn’t nearly as detailed or complex as an HTS code.

If you need help finding the proper code for your product, our Product Classification Trade Wizard is the easiest way. Simply select import or export and enter a search term.

videos.full_text: As an exporter, you’re probably familiar with Schedule B codes, but you may not be as familiar with the role of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule, or HTS, codes. I’m Kari Crane, editor of Shipping Solutions’ International Trade Blog Passages. In this video, I’ll explain HTSUS basics, including what it is, when it should be used and why Schedule B codes are a better option for companies that ONLY export. But before we get started, make sure you subscribe to this channel so you don’t miss any of our Basics of Exporting videos, sharing practical advice for exporters and importers. The Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States, known as HTSUS or simply HTS, is used by U.S. Customs and Border Protection to classify imported goods and determine duty rates. Goods are classified based on their material composition, product name and intended function. The HTS is a 10-digit code designed so that each article falls into only one category. It is divided into chapters, each of which has a 2-digit number. Each product category within the various chapters is designated by 4, 6, 8 or 10 digits. The 4-digit categories are called headings. The 6-, 8- and 10-digit classifications are called subheadings. HTS Codes: An Example Let’s look at an example for umbrellas. Put following image on the screen: This example is for “hand-held umbrellas chiefly used for protection against rain." U.S. HTS Codes have four components: The first two digits are the Chapter—66 in this case. The next two digits make up the Heading. The heading dictates the specific category within any particular chapter. Then comes the Subheading. These digits get even more specific, defining subcategories of products. Finally, you have the last four Extra digits. Countries can use an additional 2 to 4 digits here for country-specific categorizations. The United States relies on 10-digit codes, or HTSUS numbers. I’ll put a link below to the International Trade Commission website where you can search for the HTSUS code for your product. The HTS uses the same structure of the Harmonized System, or HS, administered by the World Customs Organization, which is a universal classification tool used across the globe. There are 6 digits in an HS code. Many governments add additional digits to the HS number to further distinguish products in certain categories. These additional digits are typically different in every country—that’s where HTS codes come in. An HTS code takes the same form as an HS code for the first 6 digits and then has 4 differing last digits. Schedule B and HTS codes are separate entities that are used for exporting and importing respectively. Schedule B codes are a 10-digit subset of HTS codes for U.S. EXPORTERS. They are maintained by the U.S. Census Bureau and a way for the U.S. government to monitor U.S. exports. As with HTS codes, the first 6 digits of a Schedule B code should be the same as an HS number, but the last 4 digits may differ from the HTS code. If you’re doing both importing and exporting, you are required to use HTS codes for your imports, so you might as well use those codes for your exports as well. But do know that there are some HTS codes that cannot be used for export. Look for a link below to the Census Bureau website to see which HTS codes this applies to. If you’re only exporting, using the Schedule B code is the easiest way to go. It isn’t nearly as detailed or complex as an HTS code. If you need help finding the proper code for your product, our Product Classification Trade Wizard is the easiest way. Simply select import or export and enter a search term. There’s a link below to give it a try for free. If you liked this video, like it, share it, and subscribe to our channel for more videos sharing real, practical advice for exporters. You’ll also find 100s of articles about every aspect of exporting at shippingsolutions.com/blog. Look for a link below.

classification ensures your goods are assessed with the correct duties and taxes,
helping you avoid costly penalties and delays. Tariff classification involves assigning your
product a specific code from the Harmonized Tariff Schedule, or HTS. This code determines
the duty rate, applicable trade programs, and even potential import restrictions.
To classify your goods correctly, start by understanding the HTS structure. It’s
based on a structured system of headings and subheadings that describe various
product categories. Careful attention to detail is required to match your product’s
characteristics to the most accurate code. Incorrect classification can lead to
underpayment or overpayment of duties, fines, or even seizure of your goods.

or trigger unnecessary regulatory scrutiny. To ensure accurate tariff classification,
start by reviewing the General Rules of Interpretation, or GRI. These rules act
as your guide through the classification process, helping you navigate complex product descriptions
and find the correct HTS code for your goods. If you’re uncertain about a classification,
consider requesting a binding ruling from CBP to gain clarity and avoid potential errors.

so staying informed about changes is essential to maintaining compliance and
avoiding surprises with your imports. Navigating tariff classification can

metadata.title: Customs Penalty Mitigation: Negotiating with CBP | Jennifer Diaz
metadata.author: Meaningful Mediation
metadata.shortDescription:
How do you negotiate a customs penalty when the other side is U.S. Customs and Border Protection and there is no mediator in the room?

In this episode of the Meaningful Mediation Podcast, host Patrick Russell (Florida Supreme Court Certified Mediator and Qualified Arbitrator) sits down with Jennifer Diaz, founder of Diaz Trade Law, P.A., a customs and international trade attorney Board-Certified in International Law by The Florida Bar.

Jennifer has counseled importers and exporters on customs matters since 2006, first at a South Florida firm, where she became a partner and led its customs and international trade group, and since 2016 at her own firm. Her clients call her when CBP, the FDA, or OFAC arrives with a detention, a seizure, or a penalty notice.

Jennifer explains who is really on the other side of a customs dispute, how the reasonable care standard and the levels of culpability (negligence, gross negligence, fraud) drive the size of a penalty, and how customs penalty mitigation works through petitions, mitigating factors, and inability-to-pay arguments. She walks through the hard call of a prior disclosure or voluntary self-disclosure, why trade fraud is now a top federal enforcement priority, what happens when a traveler's cash is seized at the airport, and when a claim and cost bond beats a petition.

Patrick and Jennifer also discuss why customs disputes almost never go to mediation, how she values a settlement against CBP's own mitigation guidelines, and her top three negotiation tips for dealing with a counterpart that holds most of the power.

And you see all sorts of crazy scenarios, but each one requires its own kind of thought process in terms of how we want to try to argue and try to get the best results for our clients. Like which which mechanism of lobbying is best? Is it written? Is it Is it a verbal appeal to somebody? Is it trying to get it into an attorney's hands? They're trying to move it to Customs Council and or the Department of Justice to try to settle? Are we trying to just keep it locally at the paralegal level? You know, everything is involving a little more strategy than it has in the past. >> Yeah. Well, one lesson there, count your money before you get to the airport. >> Yeah. What happens quite often in those situations is you have over 10 grand. Like I've heard all sorts of stories. I was selling a house in whatever other country, my family member gave me whatever currency. It It doesn't matter what the rationale is, and the government doesn't care that you have the money per se as long as it's not illicit drug money. That's a different story. We have had drug sniffing dogs sniff and find currency and then have the DEA seize it. You know, that's a separate animal versus you have over 10 grand for whatever legitimate reason, then it's our job to prove that it came from a legitimate source. It's intended to be used for a legitimate use. And quite often we see people that had global entry and now it's revoked. And now every time they're traveling, they're going through secondary examination. So imagine every single time you traveled internationally, well, Mr. Patrick, great, good to see you again. Come to the room. So where are you going this time, buddy? How much money do you have on you this time? Have any Rolexes, any watches on you this time? What exactly do you do for a living again? Where were you going? Why were you headed there? What's going on there? What are you doing? You know, they're trained investigators. They're trained to get under your skin. So you see people losing their patience with that. Not a good call because these guys have access to your travel record. They're going to say not a nice guy, was very irritated, escalated. I mean they can get law enforcement and they are their own law enforcement, but they can also get local law enforcement to arrest you. We've had people handcuffed and arrested at the scene, too. So I I would say be very very nice to your local TSA/CBP/anyone at the border in any sort of mechanism of enforcement because it can get ugly really fast. >> Yeah. Well, let's pivot over to what I call the defining moment. >> Sure. >> So every practice has one matter or one event, something that um which you learned something, whether it's about yourself, the other side, or your practice that you still carry today. Tell me what yours was. >> I have a couple, but first is you know, I had a very lucky break with a larger firm when I first started out and I was there for 10 years before I decided to start my own practice itself. So becoming an entrepreneur was definitely my my defining career moment for myself and that I think is a huge moment for anybody who's willing and able to take that leap of faith in themselves and to create their own entrepreneurial journey, which is a crazy, fun, awesome roller coaster in its own way, but really rewarding. And then when it comes to client matters, I will say there was a and there always are we have a few of these, but where you take the matter really personally >> Mm. >> and you take it home with you and good and bad and there's some where it's not necessarily a fair result. On my side, the other side is always the US government, period. You know, I it's I don't have conflicts in that regard because it's it's my client versus US Customs versus a government agency in some way, shape, or form. That's it. And it's not always fair. know, the the stories are not always fair, the situations are not always fair, the outcomes are not always fair. But there is a lot of advocating that we have to do on our side. And it's On the one hand, I've had to learn to try to not take these things personally. It's somebody's business versus freedom for the most part, you know, when you're not dealing with the criminal implications. But we really do have our own mantra and like values at my firm itself to really work to get the best damn results we could possibly get for our clients. Like our job is to take the matter as seriously as possible and to work through the scenarios to get the best results we possibly can. And in some instances, like the one case I'm thinking of, was that trade show case where they brought back their life savings, their life savings in cargo, and everything's on the line, and they missed a cleared it. They forgot a few items. Are they purposely trying to screw the man? No. They weren't. They were up in the middle of the night trying to recreate what they had, what they didn't have, and they screwed up because they're human. When's the last time anybody made a mistake? Oh, wait, all the time. Ask my daughter. I make mistakes every day. She'll tell you, you know? So did they purposefully intend to No. So I'm writing my 8 million page petition and getting all And then it wound up turning into a criminal matter as well. The government's alleging, I don't know, you smuggled. How dare you? It was an artifact. And it wound up getting so intense that they actually needed It was a grand jury, and they actually needed a witness, like an evidentiary witness, and they were scared to be there in any way, shape, or form. So I offered to help them in that regard, and I wound up testifying. I will never do that again. It was terrible. It was all sorts of terrible. They wound up, thankfully, settling the matter, getting all of their goods back, but it was just the whole thing was a terrible, terrible experience, and I wound up getting like way too entwined and personal in it, you know? So I will say it's hard to like find a line, you know? And to make a black and white line when you really, really like wind up liking your clients and like liking them for who they are and wanting the best for them, but at the end of the day it's like we're here to perform a specific job function and trying not to take it so personally and take it home with you. It's hard. I mean, when you go home you should be able to go home, enjoy a glass of wine and forget about your crazy day and you know, enjoy the gray hairs that come with it in the glass of wine, but I we have so many crazy matters now where the numbers are just so astronomical and the government saying you owe 60 plus million dollars. Like no, that can't be real. This can't be real. There's 100 million dollars on the line. It's like come on. This is a small company. Like it's a tiny, tiny business. This can't be true. And some of these scenarios are just getting razier and razier and we're seeing the government use subpoena power and bang down doors. I've heard of a crazy story where the government banged down a door and next thing you know, their poor dog had a little heart attack and died. Like crazy, crazy, all sorts of crazy stories. So those aren't going to go away. So it's how do you segregate and separate that to get the best for your client and to also have the ability to like do your job, function well, sleep a night yourself and not take it home with you, you know? Those are hard. >> Yeah. >> And in some instances we find ourselves caring more about our cases than, you know, our clients do. It's like I want you to comply. I want you to do the right thing and it's like eh, okay. Well, maybe not a fit. So having to to learn which matters to take on and which matters not to take on, that's that's huge too. Sometimes it's just not worth it. >> I think all lawyers struggle, those that are really trying to do the right thing, they struggle with not taking things personally because you are their advocate, you're their shield, you can be their sword depending on what side of the fence you are. And it's really hard to cut that line and when you keep on that line too long and you become the client, I mean, for example, if you ever have your own personal legal problem, you know, could be a car accident, whatever it is, parking ticket, whatever, does that not bother you a lot? Right? Because it's your own problem. So now all of a sudden you are putting that on for all your clients. So you're now absorbing all of that. Every case is a personal case. And that really that's what leads to a lot of the burnout in our profession when people can't draw that line. Um and you start losing perspective, too. >> I mean, what I like to be able to say and do and what we really take pride in is like when you have an import issue, you come to us and we take on your issue as if it's our own and we work through it and advocate and then try to get the best, you know, that that's our jam. And it's great when it doesn't become personal. It's very strange when it does and it 's not the norm, but it's just a matter of how close you get to those clients and there are some clients you just wind up like loving them because they're an awesome person and it's really hard to not like get close with them when you're spending so much time on a matter. And it's brutal when you think that some unjust, unfair outcome or, you know, something is happening, the process itself, it's not always fair. I mean, our our systems are not always fair fabulous systems. You're hopeful that the end result will be one that is adequate and or fair and or just, but it doesn't always happen that way and that's really hard to accept. >> Yeah. >> Especially given our pursuit of justice, right? Truth and justice. >> That's right. >> how often do you actually have a mediation in your business? Do you at all? Is there any mediations in any of this stuff? >> No, sadly. I mean, it'd be nice if there were in some instances, but no. Typically, the way our world works is you make a conscientious decision. Like, for example, if your goods are seized, you don't have a choice of a mediation. You have a choice of abandoning the goods. The government would love that, right? Less work. >> Okay. >> You can petition. You can fight. You can file a claim and cost bond. You can file an offer and compromise, but there is no let's go to a third-party mediator to solve this dispute. Um like, for example, FMC disputes have their own mediation, for example, but it's few and far between when other agencies do the same thing and see the value in that, which I think it would be a great solution to some instances where you have the back and forth, but we wind up having disputes that go to the Court of International Trade in New York. So, for example, if the government imposes a $10 million penalty and you don't pay it and the government winds up filing their complaint itself, you're going to the CIT and dealing with the judge itself. I I wish there are more mediations per se that happen at that level, too, but it's it's sadly few and far between. I think it would be a great workaround for some of these disputes to have a third party telling the government to settle for X, you know? But there are there are settlements that do happen and at times, depending on where you are, for example, in the claim and cost bond process for a seizure, you can get a settlement with the government itself, with the government's lawyer. That's the Office of Chief Counsel for Customs, like Customs' own lawyer, or the Department of Justice if the case is referred to the US Attorney's Office. So, there is like a portion where you can negotiate a settlement per se, but you're doing so with the other side, not with the benefit of a third party. >> It's interesting because mediation has proliferated to all areas, but somehow it's not there, which she would seem to be a good fit um to move things along and maybe it will dispose of even if it disposes of 25% of the cases, that still frees up a lot of time, right? >> I like it. >> Yeah. Well, well, why don't we switch over then? If we're not going to talk about mediation per se, let's talk about negotiation. >> Sure. >> But one of the things I like to ask everybody is what are their top three tips for better negotiation outcomes. Now, you do negotiate. So, if someone has listening someone who is listening has a difficult negotiation on their calendar and maybe they only have about 10 minutes to prepare, give me your top three tips for getting a better outcome. >> Never take no for an answer from someone that does not have the power or authority to say yes. Quite often, you're dealing with a lower level officer and or paralegal and or import specialist and they have a boss who has a boss who has a boss. We get told no consistently and we're like, is that really the final answer? And you ask for supervisors over and over and over again until you get to the right person who can have hopefully a more rational thought process like, no, you can't have this extension or can't have this. Well, really? Can I not? Is that really Is that really the right answer? And when we keep going above and above and above, quite often you get to a more fair answer. What I'm seeing annoyingly is that trend is proving more and more true over the last year or so where enforcement and a hard-handed approach is becoming more and more of the new normal, so you're hearing a lot more noes before you get to the yes. It's it's harder to fight for those yeses. So, goes to the second part. If you're not persistent in my world, it's like being the phone caller who has to call and call and call people and hear the noes and noes and noes, you know. You have to be able to handle rejection and get the hell over it because you're going to hear noes. That doesn't mean that's the final answer, but you have to be persistent. You have to persistently know like where to climb, where to go, and who to go to. And you're often going to hear what you don't want to hear. So, being able to A, not take rejection so seriously. B, go back and keep understanding the the what's the the road map on the the org chart to know who's on top of who and where where the top of the list is. And being able to be persistent enough to not give up because it's really easy to say, all right, the answer is nobody. We got to give up. It's It's unfortunate, but it takes a lot more willpower to keep going and to have more and more of that persistence. But I do find that that pays. And then we often have to analyze trends and see what's working, what's not working. And sometimes we have to change our approach. So, it's I've been filing petitions for 18 years and getting great results on those. And now I'm like, it's taking too long to get back. We got to change our approach. Now we have to file more claim and cost bonds and think about how we're doing things and maybe we have to divvy up, you know, what we're doing and how we're doing it and how we're making these decisions. And depending on the value of the merchandise and what port it is, we're going to have to think differently. And it's being able to shift that strategy consistently. So, it's you have to keep your brain active. You're never resting on your laurels and not knowing who to call, when to call them. So, don't give up. Be persistent. Don't take that no for an answer. Keep up with what's going on in your industry, your trends, and being able to be shifty and change approaches when you need to. And staying stagnant is not going to get you anywhere in my world. >> Yeah. So, don't accept no, persistence, and be flexible. >> I like that. >> up to date. Yeah. Okay, I like that. Very good. Um, how about this one? How do you actually determine or calculate a settlement value for your clients? >> It's a good question. Um, in some instances, I tell my client that you can't put good money after bad. So, for example, we've had instances where an importer says, I went to my customs broker and they gave me bad information. And I'm like, okay. I got it. You feel like you got screwed. You feel like you got crap info. What did you pay for that? Oh, nothing. They just told me. Okay, and you relied on that and did none of your own research in any way, shape, or form. You need a new attorney after that. I mean, I did a damn good job for you. If you have a problem paying that, we're going to we're going to have different words then. You know? So, when you get what I would call great results in line with customs own mitigation guidelines, like customs says if X dollars in currency or C's, you should have X penalty in X range. If you're getting within that range or better, great. I think that's a great result. And I think in my world, it's nice that customs really has guidebooks out. Now, what's interesting is there's a new executive order that just came out and actually in a couple of weeks, there should be new guidelines. And the idea from the government side is they're going to be stricter and they're going to be different and it's going to be harder. And if you're a repeat offender, you're not going to get the same mitigation, for example. We're going to see what those look like, but it's going to be harder potentially to get the settlements that we've been able to get and that mitigation that we've been able to get. So we always start with the benchmark. What are the basics? Where where is the government typically standing? But now we may have to get even more creative because the benchmarks are going to be changing as well. So it it's easy to say if you have X dollars, 4 million, typically the mitigation guidelines are 10 to 30%. That's still 400 grand. But now being able to see what's going to happen towards the end of the year, I think we're going to have a whole different conversation and thought process about the guidelines maybe not being fair after that. So then what are we going to have to do? We're going to have to continue our flexible approach and how we do things thereafter because maybe it's going to have to turn to more litigation than we ever wanted before in order to get that fair result. You know, you start with a penalty petition and then if you don't like your results, you get a supplemental petition considered by a different group of people. And that requires a different outlook and a different strategy like you are you are doing. It's tough to keep up, but it's what you need to do to do a good job. Um well, I think we're at our time, Jennifer. It's been fascinating, but before we close, I want to give you the floor for a minute. One, tariffs, tariffs, tariffs. You know, there are $166 billion on the line and only about a hundred billion of it refunded. You know, some people are leaving money on the line, like they don't want the tariff in some way, shape or form, or they don't know what to do about it or how to get their money back in any way, shape or form. If you hear of anybody who's imported, period, who's paid any IETA tariffs, call Diaz Trade Law ASAP to work on your refund. It's crazy. If you don't want your money, I'll take it. I will help you get it back and I will keep it. If you don't want it, just tell me. I'll do all the work for you. I'll help you get the money back and I'll have it. Makes no sense. Why would you leave money on the table? Why? I I don't get it. I don't get it. And causes, I'm a sucker for animals. So if anybody else loves animals, the Humane Society always has a great walk for the animals, big advocate for adorable animals, adorable rescues, and it's one of those adopt don't shop commercials for me always. So take care of your lovely four-leggens who absolutely save your little hearts because we all need something, you know? It's like I always ask other lawyers and other professionals that are in crazy fun worlds like all of us are, what's your vice? What's your go-to? Or what's your thing? Like what is your outlet in some way, shape, or form? And I find petting a dog is like so therapeutic and delicious, you know? Like what is it that brings you joy? Whether it's looking at birds, petting dogs, playing poker, I don't care. What is it, you know? But like we all need something. And to some crazy people, it's working out. So for me, it's dogs, coffee, and ice cream. So you know, whatever it takes. >> [laughter] >> WHAT A COMBINATION. ALL RIGHT. WELL, I think that's a great place to land. So Jennifer, thank you so much for being here. Um I've learned a lot about tariffs and and all these penalty phases and all these wonderful crazy things that happen at our airports and ports. What Is the Visa Mastercard Settlement Judge Approval Case About? | 2026?

On June 9, 2026, a U.S. judge approved a revised $38 billion settlement between Visa, Mastercard, and merchants who accused the card companies of charging excessive fees for credit card payment processing. This settlement follows a rejected $30 billion deal from two years ago and involves about 18.6 million merchants who submitted claims before a February 2025 deadline. Key changes include allowing merchants to decline certain cards or offer discounts for cheaper options. This landmark case reshapes how interchange fees impact merchants and consumers. videos.full_text: What is the Visa-Mastercard settlement judge approval case about? 2026. What is the Visa-Mastercard settlement judge approval case about? This $38 billion deal could change how merchants handle credit card fees, and it's just been approved after years of legal battles. The heart of this case is a massive $38 billion settlement between Visa, Mastercard, and merchants who claim the card companies charged too much to process credit card payments. This settlement is a revision after a previous $30 deal was rejected by a judge 2 years ago as insufficient. The new amount aims to finally resolve years of litigation and financial disputes over interchange fees. This case affects about 18.6 million merchants across the US who were invited to submit claims for damages ahead of a February 2025 deadline. These merchants alleged that Visa and Mastercard's interchange fees, the charges paid by stores to accept credit cards, were too high, impacting their profits for years. The settlement approval means these businesses can now finally seek compensation. The legal process started with a court approval of the damages portion back in 2019, allowing merchants to send in claims. Nearly 2 years ago, a judge rejected the initial $30 settlement, calling it insufficient. The revised $38 billion settlement was announced last November and has now received final judge approval on June 9, 2026, bringing the long-running litigation closer to a resolution. As part of the settlement, Visa and Mastercard agreed to new rules that give merchants more control. Stores displaying their logos can now decline certain types of credit cards, since interchange fees vary by card. They can also offer discounts to customers who choose cheaper card options. This could change how you pay with plastic at stores, potentially saving merchants and maybe you money. What this means for you is that merchants might start steering you toward cheaper credit or debit cards or offer discounts for using them. This could impact your buying habits and how much you pay at checkout. The $38 billion settlement marks a major win for merchants, but also signals changes in card payment practices. Stay informed and subscribe for updates on how this develops.

metadata.title: WEBINAR - IEEPA Tariff Refunds: Recover Overpaid Duties and Maximize Cross-Border Savings
metadata.author: Leyton USA
metadata.shortDescription:
Originally aired on April 23, join Jean-Daniel Vermette and experts from Descartes to learn how importers can recover overpaid duties under IEEPA tariffs.
With recent legal changes and a new refund mechanism in place, businesses now have a real opportunity to reclaim costs—if they understand the process.
👉 In this session, you’ll learn:
• Why refunds are now possible
• How the CAPE system and ACE portal work
• Key eligibility criteria and timelines
• Common pitfalls to avoid
• How to maximize your refund
💡 A practical session to help you navigate the process with confidence.

metadata.author: Commercial Funding Marketplace
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, we explain the step‑by‑step process of the IEEPA Tariff Refund Buyout and how importers can monetize eligible IEEPA tariff refund claims while reducing timing and regulatory uncertainty.
We walk through how the buyout structure works from start to finish — including how claims are reviewed, why participation agreements are used, and what documentation is required for a claim to move forward. We also explain the role of the importer as the ongoing claimant, how litigation may factor into the process, and what happens once a refund is ultimately issued.
This overview is intended for importers, CFOs, customs brokers, attorneys, and advisors who want a practical understanding of how IEEPA tariff refund claims can be converted into liquidity.
Topics covered include:

What an IEEPA tariff refund buyout is
How the claim participation structure works
Why IEEPA claims are not transferable
Documentation and due diligence requirements
The role of the ACE Portal Customs Report
Litigation considerations, if required
How refunds are received and settled

This video is for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal, tax, or investment advice. Each transaction is subject to documentation review, agreement execution, and applicable legal requirements.
For additional information, visit:

metadata.title: Navigating Duty Drawback Claims for Exported Goods
metadata.author: Scarlett Jones
metadata.shortDescription:
ISF Template | 562-453-7357 | isf@isftemplate.com | www.isftemplate.com

In this video, we'll explore how to handle duty drawback claims for exported goods, providing valuable guidance for exporters and customs brokers navigating the process of seeking refunds on previously paid customs duties. Duty drawback is a mechanism that allows exporters to reclaim duties paid on imported materials used in the production of exported goods. We'll discuss key concepts and procedures involved in filing duty drawback claims, including eligibility criteria, documentation requirements, and the application process. Additionally, we'll examine common challenges and pitfalls associated with duty drawback claims and provide practical tips for maximizing refunds and ensuring compliance with customs regulations. Understanding the duty drawback process is essential for exporters to optimize cost savings and enhance competitiveness in global markets. Join us as we demystify duty drawback claims for exported goods and offer valuable insights for navigating this aspect of international trade. #usimportbond #isfcustomsbroker #uscustomsclearing #isfentry 

Video Disclaimer Here: This video is designed for education and is unaffiliated with US government bodies..

- Alex Nederlof | Sr Director Engineering Customs & Financial Services, Flexport
