metadata.title: Anti-Dumping Duties (ADD & CVD): The Hidden Customs Trap That Bankrupts Importers
metadata.author: Ask The Customs Manager
metadata.shortDescription:
Protect your bottom line by understanding Anti-Dumping Duties (ADD) and Countervailing Duties (CVD) — the hidden customs penalties that can wipe out importers who only think about standard duty rates and VAT. In today’s video, we break down what these punitive duties are, why they matter, how “Scope of the Order” can trap you long after goods enter the country, and the exact steps you should take to avoid catastrophic retroactive bills from Customs.

🔍 What you’ll learn in this video
• What Anti-Dumping Duties (ADD) and Countervailing Duties (CVD) really are — and how governments use them in trade wars
• How ADD/CVD aren’t tied to HS codes, but to written legal scope descriptions
• Why a standard duty rate of 0% doesn’t protect you
• How a post-clearance audit can trigger 50%–300% duties plus interest and fines
• Real-world risks of incorrect product classification
• The importance of requesting a formal Scope Ruling before shipping

👉 Don’t let Customs surprise you with a bill you didn’t plan for.

If you’re serious about global trade compliance, margins, and risk management, we’ve got resources to help you:

✔ Free Expert Call: Speak directly with one of our customs and trade specialists — no obligation.
✔ Professional Training: Practical courses on customs compliance, export controls, sanctions, duty savings, classification, valuation, and more. Many formats available including live online, on-demand, and corporate sessions.
✔ Weekly Newsletter & Trade Intelligence: Stay ahead with regulatory updates, compliance alerts, and strategic insights across the U.S., EU, and UK markets.

Learn how to protect your business, avoid costly audits, and build a compliance framework that works in the real world.

📌 Get full details, tools, training options, and expert support at https://www.customsmanager.org/
 — your hub for customs compliance, risk mitigation, and global trade intelligence.

➡️ Free Expert Call: Book a 30-minute consultation with a customs professional
➡️ Training & Education: Practical, real-world customs courses for importers, exporters, brokers and compliance teams
➡️ Trade Intelligence & Newsletter: Keep up with ever-changing customs, export controls and sanctions

Stay compliant. Save money. Trade smarter. 🚢
#CustomsCompliance #ExportControls #Sanctions #CustomsClearance #TradeIntelligence #CostSaving #CustomsTraining #GlobalTrade #CustomsConsultancy

and you think your standard duty rate is
the only tax you need to worry about,
you are walking into the most lethal
financial trap in global trade. Welcome
back. Today we are talking about a
customs mechanism that literally
bankrupts unprepared importers
overnight. It is not standard import
duty. It is not VAT. It is anti-dumping
and counterveailing duties commonly
known as ADD and CBD. If you have never
heard of these or if you think they only
apply to massive multinational steel
corporations, you need to listen very
carefully because in the current
geopolitical climate, trade wars are
escalating and governments are using
these punitive duties to aggressively
protect their domestic industries from
cheap foreign imports. Let's get the
definition straight. Anti-dumping duties
are applied when a foreign supplier
sells a product in your country for less
than its fair market value.
Counterveiling duties are applied when
that foreign supplers's government is
secretly subsidizing their
manufacturing, allowing them to
illegally undercut local prices. To
punish this, your customs authority does
not just add a 5% or 10% tax. They
impose penalty duties that can range
from 50% to over 300% of the commercial
value of the goods. Imagine buying a
container of aluminum parts for $50,000
and customs sends you a bill for
in taxes. It destroys your business
model instantly.
But here is the real trap that catches
innocent importers, the scope of the
order. Most importers rely entirely on
their HS code. They tell their broker
the HS code. The broker checks the
system, sees a 0% standard duty rate,
and clears the goods. But anti-dumping
orders are not strictly tied to HS
codes. They are tied to a written legal
description of the physical product
known as the scope of the order. You
could be importing a specialized
furniture piece completely classified
under a standard furniture HS code. But
if that item contains a specific type of
extruded aluminum from a targeted
country, it might fall under the scope
of an aluminum extrusion anti-dumping
order. Your HS code won't flag it. Your
broker might miss it. and your goods
will clear customs normally. You might
think you got away with it, but you
didn't. Anti-dumping duties are heavily
audited post clearance. A year later, a
customs investigator reviews your entry,
reads the physical description of your
goods, and realizes it fell within the
scope of an ADD order. They will issue a
retroactive bill for the 250%
penalty duty plus interest plus fines
for a false declaration.
So, how do you protect yourself? You
cannot just trust your supplier and you
cannot blindly trust your freight
forwarders automated software. [music]
If your product is made of metal, wood,
paper, plastics, or certain chemicals,
you must manually check the active
anti-dumping registers in your
destination country. You have to read
the actual text of the scope. If there
is any ambiguity, if you're even
slightly unsure whether your product is
included, you must apply for a formal
scope ruling from the government before
you put that cargo on a ship. A formal
ruling is legally binding and protects
you from surprise audits. Hoping that
customs won't notice your specific
product variation is not a strategy. It
is financial suicide.

metadata.author: NCBFAA Educational Institute

Please join us for this educational webinar on Best Practices for Anti-Dumping and Countervailing Duty (AD/CVD) where you'll hear directly from Alexander Amdur, the Director for AD/CVD Policy and Program Division within the Office of International Trade (OT) at U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CEP). Mr Amdur will be available to answer any AD/CVD questions and provide guidance on a variety of AD/CVD topics including: 
 
 
* Using Ace to manage AD/CVD entries including Post Summary Corrections (PSCs)​

* Due Diligence for suppliers and supply chain involving export-specific rates

* Managing the written scope of AD/CVD orders and estimation of AD/CVD duties due on imports
 
Ad/CVD cases are on the rise with over 452 new petitions filed in 2015, the highest number in over 14 years. CBP has indicated that AD/CVD Enforcement is a top Priority Trade Issue (PTIs) and customs brokers are also ebing held to a higher standard for collecting data from importers when it comes to PTIs such as AD/CVD. Lisa Gelsomino from Avalon Risk Management and co-chair of the COAC Trade Enforcement and Revenue Collection Subcommittee will help moderate the webinar and provide updates from teh COAC AD/CVD Working Group, including new AD/CVD provisions under the Trade Faciliation and Trade Enforcement Act.

segments.text: So welcome to today's webinar! If I were
to ask you what your greatest concern
about anti-dumping and countervailing is,
what would you say? Well I hope that in
today's webinar, as we go over the basics,
I answer a lot of those questions. And if
not, we're going to open up the floor and
try to get some of these answered here today
as well as by licensed Customs Brokers
after the webinar as well. My name is
Tyler Zaichkin, I'm the National Sales
and Marketing Manager at TRG and I have
been working in this industry for just
over five years, learning all I can about
these complex topics. Trade Risk Guaranty,
we are an insurance agency specializing
in international trade.
We've been in business since 1991 and
we're located in beautiful Bozeman,
Montana. Now we do things a little bit
differently;
traditionally in the market the insurance
products that we sell, U.S. Customs bonds
and cargo insurance, are sold through third
parties like a Customs broker or a Freight
Forwarder. Our business model has us
selling directly to importers and
exporters. And over the past 25 years
we've worked with over 13,000 companies
just like yours to help them grow and
save money on some of these very niche
insurance products. Throughout the
webinar we will be monitoring our Facebook
page, Trade Risk Guaranty, as well as our
Facebook group, International
Trade Professionals - TRG. We'll send
you links to both of these after the
webinar as well, we encourage you to join
and come here to discuss with fellow
importers and exporters the different
things you have going on within your day
as well as to get some of your most
common questions answered. So let's get
started! I'm going to start off by saying
you know I've been in this industry for
a long time and we represent a lot of
information here today, but this is just
the basics. And so if you ever have any
questions you're definitely welcome to
come to us here at TRG and we can have
our team of licensed Customs Brokers
answer those questions for you as well
as going directly to your broker who can
help you out as well.
But in today's webinar we're going to be
covering a few topics here;
first we're going to be talking about
what dumping and subsidized exports are,
next we're going to go into the
definition of anti-dumping and
countervailing duties. After that we're
going to cover the history of
anti-dumping and countervailing in the
United States. One of the big, and maybe
the biggest portion, of the webinar
itself is going to be on the petitions
for anti-dumping and countervailing
relief. Now we're talking about the
investigation process, and the
determination of anti-dumping duties and
countervailing duties, as well as the
administrative review and sunset review
process.
Ok so first question; what is dumping?
Well dumping occurs when a foreign
producer sells a product in the United
States at a price that is below that
producer sales price in the country of
origin, their home market. It's either
that or it is selling at a price that is
lower than the cost of production. So a
foreign producers selling imports at
prices below American products is not
necessarily dumping. So just because a
foriegn producer can sell a product at
less than you would buy it here in the United States
from a domestic producer, doesn't
make the import dumping. It's when the
price is below that producers price in
their home market. Subsidized exports are
a little bit different. So although
related, subsidized exports are exports
from industries and products in which
foreign governments
provide financial assistance to benefit
the production, manufacturer, or
exportation of goods. Now this doesn't
mean just a cash subsidy. Subsidies can
take place in many forms such as direct
cash payments, credit against taxes, and
loans at terms that do not reflect
market conditions. So 'dumping' is
rectified with 'anti-dumping duties' and
'subsidized exports' are rectified with
'countervailing duties'.
Let's look at the definition
of both of those. An anti-dumping duty is a
protectionists tariff imposed on
foreign imports believed to be priced
below market value and causing material
harm to the domestic market. Now both of
those conditions must be met; both the
price below market value and causing
material harm to the domestic market.
Countervailing duties are a little bit
different.
They are still a protectionists tariff
imposed on foreign imports but these are
imports believed to be subsidized by a
foreign government, and again, causing
material harm to the domestic market. So
those two criteria must be met for both
anti-dumping duty and countervailing
duty to be applied. So it must
either be priced below market value and
causing material harm or subsidized by a
foreign government and causing material
harm. So anti-dumping specifically goes
back a long way, you know it's something
that that our government has been
working on here in the U.S. since the
1890s to work to rectify the
situation. Now initially in the 1890s
and all the way up to this
Anti-dumping Act of 1916, the focus of
legislation was on antitrust and
monopolies. It was not specifically
about the duties themselves but instead
trying not to have monopolized
industries here in the United States. So
the first act, Anti-dumping Act of 1916
was focused on dumping related to
predatory pricing, pricing that would
force competitors out of an industry. And
it was enforced not through duties but
instead through legal proceedings and
criminal proceedings. So a little bit
different than how we think about it
today, the Anti-dumping Act of 1921,
happening five years later, is a little
bit closer to how we do it today. In fact,
a lot of the acts that we talk about today
are going to be based specifically
on this first Anti-dumping Act of 1921.
So this was focused, instead of on
predatory pricing, instead on just the
discrimination of price.
And instead of enforcing it through
criminal proceedings and legal
proceedings, it was enforced through
higher import duties much like what we
see today. The Tariff Act of 1930
may be something you're more
familiar with as this is still part of
how today's legislation is built. So
originally the Tariff Act of 1930
defined anti-dumping and countervailing
duties under subtitle four. The act
itself authorized investigation of
unfair competition related to these
imports. From there in 1947 the World
Trade Organization came together at the United
Nations conference on Trade and
Employment, and came together to
create an agreement on tariffs and trade.
It's called the General Agreement on
Tariffs and Trade, or GATT 1947. These
specific negotiations and
rulings went into effect on January 1, 1948.
Now the article that they
came up with here, Article 6, was based on
the U.S. Anti-dumping Act of 1921.
So it brought it all together from a
world perspective to keep us all
globally on the same page with anti-dumping
and countervailing. The laws did
change a little bit over time and
different parties became involved in the
United States determining anti-dumping
and countervailing, but major changes
didn't happen again until the Trade Act
of 1974. So this expanded the definition
of dumping to include home market sales
below the average cost of production.
This, again, five years later the Trade
Agreements Act of 1979
made the biggest changes overall and
this is where most of how are our
legislation works today was based on
this Trade Agreements Act of 1979.
So this repealed the
Anti-dumping Act of 1921 and it also
revised the Tariff Act of 1930.
So it got rid of Title Four and
was enacted as Title Seven to the
Tariff Act of 1930.
It shorten the time limits on dumping
and subsidized export investigations and
it allowed the use of best information
available when foreign firms did not
provide requested information. So this
brings us back to today. And as you may
or may not know anti-dumping all
starts with a petition. So let's talk a
little bit about that petition process
and how that begins to affect you as an
importer. So any interested party may
file an anti-dumping, excuse me, not 'any
interested', I'll define 'interested
parties', but an interested party may file
an anti-dumping or countervailing duty
petition... alleging that an industry in
the United States is materially injured
or threatened with material injury or
that the establishment of an industry is
materially retarded by reason of imports
that are being, or are likely to be, sold
in the United States at less than fair
value, or by reason of imports that are
being subsidized by governments of one
or more countries. So let's dissect this
a little bit. First
what parties can file these petitions? So
petitions can be filed by 'interested
parties' including manufacturers,
producers, and wholesalers; domestic
unions, trade associations, and business
associations; in the case of agricultural
products it could be a coalition of
agricultural processors, producers, or
growers; and it could actually be a
coalition of unions or manufacturers
and producers as well. These are U.S.
domestic entities that can file these
petitions. Now the petitions themselves
need to talk about two different
things that are going on, those two items
that we talked about earlier. Is it
dumping or subsidized export? And does it
cause material injury
to the domestic market? So, what is
material injury? It is an injury of
consequence or importance and it
has to be substantial in nature. So this
isn't an injury that would be "oh well it
makes a little bit of a difference to
the industry if there's this ant-dumping".
It has
to be a substantial cause. The next piece
is the fair market value and
this is talking about,
specifically, whether or not those goods
are being sold at below what they would
be sold in their home
country. So less than fair market value
is defined as a price that is below
the sales price in the country of origin,
that home market. When looking at this data,
if that home market data isn't available,
you can use a surrogate
third-country to base your
data off of. Now in the absence of both a
home market and third country data a
cost plus profit constructed value
approach may be used. Now all of these are
used to prove that the imports are
being sold at a price that is less than
the sales price in the country of origin.
So when this petition is filed, it is
filed jointly between two different U.S.
government entities; the U.S. Department of
Commerce and the U.S. International Trade
Commission. They both have different
responsibilities in the petition process
when determining if goods being imported
should be subject to anti-dumping or
countervailing duties. The Department of
Commerce determines whether foreign
producers are dumping goods or receiving
financial assistance to benefit the
production, manufactur, or exportation
of goods. So they're looking specifically
at that portion of it. Is it
dumping? Is it a subsidized export? The
International Trade Commission is
determining whether the domestic
industry is suffering material injury as
a result of the imports of dumped or
subsidized products. So they both have
these different responsibilities and
work together to determine whether or
not goods being imported should have a
tariff imposed for anti-dumping or
countervailing. So here's the process of the
investigation itself. It's a five-point
process starting with an initial
investigation by the Department of Commerce.
I'm not going to go over the exact days
they're all listed here and there are
some adjustments that can be made to
those throughout the process depending
if the company or the
department gets back up or not, but I'm
going to go through the process itself.
So the first part of the process
is this initial investigation and it is by
the Department of Commerce. And what
they're looking for is an initial
indication that foreign producers are
either dumping or receiving financial
assistance, so they are those subsidized
exports? If that does come back in the
affirmative,
then the U.S. International Trade
Commission takes over looking to see
whether that dumping or subsidized
export is causing materials harm. And
they're just doing a preliminary
investigation to see if that harm
is happening. If that comes back in the
affirmative, it moves back to the
Department of Commerce who does the
exact same thing from a standpoint of
whether or not the goods that are receiving
financial assistance are being dumped.
So if the preliminary investigation from
both the USITC and the Department of
Commerce comes back in the affirmative,
then Commerce will initiate their first
preliminary determination and ask
Customs to suspend liquidation of entries
and collect cash deposits based on their
initial estimate of what a duty rate
would need to be. So this is that first
part of the process where your goods are
now suspended and
Customs starts asking you for a cash
deposit for anti-dumping duty and
countervailing duty. The process
does not stop here however, it still goes
under the investigation to a final
determination from both Commerce and the
U.S. International Trade Commission. So
let's look further into that. So from
there, it goes back to Commerce to look
for the final determination and then back to
the USITC for their final determination.
If both Commerce and the International
Trade Commission make affirmative final
determinations of injury, Commerce then
issues an anti-dumping or countervailing
duty order to Customs and Border
Protection.
This is based on that final
determination. At this point cash
deposits must be made at the rates
established in the final determination
for all entries of subject merchandise
on or after the date of the preliminary
determination.
So what that means is that if you haven't
been paying attention, if you haven't been
filing anti-dumping entries, you haven't
been paying these cash deposits; all the
sudden the final determination happens.
Now you are responsible for paying
deposits for all of your past entries up
to that preliminary determination. So
that could be a couple of months that
you've had entries that you weren't
expecting additional duties on, that now
you need to go back and put cash
deposits on. Those entries now are
suspended if you didn't calculate them in
that way and it's something that is
completely unexpected for a lot of
companies. These entries will remain
suspended until the administrative
review period. That's what we're going to
talk about next. So you're goods,
you've imported them, you didn't know
they were subject to anti-dumping or
countervailing, a preliminary
determination was made that they
probably are, you didn't see it,
the final determination was made, and now
all of your entries from a few months
ago that were subject to this
petition are being suspended and asked
for additional deposit on the duty. So,
this is a deposit, when
does the duty get finalized? And that's
the question for a lot of importers.
You see these big anti-dumping duty
rates may be see 30%, or 50%,
or 100% anti-dumping
duty you weren't expecting it and then
you're told it's actually a deposit.
It's actually not the finalized duty but
a deposit on the entry itself. So now you
want to know when does that entry
get finalized? When does it become
liquidated and gets out of the suspended
entries? Liquidate my entry,
let me know what the final
number is. And that happens during an
Administrative Review period. So the
Administrative Review period, it usually
happens annually. And interested parties
must actually request an Administrative
Review annually, if they don't we'll talk
about that here in a second. But
interested parties may annually request an
Administrative Review of anti-dumping
and countervailing orders. This request
must be made in the anniversary month of
the publication of the anti-dumping and
countervailing duty ordered. Commerce
uses this and makes a determination of
the duties to be assessed on specific
entries made during the previous 12
month period or longer for that first
Administrative Review period. So again,
using that example; you're good, you
didn't know they were subject
anti-dumping and countervailing, you got
this additional duty rate, your entries
are suspended, you go through this entire
process, a year later an administrative
review period happens where they
actually decide what the finalized duty
rate will be. So you made your deposits,
they come out the finalized duty rate,
during that process they also review and
establish new cash deposit rates for the
next year for each company. So
anti-dumping duty is not for a country
it's not for a product, although both of those
are included,
they're looking at specific
manufacturers within that as well. So
with that they determine what the
next was going to be the determine what
the rate should have been for the
previous 12 months or longer, and then
have no reviews requested for particular
exporter, entries of that exporter's
merchandise will be assessed at the cash
deposit rate in effect at the time of
entry. So if the review process doesn't
happen for your manufacturer, for your
goods, then they use that cash deposit
rate as the finalized number typically
they're going to look at it, revise it
and it could be something that you get a
refund on your cash deposit or you owe a
little bit more, or significantly more than
what you made in that initial cash
deposit when they do that
Administrative Review. So that's
going to happen for a few years, the
Administrative Review period every year
for a few years, but on the fifth year
Commerce and the United
States International Trade Commission
are going to do a Sunset Review. So since
1995 Commerce and USITC have been
required to conduct a review on the
fifth anniversary of the anti-dumping or
countervailing order. These are
automatically initiated. So 30 days prior
to the fifth anniversary, they're going
to start this review period. Both the
USITC and Commerce, and what the review
period is for is to determine whether
revoking the order would be likely to
lead to continuation or reoccurrence of
dumping subsidies and material injury. So
this is the entire process from start to
finish; it starts with the petition from
the industry, goes all the way through,
anti-dumping orders are issued,
countervailing orders are issued, you're
asked to put a deposit down until the
finalized duty rate is calculated
which happens during that Administrative
Review period. After the Administrative
Review period after, you know, five years
later the Sunset Review happens and they
ask; is this going to continue? The
question is, it really comes down to that
product in that industry and some do,
some don't, some manufacturers decide not
to sell it at that low price, some
continue to sell at the low price, some
products will have anti-dumping, some

know what your goods are and if they are

And so if you ever have any questions you're definitely welcome to come to us here at TRG and we can have our team of licensed Customs Brokers answer those questions for you as well as going directly to your broker who can help you out as well. But in today's webinar we're going to be covering a few topics here; first we're going to be talking about what dumping and subsidized exports are, next we're going to go into the definition of anti-dumping and countervailing duties. After that we're going to cover the history of anti-dumping and countervailing in the United States. One of the big, and maybe the biggest portion, of the webinar itself is going to be on the petitions for anti-dumping and countervailing relief. Now we're talking about the investigation process, and the determination of anti-dumping duties and countervailing duties, as well as the administrative review and sunset review process. Ok so first question; what is dumping? Well dumping occurs when a foreign producer sells a product in the United States at a price that is below that producer sales price in the country of origin, their home market. It's either that or it is selling at a price that is lower than the cost of production. So a foreign producers selling imports at prices below American products is not necessarily dumping. So just because a foriegn producer can sell a product at less than you would buy it here in the United States from a domestic producer, doesn't make the import dumping. It's when the price is below that producers price in their home market. Subsidized exports are a little bit different. So although related, subsidized exports are exports from industries and products in which foreign governments provide financial assistance to benefit the production, manufacturer, or exportation of goods. Now this doesn't mean just a cash subsidy. Subsidies can take place in many forms such as direct cash payments, credit against taxes, and loans at terms that do not reflect market conditions. So 'dumping' is rectified with 'anti-dumping duties' and 'subsidized exports' are rectified with 'countervailing duties'. Let's look at the definition of both of those. An anti-dumping duty is a protectionists tariff imposed on foreign imports believed to be priced below market value and causing material harm to the domestic market. Now both of those conditions must be met; both the price below market value and causing material harm to the domestic market. Countervailing duties are a little bit different. They are still a protectionists tariff imposed on foreign imports but these are imports believed to be subsidized by a foreign government, and again, causing material harm to the domestic market. So those two criteria must be met for both anti-dumping duty and countervailing duty to be applied. So it must either be priced below market value and causing material harm or subsidized by a foreign government and causing material harm. So anti-dumping specifically goes back a long way, you know it's something that that our government has been working on here in the U.S. since the 1890s to work to rectify the situation. Now initially in the 1890s and all the way up to this Anti-dumping Act of 1916, the focus of legislation was on antitrust and monopolies. It was not specifically about the duties themselves but instead trying not to have monopolized industries here in the United States. So the first act, Anti-dumping Act of 1916 was focused on dumping related to predatory pricing, pricing that would force competitors out of an industry. And it was enforced not through duties but instead through legal proceedings and criminal proceedings. So a little bit different than how we think about it today, the Anti-dumping Act of 1921, happening five years later, is a little bit closer to how we do it today. In fact, a lot of the acts that we talk about today are going to be based specifically on this first Anti-dumping Act of 1921. So this was focused, instead of on predatory pricing, instead on just the discrimination of price. And instead of enforcing it through criminal proceedings and legal proceedings, it was enforced through higher import duties much like what we see today. The Tariff Act of 1930 may be something you're more familiar with as this is still part of how today's legislation is built. So originally the Tariff Act of 1930 defined anti-dumping and countervailing duties under subtitle four. The act itself authorized investigation of unfair competition related to these imports. From there in 1947 the World Trade Organization came together at the United Nations conference on Trade and Employment, and came together to create an agreement on tariffs and trade. It's called the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, or GATT 1947. These specific negotiations and rulings went into effect on January 1, 1948. Now the article that they came up with here, Article 6, was based on the U.S. Anti-dumping Act of 1921. So it brought it all together from a world perspective to keep us all globally on the same page with anti-dumping and countervailing. The laws did change a little bit over time and different parties became involved in the United States determining anti-dumping and countervailing, but major changes didn't happen again until the Trade Act of 1974. So this expanded the definition of dumping to include home market sales below the average cost of production. This, again, five years later the Trade Agreements Act of 1979 made the biggest changes overall and this is where most of how are our legislation works today was based on this Trade Agreements Act of 1979. So this repealed the Anti-dumping Act of 1921 and it also revised the Tariff Act of 1930. So it got rid of Title Four and was enacted as Title Seven to the Tariff Act of 1930. It shorten the time limits on dumping and subsidized export investigations and it allowed the use of best information available when foreign firms did not provide requested information. So this brings us back to today. And as you may or may not know anti-dumping all starts with a petition. So let's talk a little bit about that petition process and how that begins to affect you as an importer. So any interested party may file an anti-dumping, excuse me, not 'any interested', I'll define 'interested parties', but an interested party may file an anti-dumping or countervailing duty petition... alleging that an industry in the United States is materially injured or threatened with material injury or that the establishment of an industry is materially retarded by reason of imports that are being, or are likely to be, sold in the United States at less than fair value, or by reason of imports that are being subsidized by governments of one or more countries. So let's dissect this a little bit. First what parties can file these petitions? So petitions can be filed by 'interested parties' including manufacturers, producers, and wholesalers; domestic unions, trade associations, and business associations; in the case of agricultural products it could be a coalition of agricultural processors, producers, or growers; and it could actually be a coalition of unions or manufacturers and producers as well. These are U.S. domestic entities that can file these petitions. Now the petitions themselves need to talk about two different things that are going on, those two items that we talked about earlier. Is it dumping or subsidized export? And does it cause material injury to the domestic market? So, what is material injury? It is an injury of consequence or importance and it has to be substantial in nature. So this isn't an injury that would be "oh well it makes a little bit of a difference to the industry if there's this ant-dumping". It has to be a substantial cause. The next piece is the fair market value and this is talking about, specifically, whether or not those goods are being sold at below what they would be sold in their home country. So less than fair market value is defined as a price that is below the sales price in the country of origin, that home market. When looking at this data, if that home market data isn't available, you can use a surrogate third-country to base your data off of. Now in the absence of both a home market and third country data a cost plus profit constructed value approach may be used. Now all of these are used to prove that the imports are being sold at a price that is less than the sales price in the country of origin. So when this petition is filed, it is filed jointly between two different U.S. government entities; the U.S. Department of Commerce and the U.S. International Trade Commission. They both have different responsibilities in the petition process when determining if goods being imported should be subject to anti-dumping or countervailing duties. The Department of Commerce determines whether foreign producers are dumping goods or receiving financial assistance to benefit the production, manufactur, or exportation of goods. So they're looking specifically at that portion of it. Is it dumping? Is it a subsidized export? The International Trade Commission is determining whether the domestic industry is suffering material injury as a result of the imports of dumped or subsidized products. So they both have these different responsibilities and work together to determine whether or not goods being imported should have a tariff imposed for anti-dumping or countervailing. So here's the process of the investigation itself. It's a five-point process starting with an initial investigation by the Department of Commerce. I'm not going to go over the exact days they're all listed here and there are some adjustments that can be made to those throughout the process depending if the company or the department gets back up or not, but I'm going to go through the process itself. So the first part of the process is this initial investigation and it is by the Department of Commerce. And what they're looking for is an initial indication that foreign producers are either dumping or receiving financial assistance, so they are those subsidized exports? If that does come back in the affirmative, then the U.S. International Trade Commission takes over looking to see whether that dumping or subsidized export is causing materials harm. And they're just doing a preliminary investigation to see if that harm is happening. If that comes back in the affirmative, it moves back to the Department of Commerce who does the exact same thing from a standpoint of whether or not the goods that are receiving financial assistance are being dumped. So if the preliminary investigation from both the USITC and the Department of Commerce comes back in the affirmative, then Commerce will initiate their first preliminary determination and ask Customs to suspend liquidation of entries and collect cash deposits based on their initial estimate of what a duty rate would need to be. So this is that first part of the process where your goods are now suspended and Customs starts asking you for a cash deposit for anti-dumping duty and countervailing duty. The process does not stop here however, it still goes under the investigation to a final determination from both Commerce and the U.S. International Trade Commission. So let's look further into that. So from there, it goes back to Commerce to look for the final determination and then back to the USITC for their final determination. If both Commerce and the International Trade Commission make affirmative final determinations of injury, Commerce then issues an anti-dumping or countervailing duty order to Customs and Border Protection. This is based on that final determination. At this point cash deposits must be made at the rates established in the final determination for all entries of subject merchandise on or after the date of the preliminary determination. So what that means is that if you haven't been paying attention, if you haven't been filing anti-dumping entries, you haven't been paying these cash deposits; all the sudden the final determination happens. Now you are responsible for paying deposits for all of your past entries up to that preliminary determination. So that could be a couple of months that you've had entries that you weren't expecting additional duties on, that now you need to go back and put cash deposits on. Those entries now are suspended if you didn't calculate them in that way and it's something that is completely unexpected for a lot of companies. These entries will remain suspended until the administrative review period. That's what we're going to talk about next. So you're goods, you've imported them, you didn't know they were subject to anti-dumping or countervailing, a preliminary determination was made that they probably are, you didn't see it, the final determination was made, and now all of your entries from a few months ago that were subject to this petition are being suspended and asked for additional deposit on the duty. So, this is a deposit, when does the duty get finalized? And that's the question for a lot of importers. You see these big anti-dumping duty rates may be see 30%, or 50%, or 100% anti-dumping duty you weren't expecting it and then you're told it's actually a deposit. It's actually not the finalized duty but a deposit on the entry itself. So now you want to know when does that entry get finalized? When does it become liquidated and gets out of the suspended entries? Liquidate my entry, let me know what the final number is. And that happens during an Administrative Review period. So the Administrative Review period, it usually happens annually. And interested parties must actually request an Administrative Review annually, if they don't we'll talk about that here in a second. But interested parties may annually request an Administrative Review of anti-dumping and countervailing orders. This request must be made in the anniversary month of the publication of the anti-dumping and countervailing duty ordered. Commerce uses this and makes a determination of the duties to be assessed on specific entries made during the previous 12 month period or longer for that first Administrative Review period. So again, using that example; you're good, you didn't know they were subject anti-dumping and countervailing, you got this additional duty rate, your entries are suspended, you go through this entire process, a year later an administrative review period happens where they actually decide what the finalized duty rate will be. So you made your deposits, they come out the finalized duty rate, during that process they also review and establish new cash deposit rates for the next year for each company. So anti-dumping duty is not for a country it's not for a product, although both of those are included, they're looking at specific manufacturers within that as well. So with that they determine what the next was going to be the determine what the rate should have been for the previous 12 months or longer, and then have no reviews requested for particular exporter, entries of that exporter's merchandise will be assessed at the cash deposit rate in effect at the time of entry. So if the review process doesn't happen for your manufacturer, for your goods, then they use that cash deposit rate as the finalized number typically they're going to look at it, revise it and it could be something that you get a refund on your cash deposit or you owe a little bit more, or significantly more than what you made in that initial cash deposit when they do that Administrative Review. So that's going to happen for a few years, the Administrative Review period every year for a few years, but on the fifth year Commerce and the United States International Trade Commission are going to do a Sunset Review. So since 1995 Commerce and USITC have been required to conduct a review on the fifth anniversary of the anti-dumping or countervailing order. These are automatically initiated. So 30 days prior to the fifth anniversary, they're going to start this review period. Both the USITC and Commerce, and what the review period is for is to determine whether revoking the order would be likely to lead to continuation or reoccurrence of dumping subsidies and material injury. So this is the entire process from start to finish; it starts with the petition from the industry, goes all the way through, anti-dumping orders are issued, countervailing orders are issued, you're asked to put a deposit down until the finalized duty rate is calculated which happens during that Administrative Review period. After the Administrative Review period after, you know, five years later the Sunset Review happens and they ask; is this going to continue? The question is, it really comes down to that product in that industry and some do, some don't, some manufacturers decide not to sell it at that low price, some continue to sell at the low price, some products will have anti-dumping, some won't. So it's really important that you know what your goods are and if they are subject to specific anti-dumping and countervailing duty orders. So we covered a few topics here over the last 20 minutes or so and it really is just the basics. You can see that this is a very complicated, very complex part of this industry. It involves multiple departments; the Department of Commerce, the International Trade Commission, and Customs collecting duties. And it really is something that every important must understand when bringing in goods to the United States. So we covered a few topics today. Again, those are dumping and subsidized exports, anti-dumping and countervailing duty definition, the history of anti-dumping and countervailing duties, petitions for anti-dumping and countervailing relief, investigation and determination from the Department of Commerce and International Trade Commission, that Administrative Review period, and the Sunset Review. I'm sure a few of you are going to have some questions, here are a few different resources that you can access that are going to help answer all of your questions both from a government or legislative point of view as well as a simplified point of view. So I encourage you after the webinar to check out all six of these resources and pay attention to all of those. We are actually going to hold a continuation of this webinar on March 30th so that's five weeks from today exactly the same time 1pm Eastern / 10am Pacific. And we're going to go more in-depth into this topic. Specifically into discussing how to monitor the open petitions, how to calculate what type of cash reserves you should keep to be prepared for that Administrative Review period, how to mitigate your business risk, and a lot more. We're going to invite a few licensed Customs Brokers to be on the call with us to answer some of your more very specific questions. So I encourage you to join us for that. This link here at the bottom http://bit.ly/adcvd-p2 is the link to sign up for that. We're going to be sending that out to everyone as well and again this will be the more in-depth version of what we talked about today. I wanted to take a minute to go over what Trade Risk Guaranty is, again, we are an international trade insurance agency. We work directly with importers and exporters and we've been doing this for 25 years. We've got over 13,000 clients that we work with every day, specifically discussing these complex topics and helping them navigate through this world of Customs. We're an additional resource for them with their Customs Broker and Freight Forwarder. So our model does help save time and money, and our multi-year billing cycles are significantly less, usually on the Customs bond, than what the average would be. Typically people are paying somewhere between $475 and $525 for their Customs bond and we are down to $225 a year with our multi-year pricing on that $50,000 bond. You can continue to work with any broker or forwarder of your choice and then our in-house claims assistance from licensed Customs brokers are going to help you navigate any issues that come up along the way. Thank you so much for coming I can't tell you how much we appreciate it. It's our goal to help educate the import community and make this information as understandable as possible. These are complex topics and when you read the legislation and you read Customs and you read all of these items, it can be very difficult to understand. So it's our goal to simplify this process and specifically give you ways to protect your business and that is what our next webinar is about. So use any of the information provided to contact TRG if you have any questions at all I'd love to either chat with you on the phone or email back and forth, whatever works for you. Again, thank you so much for coming today, we'll have this webinar up quickly and answer as many questions as we can thanks again.

And if a new provision has no corresponding old one, the codifiers simply give it a new section of its own. The 1930 Act carries the most weight. It was moved wholesale into chapter four. And the codifiers opened a new numbering range for it. 1,000 was added to the section numbers of the original Act. Section 321 of the [clears throat] original Act became section 1321 in the code. Section 514 became section 1514. And right here hide the two traps my students fall into most often when they look things up in the code. Trap number one. >> [clears throat] >> Look for a provision in the code using the original act's number and you will never find it. You read in a book about section 305 of the 1930 Act. You turn to 305 in the code. That address does not exist. It actually lives at 1305. Add 1000 first, then look. Trap number two, in the table of contents, you see a number with nothing after it but the word repealed. That is the provision's tombstone. The place is kept, the content is gone. Where did the content go? Two possibilities. Either a later act carried it away to a new address or Congress repealed it, put it to death. To find out which, read the note underneath it about its origin. >> [clears throat] >> In English, the historical and revision notes, it spells everything out. There is also a similar looking word, omitted. That is not a repeal. It means the provision was left out in codification, mostly because it was moved to another title or because it was a one-time transitional provision. >> [clears throat] >> Why are there tombstones? Because the code is arranged in exactly the opposite way from the statutes at large. The original acts passed by Congress are arranged by time. The compiled code is arranged by present ownership, where each provision belongs now. Every living provision has, in the code, a basically fixed position. It is simply updated and reinforced over and over by the provisions of new acts. And every abandoned provision stays forever in the chapter of the act it came from. Those that were carried away move with the new act. Those that were not stay at the old address and slowly become tombstones. Our chapter three in the table of contents titled the tariff and related provisions holds exactly those fragments that were never carried away. They run to section 580 and more than half of them are already repealed. Finally, let me talk about its relationship with the CFR. This is the part that lands on real work and on the exam. I often give my students an analogy. 19 USC is the classical text, the root. Title 19 of the CFR is the plain language version. An operating manual that Customs writes for itself based on the code. Whenever Customs needs a provision for its work, it takes the corresponding text out of the code. It writes it up as operating rules. It compiles it into a part and it adds it to the book called CFR title 19. What it doesn't need, it doesn't take. In recent years, for example, new parts have been added. Parts 149, 165, 182, [clears throat] 190, and others. This explains the biggest puzzle my students run into with the CFR. Why do the part numbers jump? You flip through it. After part 149 comes not 150, but 151. After part 152, it jumps straight to 158. The numbers missing in between are not missing pages. They are reserved spaces. When a new need arises later, a new part is added into an empty space. When a new provision is added to the code or an old one is changed, Customs takes that provision out of the code. It revises it. And it adds it into the corresponding part of the CFR. In recent years, parts 18 and 111, among others, have seen relatively large changes. So, the sequence is this. Congress amends the acts. The codifiers amend the USC accordingly. And Customs amends the CFR accordingly. From now on, when you see a citation in the CFR like issued under 19 USC 1641, you will know which provision of the code it comes from. You can check for yourself. Section 1305 landed in part 12 at section 12.40. Section 1307 landed at sections 12.42 through 12.45. The withhold release orders you see so often these days are right there in those sections. All right, let me sum up today's framework and fix our terminology so it is easy for everyone to follow. An act is what Congress passes, archived word for word in chronological order. The code is what the codifiers compile, provision by provision, classified [clears throat] by subject. A provision, a section, is the individual rule the codifiers extract from the acts and place into the code. And the CFR is the operating manual Customs compiles from the code. With this framework in hand, when you open the code and read the CFR on your own from now on, you won't be confused. And you won't get lost. The attachment to this video is a table of contents of 19 USC that I compiled following this very logic to make your look-ups easier. If you would like to learn more about the Customs Broker Exam, you are welcome to visit my website customsclass.com. >> [clears throat] >> Thank you, everyone.

metadata.shortDescription:
CBP just liquidated your entry at a higher duty rate, and you're sure the classification is wrong. This video maps out, step by step, how to actually challenge that decision, from the first protest filed with CBP all the way into a Court of International Trade lawsuit, including the hard deadlines at every stage.

(410) 220-2800
https://www.fdaimports.com
Serving importers and FDA-regulated businesses nationwide

In this video, Benjamin England breaks down:
What CBP decisions you can challenge, and exactly when the liquidation clock starts
How to file a protest under 19 U.S.C. section 1514, and the 180 day deadline to do it
When to request further review from CBP on a tough legal question
How a request for accelerated disposition can force CBP's hand after two years of waiting
Why you must pay the duties in full before you can sue CBP in court
How to file in the Court of International Trade under 28 U.S.C. section 1581(a)
What evidence actually wins a protest case once you're in front of the court
Why the IEEPA tariff fight follows a completely different track than a classification protest

Benjamin England is a 17-year FDA veteran who served as Regulatory Counsel to the Associate Commissioner for Regulatory Affairs, the top regulatory law role at the agency, and previously worked as a Consumer Safety Officer, Compliance Officer, and Senior Special Agent with the FDA Office of Criminal Investigations. He holds a JD summa cum laude from the University of Miami School of Law and is admitted to the bars of Florida, Maryland, and the District of Columbia, representing importers and FDA-regulated businesses nationwide on trade and regulatory compliance matters.

This video is for educational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. Every case is different. Consult with a qualified attorney about your specific situation.

WATCH NEXT:
BEngland (FDAImports) on the SCOTUS IEEPA ruling
https://youtu.be/7ZCoEhHiI90

The FDA & Customs TRAP That Will Cost You THOUSANDS
https://youtu.be/bC-VRhF9JH0

Chapters:
0:00 Why Customs Deadlines Are Unforgiving
1:40 Know What You Can Challenge and When the Clock Starts
3:20 Filing the Protest
5:30 The Wait, and Forcing a Decision
7:10 Paying First and Filing in the Court of International Trade
8:40 Building Your Evidence and the Realistic Timeline

#CustomsLaw #FDACompliance #CBPCompliance #ImportCompliance #TariffClassification #CourtOfInternationalTrade #TradeCompliance #CustomsProtest #IEEPA #FDAImports #RegulatoryCompliance #FDAAttorney #ImportLaw #CustomsCompliance #PortOfEntry #TradeLaw #BenjaminEngland #FDAVeteran #ImportersRights #CBPLiquidation

segments.text: CBP just liquidated your entry at a higher duty rate.
You're sure the classification is wrong.
So how do you actually fight that decision, from the first filing at CBP all the way into federal court?
That's exactly what this video maps out.
Step by step.
Because the clock generally starts the day that notice posts, although certain entries can legally liquidate before notice is posted.
Miss one step, and CBP's decision becomes final.
Against everyone.
Including you.
Here's why I care about getting this right.
I spent 17 years inside the FDA.
I was a Senior Special Agent with the Office of Criminal Investigations.
I wrote the initial statement of work for PREDICT, the system FDA uses to risk-screen import shipments at the border, and I managed that program.
That's the government side of how FDA-regulated imports get flagged and reviewed at the border, while customs classification disputes like yours go through CBP's separate customs process.
Now I sit on the other side of the table, with importers.
And the number one mistake I see?
Treating a customs dispute like a phone call you'll get around to.
It isn't.
It's a sequence of hard deadlines.
So let's go through them in order.
Step one.
Know what you can challenge, and when the clock starts.
Under 19 U.S.C.

section 1514, CBP decisions on classification, the rate and amount of duty, appraised value, and the liquidation of an entry are final and conclusive unless you protest them, subject to limited statutory exceptions.
For most tariff fights, the trigger is liquidation.
That's CBP's final computation of the duties on an entry.
By statute, CBP generally has one year from the date of entry to liquidate, and it can extend that, up to four years total.
But statutory or court-ordered suspensions can extend liquidation beyond that period.
Here's the trap.
Under CBP's regulations, the date of liquidation for entries actually liquidated by CBP is generally the date the notice is posted on CBP's public website.
Entries deemed liquidated by operation of law can have an earlier effective date.
Not the day your broker emails you.
Not the day you notice the bill.
So watch your entries.
Step two.
File the protest.
Section 1514 gives you 180 days after the date of liquidation to file.
That's the deadline.
Put it on the calendar the day liquidation legally occurs, not the day you finally get around to it.
The protest can be filed electronically in ACE, CBP's Automated Commercial Environment, or on CBP Form 19.
The importer, the consignee, the surety, an authorized agent like your customs broker, or certain other parties authorized by statute can file it.
And what goes in it matters.
The statute requires the protest to set forth, distinctly and specifically, each decision you're contesting, the merchandise affected, and the nature of and reasons for your objection.
Only one protest can be filed per entry, with a limited exception for separate categories of merchandise.
You can amend it to add objections to other decisions.
But only before that 180-day window closes.
Additional arguments supporting a decision already protested can generally be submitted before CBP disposes of the protest.
Step three.
Decide whether to ask for further review.
You can file an application for further review with your protest, inside the same protest period.
It sends your protest to a higher level of review within CBP.
CBP's regulations limit it to certain situations, like a decision that conflicts with an existing CBP ruling, or a legal question CBP or the customs courts haven't ruled on before.
If your case fits, it's worth considering.
Step four.
The wait.
And this is where a lot of importers get stuck.
Under 19 U.S.C.
section 1515, CBP generally has two years from the date you file to allow or deny your protest.
But missing that deadline alone doesn't automatically mean the protest is denied.
Two years.
You do have a lever.
It's called a request for accelerated disposition.
You can send it by certified or registered mail at the same time as your protest or anytime after.
If CBP doesn't allow or deny the protest within 30 days of mailing, the protest is deemed denied by law on day 30.
That deemed denial is your ticket to court, provided you meet the court's filing requirements.
The tradeoff?
Once you request it, you lose the ability to amend the protest.
So get the protest right first.
And remember, your window to go to court doesn't open until there's a denial, actual or deemed.
Step five.
Pay.
This one surprises people.
Under 28 U.S.C.

section 2637, you can only bring a case challenging a denied protest to the Court of International Trade if all liquidated duties, charges, and exactions have been paid when you file, subject to a limited statutory exception for sureties.
You pay first.
Then you fight to get it back.
Step six.
File in the Court of International Trade.
Under 28 U.S.C.
section 1581(a), the CIT has exclusive jurisdiction over civil actions contesting the denial of a protest.
Not your local federal court.
The CIT.
Your deadline, under 28 U.S.C.
section 2636, is 180 days after the date CBP mailed its notice of denial, or 180 days after a deemed denial.
Under the court's rules, a protest case starts with a summons.
The complaint can come later.

The case goes on the court's Customs Case Management Calendar, and you generally have 24 months to file a complaint or otherwise move the case forward, unless you obtain permission to remain on the calendar.
Otherwise, the case can be dismissed for lack of prosecution.
The maximum time on that calendar is 48 months.
Step seven.
Build your evidence.
This is where cases are won and lost.
By statute, CBP's factual determinations are generally presumed correct.
The burden of challenging those determinations is on you, although the court independently decides questions of tariff law.
But here's the good news.
In a protest case, the court makes its decision on the record made before the court.
You're not stuck with whatever was in CBP's file.
You get to build your own record.
So what does that record need?
Your entry summaries and commercial invoices.
Product specifications, drawings, and technical literature.
Samples, if they exist.
Lab or engineering reports showing what the product actually is and how it functions.
Evidence of how it's marketed, sold, and used.
Any CBP rulings on similar merchandise, and every piece of correspondence you had with CBP before liquidation, including requests for information and notices of action.
One more rule.
The court can consider a new argument, but only if it involves the same merchandise and the same decision you protested.
So your protest defines the fight.
A sloppy protest can shrink your case before it starts.
So what's the realistic timeline?
Add it up.
Generally up to a year for liquidation, sometimes longer.
Up to 180 days to protest.
Generally up to two years for CBP to decide, unless you accelerate it.
Another 180 days to file in the CIT.
Then litigation.
And if either side appeals, the case goes to the U.S.
Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit.
You're measuring this in years, not months.
That's why the early steps matter so much.
They're the ones you control.
Now, one important distinction.
Everything I just walked through is the protest track, built for disputes over how CBP applied the law to your entry.
Classification, valuation, the amount of duty.

Whether a tariff was lawful in the first place, like the IEEPA tariffs the Supreme Court struck down in February 2026, is a different fight, generally brought under section 1581(i), with its own two-year deadline measured from when the claim accrues.
Here's the part that trips people up.

CBP has been refunding a lot of IEEPA duties through its own administrative process, called CAPE, not through a protest, and filing a protest on an entry eligible for that process can complicate the refund instead of speeding it up.
Some entries that are already finally liquidated are being handled through litigation in the CIT, while certain refund orders remain on appeal to the Federal Circuit.
CBP has also expanded CAPE to process certain finally liquidated entries covered by court orders.
And in October 2026, the CIT certified a class covering certain importers who paid IEEPA duties but never filed their own lawsuits.
That doesn't automatically guarantee refunds, but it may provide another path to relief.
So if IEEPA duties are your issue, don't assume this roadmap is your path.
Talk to counsel about which track your entries are actually on before you file anything.
Which brings up a question I hear constantly.
If the Supreme Court already ruled, why would you need to file anything at all?
I answered exactly that in another video.

It's called "If You Weren't in the Supreme Court Case, Your Refund May Not Be Automatic: What Importers Need to Do Now." It explains why importers who weren't parties to that case may need their own action in the Court of International Trade, depending on their circumstances.
Watch that next, and then come back to this roadmap.
Because deadlines don't wait for you to figure out which track you're on.

metadata.title: After the Midterms, Can Congress Undo Tariffs? Follow One Toy
metadata.author: Trade Winds Report
metadata.shortDescription:
After the midterms, can Congress actually unwind US tariffs? We follow one tariff line, a box of classroom toys, through the Supreme Court ruling, the Section 122 clock, the longer-lasting Section 232 and 301 tariffs, and the veto math. The short version: refunds go to importers, not shoppers, and the tariffs still in place are the hardest for Congress to remove.

00:00 One toy, one tariff line
01:05 What the Supreme Court did
01:59 Four layers, four off switches
02:34 Refunds go to importers
03:42 The 150-day clock
04:51 The layers that stay
05:33 Congress and the veto math
06:37 Both sides of the ledger
07:41 What changes on your receipt

Sources:
https://www.ey.com/en_us/insights/strategy/macroeconomics/what-the-supreme-court-ruling-against-ieepa-tariffs-means-in-practice
https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/LSB11398
https://www.klgates.com/thought-leadership/Summary-Supreme-Court-Decision-on-IEEPA-Tariffs-2-20-2026
https://www.sidley.com/en/insights/newsupdates/2026/02/us-supreme-court-issues-international-emergency-economic-powers-act-tariff-decision
https://www.wiley.law/alert-Trump-Imposes-Section-122-Tariffs-After-Halting-IEEPA-Tariffs-Previews-New-Section-301-Investigations
https://globaltradealert.org/reports/S122-US-Tariff-Estimates
https://www.skadden.com/insights/publications/2026/05/us-trade-court-strikes-down-section-122-tariffs
https://www.gibsondunn.com/section-122-global-tariffs-invalidated-by-the-court-of-international-trade-ruling-and-next-steps/
https://www.supplychaindive.com/news/cbp-has-paid-100b-in-ieepa-tariff-refunds/827257/
https://www.cato.org/blog/ieepa-refunds-update-good-progress-still-ways-go
https://www.ups.com/us/en/supplychain/logistics-solutions/customs-brokerage/us-customs-tariff-refunds

This video is for general information only and is not investment, legal or financial advice.

segments.text: On paper, a small box of classroom toys
owes nothing at the US border. Toys like
this sit under heading 9503 of the US
tariff schedule, and the base duty on
that tariff line, the code customs uses
to decide what a product owes is zero.
Every cent this box has paid in tariffs
since 2025 was stacked on top of that
zero, and some of it may have reached
the shelf price.
It is the kind of box made by Learning
Resources, the company whose name is on
a Supreme Court tariff case.
Congress can unwind tariffs, but only by
passing a law the President signs or by
finding two-thirds of both chambers to
override a veto. The new Congress is not
sworn in until January 3rd, 2027. Note
that the largest layer on that box was
not removed by Congress at all. It was
removed by a court, and the money went
back to importers, not to the people who
bought the toys.
The detail that matters sits in court
opinions and customs filings, not
campaign speeches.
On February 20th, 2026, the Supreme
Court ruled 6-3 in an opinion by Chief
Justice John Roberts that the
International Emergency Economic Powers
Act, known as IEEPA, does not let a
President impose tariffs.
According to EY's analysis, that ruling
invalidated the IEEPA tariffs on goods
from Canada, Mexico, and China, plus the
global 10% rate and the country-specific
rates.
Note what the court did not touch. EY
points out that the ruling left the
underlying national emergency
declarations in place. The case also
said nothing about the other tariff laws
Congress passed decades ago, which
remain on the books. That is where the
rest of this story lives and where
Congress either has a grip or does not.
So think of the duty on that box as a
stack of four layers, each with its own
off switch. Layer is IEEPA switched off
by the court. Layer five is section 122
of the Trade Act of 1974, which runs on
a clock. Layer three is section 232, the
national security tariffs run through
the Commerce Department. Layer four is
section 301, the unfair trade practice
tariffs run by the US Trade
Representative.
Congress sits above all four, but its
hand rests on each switch differently.
Start with layer one because it shows
what a full unwind looks like in
practice. Customs and Border Protection
built a refund portal called CAPE.
According to Supply Chain Dive, the
agency had paid out $100 billion
in IEEPA refunds by July 31st out of
roughly $166 billion collected.
The CATO Institute estimates refunds
could eventually reach about $130
billion before interest because not
every eligible importer will file.
Follow the cargo and then follow the
check. A refund goes to the importer of
record, meaning the company that cleared
the goods through customs and paid the
duty. If that company raised its shelf
price in 2025, nothing in the law
requires it to cut that price or to pay
you back when the refund lands. Some
importers may pass part of it on where
competitors are cutting, but that is a
business choice, not a legal duty, and
it is the first thing that does not
change on your receipt.
Layer two arrived within hours.
According to Global Trade Alert, the
White House invoked section 122 on the
day of the ruling, and the law firm
Wiley documented a 10% global tariff
taking effect on February 24th. Global
Trade Alert estimated the trade-weighted
average US tariff was about 11.3% before
the ruling, 8.1% with IEEPA gone, and
11.4% once the new 10% layer went on.
Section 122 was written for balance of
payments problems, and it carries two
built-in limits. The rate is capped at
15% and it lasts 150 days unless
Congress passes a law to extend it. That
makes it the one tariff tool where
Congress holds the off switch simply by
doing nothing.
Separately, on May 7th, the Court of
International Trade ruled that the
Section 122 tariff was not authorized
either. Though the law firm Scadden
noted the relief covered only three
importer plaintiffs and the ruling's
fate on appeal was uncertain.
Layers three and four are the durable
ones and neither was before the Supreme
Court. Section 232 lets the Commerce
Department find that certain imports
threaten national security, after which
the president can set tariffs, as with
steel, aluminum, and cars. Section 301
lets the trade representative
investigate another country's trade
practices and it is the tool behind most
tariffs on Chinese goods since 2018.
Both require an investigation and a
paper record, which makes them slower to

It is the kind of box made by Learning Resources, the company whose name is on a Supreme Court tariff case. This video clarifies which tariffs are eligible for refunds, detailing effective dates for Fentanyl, Reciprocal, and APAP tariffs. What IEEPA tariffs cover (including fentanyl-related tariffs, reciprocal tariffs, and measures affecting countries like Brazil, Russia, and Venezuela)
How to identify eligible refunds using HTS Chapter 99 codes

The difference between:
Unliquidated entries (still adjustable)

metadata.title: Why Tariff Refunds Go to Importers, Not Shoppers
metadata.author: The Wax Seal
metadata.shortDescription:
In February, the Supreme Court ruled the IEEPA tariffs were not authorized. Now the refunds are being paid, with interest. But CBP says it can send that money only to the importer, or a party the importer names. Not to the shoppers who paid the higher prices.

So who actually paid, and where is the money going? Walmart says it received about $2.9 billion and cut prices on thousands of items. Amazon says it largely absorbed the tariff costs. Costco and Dollar Tree have reported hundreds of millions in refunds, and customers have sued both, saying shoppers should get that money. Nintendo, Sony and Microsoft face lawsuits from gamers who say they paid the tariffs through higher console prices.

We follow the money from the Supreme Court ruling to CBP's refund system, through what each company says it did with its refund, to an Atlanta Fed survey where 70% of firms said they expect to keep at least some of it as cash.

The lawsuits' claims are allegations, not court findings. Company figures are as the companies reported them.

Sources: the Supreme Court's ruling, CBP's refund pages, court filings, company earnings reports, Atlanta Fed research and news reporting.
News clips are shown briefly for commentary; all rights remain with their owners.

metadata.title: $126 Billion Tariff Refund — Will YOU Get Any Money?
metadata.author: Border & Bench
metadata.shortDescription:
The Supreme Court ruled that President Trump's IEEPA tariffs were unlawful—but does that mean Americans will get a tariff refund?

About $126 billion in tariff refunds had been certified and sent to the Treasury for payment as of October 2, 2026. But the money is not automatically going to shoppers.

In this video, we explain who qualifies for tariff refunds, how the CBP CAPE refund system works, and why importers—not ordinary consumers—generally receive the money. We also cover the October 8 court decision, the roles of FedEx, UPS, and DHL, consumer lawsuits, and what you can do if you paid duties on a package.

**In this video:**
- The Supreme Court's tariff ruling
- What happened to Section 122 and Section 301 tariffs
- How the $126 billion refund process works
- Who receives tariff refunds
- FedEx, UPS, and DHL refund policies
- The October 8 class certification decision
- What consumers and businesses should do next
- Three common tariff refund myths

**Important:** There is no general tariff rebate check for every American. Refund eligibility depends on the circumstances, and class certification does not guarantee that consumers will receive money.

This video is for informational purposes only and is not legal or financial advice. Check official court filings and Customs and Border Protection updates for the latest information.

metadata.title: What Is an HTS Code? | U.S. Tariff Classification Explained
metadata.author: Straightforward ITC
metadata.shortDescription:
What is an HTS code, and why does getting it right matter for U.S. imports?

An HTS code is the classification used to identify imported merchandise under the U.S. Harmonized Tariff Schedule. The code can affect duty rates, additional tariffs, special tariff provisions, statistical reporting, and other import requirements.

In this video, we explain the core concepts behind HTS classification, including:
- What an HTS code is
- How the 10-digit U.S. classification structure works
- Why classification affects more than just duty
- How the General Rules of Interpretation apply
- Why product details such as material, function, construction, and use matter
- Common mistakes, including relying on supplier codes or keyword searches
- Why old or similar-product classifications may not always be reliable

HTS classification is not simply a matter of finding the description that sounds closest. It requires reviewing the tariff language, relevant notes, product facts, and applicable classification rules.
Straightforward ITC’s HTS Code Sanity Check helps review code validity, product-to-code fit, classification red flags, reporting requirements, and areas that may need further review.

Explore the tool at straightforward-itc.com/hts-sanity-check

Important limitation: Straightforward ITC is a technology platform for trade compliance support. It is not a law firm, customs broker, or trade consulting firm, and its outputs are not legal, brokerage, or consulting advice. Results should be independently reviewed.

HTSUS CLASSIFICATION
Your Guide to Classifying Goods for Customs 

The Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) is the primary resource for determining tariff classifications for goods imported into the United States.  Classifying your goods can be tricky because parts and accessories can be classified in many different areas of the HTS.  Accurate classification is crucial for maintaining proper importing records and avoiding potential fines.  Join us to learn how to classify your goods correctly, the first time.

In This Webinar, You’ll Learn:
- Classification basics
- Understanding the General Rules of Interpretation
- Key definitions
- Tips for accurate classifying

For resources visit https://starusa.org/on-demand-webinars/htsus-classification/

Duty Optimization Through Tariff Engineering and HTS Classification
Flexport Webinar
October 3, 2024

Join Flexport for an insightful webinar that delves into the strategic practices of HTS Classification and Tariff Engineering– essential tools for importers seeking to optimize their duties and enhance profitability. In this session, we’ll break down the steps to developing a robust customs compliance strategy, starting with the foundation of accurate product classification.

Discover how understanding the Harmonized Tariff Schedule (HTS) can lead to significant cost-saving opportunities. Learn how to navigate its complexities and identify the right tariff codes to ensure compliance while leveraging the nuances of classification for tariff optimization.

Speakers:
- Jenn Park | Director, Trade Advisory, Flexport
- Beny Sirkin | Senior Trade Advisory Associate, Flexport

metadata.title: CBP ENFORCEMENT IS EVOLVING — AND CUSTOMS BROKERS AND IMPORTERS NEED TO PAY ATTENTION.
metadata.author: Simply Trade Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
In the October NCBFAA President’s Recap, Lori Mullins sits down with NCBFAA President Karen Damon to break down some of the biggest issues facing customs brokers, freight forwarders, importers, and trade compliance professionals.

Fresh off NCBFAA’s sold-out Government Affairs Conference, Karen shares what stood out from conversations with government officials and policymakers — and why advocacy on Capitol Hill matters to the trade community.

The conversation also examines CBP’s increased focus on enforcement and the growing role of the licensed customs broker as a “force multiplier” supporting trade facilitation, security, data accuracy, compliance, and revenue collection.

Plus, there’s an important deadline every licensed customs broker needs on their radar:

The 2027 Licensed Customs Broker Triennial Report and continuing education requirements.

Karen also looks ahead at two issues she believes the industry will still be talking about six months from now:

➡️ Supply-chain tracing
➡️ CTPAT obligations affecting customs brokers

If you work in customs brokerage, freight forwarding, importing, exporting, logistics, supply chain, or trade compliance, this episode is for you.


⏱️ CHAPTERS

00:00 Welcome to the October NCBFAA President’s Recap
00:58 Welcome NCBFAA President Karen Damon
01:03 NCBFAA Government Affairs Conference recap
01:20 What stood out from the Government Affairs Conference
02:00 Why advance notice on tariffs matters
03:09 Taking the trade industry’s message to Capitol Hill
04:09 Why customs brokers are a “force multiplier” for CBP
05:12 Increased CBP enforcement — what brokers should watch
05:28 Importer records, bonds & supply-chain transparency
06:25 Keeping up with rapid regulatory changes
06:44 How NCBFAA keeps members informed
07:28 What happens behind the scenes at NCBFAA
07:57 Committees, advocacy, toolkits & regulatory monitoring
09:42 Preparing for the 2027 customs broker triennial
10:58 The continuing education challenge
11:52 Don’t forget licensed customs brokers working for importers
12:08 Why NCBFAA member participation matters
12:25 How to get more involved
13:32 What will trade be talking about six months from now?
14:16 Supply-chain tracing and CTPAT obligations
16:07 What’s coming next from NCBFAA


🔗 RESOURCES

National Customs Brokers & Forwarders Association of America (NCBFAA)

Simply Trade brings the trade community together for conversations about customs compliance, international trade, tariffs, importing, exporting, freight forwarding, logistics, supply chain, and the regulatory issues affecting businesses every day.

Simply Trade is presented by Global Training Center.
