What trade issue do YOU think we’ll still be talking about six months from now?

Supply-chain tracing? CTPAT? Tariffs? CBP enforcement? Something else?

Tell us in the comments.

um to network and get involved there and

the executive order is a is a
three-legged stool. So, we have enhanced
and enforced responsibilities placed on
the importer,
the customs broker, and CBP.

evolve, we shall watch where the

premise of the executive order. I have
two things we'll be talking about six

order.

trade professionals, please file

- Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States 
- Title 19, Code of Federal Regulations

- ACE Entry Summary Business Rules and Process Document (Trade-External)

- reviewed by licensed Customs Broker 

If you want to pass the Customs Broker Licensing exam, contact Kenvic Training at 1-888-939-6996 for a trial class.

metadata.title: What Importers Get Wrong About US Customs (And It's Expensive) | Expert's Guide for Beginner
metadata.author: Trade Counsel
metadata.shortDescription:
What actually happens between ordering from a Chinese factory and getting the goods into your US warehouse? We follow one $10,000 order of plastic storage bins step by step: who the importer of record is, the HTS code, how the China tariffs stack up today (3.4% + 7.5% + 12.5% = 23.4% on our example), why US duty is charged on the goods and not the freight, the bond and broker, the Importer Security Filing deadline, which goods can be stopped, the 15-day and 10-working-day entry deadlines, and when the duty becomes final.

Chapters
0:00 A $10,000 order from China
0:31 Who is the importer of record?
1:00 The HTS code
1:29 The China tariff stack
2:21 Duty on the goods, not the freight
2:47 Importer number, bond and broker
3:16 The Importer Security Filing (24 hours before loading)
3:52 Can the goods come in? Agencies, origin marking, UFLPA
4:21 Entry, release and CBP Form 7501
4:50 When the duty becomes final
5:09 Four things to settle before your first order

Importing into the US (this series)
- Finding the right HTS code (next)
- Working out your duty
- Bill of lading, explained
- CBP Form 7501, box by box
- Getting overpaid duty back
On this channel: Incoterms: all 11 rules explained

Rates and rules as of 12 November 2026. The storage-bin order is an example; your own HTS code decides your rates.

Sources
- CBP CSMS #69326983 (23 Jul 2026), Section 301 forced labor import duties (China: 12.5%, HTS 9903.05.31)
- USTR, Notice of Actions in Section 301 Investigations (forced labor), 23 Jul 2026, Annex II
- HTSUS 3924.90.56.50; 9903.88.15 (Section 301, List 4A)

metadata.title: 11 19 2025 SmarTrade Fundamentals 2 25 Duty Drawback Opportunities
metadata.author: Thompson Hine LLP
metadata.shortDescription:
Please join us for a complimentary webinar series focusing on the basics of import regulation and customs compliance. In past years, our SmarTrade Fundamentals series explored a range of international compliance areas, including import, export, and sanctions. 2025 has seen an enormous shift in the tariff landscape and a related need for companies to dive deeply into import compliance. So, this year’s SmarTrade Fundamentals 2025 focuses on tariffs, import compliance, and trade remedies.

Our sessions will lay the groundwork with overviews of the administration’s trade actions in the first 200 days and evolving tariff evasion enforcement in the U.S. and EU. Additional sessions will focus on key areas of risk and opportunity to reduce duty exposure in this shifting landscape while maintaining compliance. Through these focused sessions, participants will gain the tools to anticipate regulatory change, manage risk, and unlock value in their trade operations.

Session 4: Duty Drawback Opportunities
Duty drawback remains one of the most effective cost-savings tools for U.S. importers and exporters. This session provides an overview of the program, compliance requirements, and practical considerations for maximizing refunds. We’ll also share tips for streamlining the claims process.

Presenters:
Samir Varma, Partner, Thompson Hine
Aaron C. Mandelbaum, Associate, Thompson Hine

metadata.title: Duty Drawback-Beyond the Basics
metadata.author: World Trade Center Denver
metadata.shortDescription:
Many companies assume they don't qualify for drawback because they don't directly export goods. Others think the process is too complex for their business model. Both assumptions leave significant money on the table. 

This webinar is part of the Colorado Tariff Navigation Series and will be an interactive discussion to learn how organizations like yours are recovering up to 99% of import duties on goods that leave the U.S. We’ll cover: 

• The three types of drawback and use cases.
• How to identify drawback opportunities, and broker cooperation, among various supply chain participants.
• How to calculate your potential refunds of import duties over the past 5 years.

Presenter:  Trisha Paige, Drawback Compliance Specialist, CITTA Brokerage

A licensed customs broker, Trisha Paige has broad expertise spanning duty drawback operations, regulatory compliance, and client advocacy. A CITTAzen since 2019, she began her journey as a drawback manager before focusing exclusively on compliance. Since then, she has presided over more than 500 Customs and Border Protection audits and claim reviews. She also works closely with new clients to navigate the complexities of assembling and submitting drawback applications. In her free time, she enjoys reading, writing short stories, and listening to music.

segments.text: Hello, I'm Alice, your virtual drawback
assistant.
Today we will be discussing the topic,
what is duty drawback?
Duty drawback is a trade refund program
administered by US Customs and Border
Protection.
It provides refunds of duties, fees, and
taxes paid on imported merchandise that
is later exported or destroyed.
Established in 1789, it's the oldest
trade refund program in US history.
Drawback is retroactive for 5 years from
the date of importation. Often this
creates a significant windfall of refund
opportunities for firsttime claimants
and it refunds 99% of duties, fees, and
taxes while customs keeps 1%.
Here's an example. A company imports
sunglasses into the United States and
pays duties and fees to Customs and
Border Protection.
The company then consolidates the
sunglasses in their warehouse. Some are
sold in the United States and others are
sold to customers abroad and exported.
The exported sunglasses are matched to
earlier duty paid imports and a drawback
claim is filed with Customs and Border
Protection allowing the company to
receive refunds.
Let's dig a little deeper into drawback.
Next, we'll talk about matching methods.
A drawback matching method is how a
qualifying export is paired with a
previous duty paid import. There are two
ways to do this. Direct identification
and HTS level substitution.
First up is direct identification.
The simplest way to think about it is
matching imports to exports at the part
skew or material level. To compliantly
use this method, customs requires lot or
serial number tracing.
For example, a vehicle has a unique
serial or VIN number. That number allows
the import to be tracked into inventory,
show being withdrawn from inventory, and
then exported. The item maintains its
identity throughout the process, and
that's what we call explicit matching.
But what about retail apparel? Clothing
doesn't come with serial numbers. In
cases like this, customs allows
companies to use a drawback accounting
method. This is essentially a structured
way of turning inventory for drawback
purposes when law or serial tracing
isn't possible.
The second matching method is HTS level
substitution.
With this method, duty paid imports can
be matched to qualifying exports that
share the same 8 or 10digit
classification.
That's right, we can ignore part numbers
entirely.
domestic, manufactured or even duty-free
exports can be substituted against duty
paid imports if they have a qualifying
HTS match. This method offers broader

segments.text: Welcome to this BGI Worldwide Logistics
training on how to generate your IEPA
duty report in the ACE portal.
In this tutorial, we'll walk through
each step from logging in to exporting
your report so you can identify entries
eligible for potential duty refunds.
Once you're logged into the ACE portal,
start by selecting accounts from the
main menu.
Then click importer.
This displays all importer accounts
linked to your login.
Click the account name you'd like to
generate a report for.
After selecting your importer account,
look to the top right corner and click
the reports button.
The BI launchpad will open.
Next, scroll down and click web
intelligence.
Keep the default options SAP BI platform
and universe selected, then click okay.
Next, select entry summary as your
report universe and click okay again.
The query panel is where you'll build
your report.
Use the search bar to find data elements
like entry summary date.
Add this field to both result objects
and query filters.
To focus on IEPA related entries, set
your filter to greater than January 1st,
2025 and click okay.
Now that you've set your filter, add the
data you need.
HTS number full, liquidation status, and
liquidation date.
When ready, click the run button to
generate your report.
Once your report appears, you can view
it on screen or export it.
Click the three dots in the upper left
corner, select export, and choose Excel.
Make sure the reports option is checked,
then click export again.
Your Excel file will download
automatically.
In your Excel file, review these key
columns.
HTS number, full, to identify I EPA
related duties, liquidation status to
confirm entry status and liquidation
date to track the 180-day protest
deadline.
To save time in the future, click save,
choose save as, and select personal
folders.
Name your report and click save.
You can access it later in the BI launch
pad under folders.
That's it. You've successfully created
and exported an I EPA duty report in
ACE.
For more trade compliance guidance,
visit BGI Worldwide Logistics online at
bgiworldwide.com
or call us at 800-987-4244.

metadata.title: BorderConnect Virtual Workshop - ACE eManifest
metadata.author: BorderConnect
metadata.shortDescription:
In this workshop we’ll be joined by BorderConnect Account Managers Egzon Muriqi and Justin Guerard as they guide you through how to register for ACE with BorderConnect, show you a detailed walkthrough of creating and submitting an ACE eManifest as well as some additional items, such as other software features, where to find helpful training resources, common shipment types used in ACE and much more.

The Automated Commercial Environment (ACE) is U.S. Customs and Border Protection’s (CBP) electronic manifest program and it’s intended to provide Customs officers with electronic pre-arrival information. For highway carriers, it involves filing an electronic manifest through CBP’s portal or with a service provider such as BorderConnect in advance of the driver arriving at the port of entry. 

The ACE program became mandatory for all carriers in 2007 where all highway carriers had to transmit their trip and shipment information electronically to CBP and failure to do so could result in a monetary penalty issued by CBP.

BorderConnect became one of the first third-party service providers to launch their own ACE eManifest solution in 2007, providing customers with a user-friendy software that had benefits and features outside the scope of the ACE data portal that made it an industry-staple for thousands of cross-border carriers.

Topics Covered in the workshop include:

- What is the difference between ACE and ACI?
- Who needs to file ACE eManifests
- Getting Started with ACE eManifest
- Common shipment types required for ACE
- BorderConnect ACE eManifest walkthrough (with PAPS)
- Helpful software features
- How to fix or correct your ACE eManifests
- ACE Training Resources

For more information on BorderConnect ACI eManifest: https://www.borderconnect.com/ace-e-manifest/ace-manifest-requirements.htm

BorderConnect ACE eManifest Software User Guide: https://wiki.borderconnect.com/index.php/ACE_Manifest_Software_User_Guide_(CBP)

Acceptable v. Unacceptable Commodity Descriptions for ACE: https://www.cbp.gov/trade/basic-import-export/e-commerce/examples-unacceptable-vs-acceptable-cargo-descriptions

Download eManifest App for iOS: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/emanifest-app/id1620694667

Download eManifest App for Android: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.borderconnect.app

BorderConnect YouTube Channel: https://www.youtube.com/@BorderConnect

BorderConnect Support Wiki: https://wiki.borderconnect.com

ACE Manifest • ACI eManifest • RNS PARS Tracking • eManifest API • U.S. In-Bond Manager • 24/7 eManifest Support and Processing • Customs Consulting

Sign up for a free 45-day software trial using special promo code EASY45 at https://www.borderconnect.com

metadata.title: Why Tariff Refunds Go to Importers, Not Shoppers
metadata.author: The Wax Seal
metadata.shortDescription:
In February, the Supreme Court ruled the IEEPA tariffs were not authorized. Now the refunds are being paid, with interest. But CBP says it can send that money only to the importer, or a party the importer names. Not to the shoppers who paid the higher prices.

So who actually paid, and where is the money going? Walmart says it received about $2.9 billion and cut prices on thousands of items. Amazon says it largely absorbed the tariff costs. Costco and Dollar Tree have reported hundreds of millions in refunds, and customers have sued both, saying shoppers should get that money. Nintendo, Sony and Microsoft face lawsuits from gamers who say they paid the tariffs through higher console prices.

We follow the money from the Supreme Court ruling to CBP's refund system, through what each company says it did with its refund, to an Atlanta Fed survey where 70% of firms said they expect to keep at least some of it as cash.

The lawsuits' claims are allegations, not court findings. Company figures are as the companies reported them.

Sources: the Supreme Court's ruling, CBP's refund pages, court filings, company earnings reports, Atlanta Fed research and news reporting.
News clips are shown briefly for commentary; all rights remain with their owners.
Photos: Kjetil Ree, 颐园居, Ajay Suresh, Beyond My Ken, Another Believer, Sam Wheeler, Tokumeigakarinoaoshima, Crisco 1492, Osh33m, Der. Bellemer, Louiemantia, Harrison Keely, Nielsoncaetanosalmeron, Aaron F. Stone, Tony Webster, Tim Evanson, KittensMittens2, AgnosticPreachersKid, APK, G. Edward Johnson (CC BY / CC BY-SA, Wikimedia Commons).

According to her lawsuit, the retailer used red stickers to mark items affected by tariffs, with some prices up as much as $1.75. In February, the Supreme Court ruled those tariffs were not authorized. Now, the refunds are being paid. On a government page, one question asks whether refunds go to shoppers. The answer names only the importer. Whether shoppers paid part of those tariffs through higher prices is the argument now playing out in courts and on earnings calls. This is the story of how a tariff can be ruled unauthorized and refunded with interest to importers and what the companies that got the money say they did next. In 2025, President Donald Trump declared national emergencies and imposed tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, a law enacted in 1977. Its initials are IEEPA. The Supreme Court's opinion lists what was imposed. There was a 25% duty on most Canadian and Mexican imports and a 10% duty on most Chinese imports. There was also a duty of at least 10% on all imports from all trading partners. On February 20th, 2026, in Learning Resources versus Trump, the court held that IEEPA does not authorize the president to impose tariffs. The vote was 6 to 3. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote the opinion, and in a section joined by two other justices, he wrote that the law, quote, contains no reference to tariffs or duties, end quote. Roberts also described how a tariff works. Tariffs, he wrote, quote, operate directly on domestic importers to raise revenue for the Treasury, end quote. Three justices dissented, Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito, and Brett Kavanaugh. Kavanaugh wrote a warning about what would come next. Quote, the United States may be to refund billions of dollars to importers who paid the IEEPA tariffs, even though some importers may have already passed on costs to consumers or others. As was acknowledged at oral argument, the refund process is likely to be a mess. End quote. A law firm summary says the ruling did not itself establish a universal administrative mechanism for refunding duties already collected. That work fell to the Court of International Trade, where Judge Richard Eaton oversees the refund cases and the Customs and Border Protection. CBP built a refund system inside its online trade portal and called it Cape. It opened on April 20th, two months after the ruling. Only the importer of record or an authorized customs broker that filed the entries can file a request. A notify party is a party the importer designates on a CBP form to receive its refund. Marketplaces summary. Refunds are only supposed to go to the people or businesses who directly imported a product. CBP says it charges no fee and that refunds are generally issued within 60 to 90 days after a request is accepted. Interest is part of it. CBP's page says, quote, Yes, interest will be included in your IEEPA duty refund. End quote. According to filings in the Court of International Trade, more than 330,000 importers paid IEEPA tariffs on more than 53 million shipments, Newsweek reported. A law firm says a CBP official's court declaration put refunds at about $126 billion by October 2nd. So CBP names the payee, the courts set the process, and a Supreme Court justice wrote on the day of the ruling that the refund process was likely to be a mess. None of that says what happened to prices. To see how that argument sounds when a company makes it, start with Nintendo, which has addressed the question in a court filing in its quarterly results and in a sale announcement. In 2025, Nintendo raised prices on several Switch products, citing market conditions, USA Today reported. The original Switch rose $40 to $339.99, and the OLED model rose $50 to $399.99. In May 2026, Nintendo announced the Switch 2 would rise from $449.99 to $499.99 on September 1st, again citing market conditions. USA Today also reported Nintendo has said its pricing decisions took into account memory, labor, shipping, and tariffs. In April, two customers filed a proposed class action against Nintendo of America in federal court in Washington State. According to the complaint, Nintendo engaged in unfair acts by, quote, raising prices due to tariffs, failing to disclose that it intended to seek tariff refunds, and retaining tariff refunds despite having passed the costs to its customers, end quote. Those are allegations, not findings. Around July 20th, Nintendo asked the judge to dismiss the case. Its lawyers wrote that the plaintiffs, quote, received exactly what they paid for, Nintendo products that plaintiffs knowingly and voluntarily purchased at the advertised price, end quote. And, quote, nor is there anything unjust about Nintendo retaining money that it may receive from the government as tariff refunds, end quote. Lawyers at Holland & Knight listed defenses that businesses could raise in cases like this, that unjust enrichment is often unavailable where an express contract governs and that the charges were imposed while the tariffs were still legally in effect. On August 6th, Nintendo published its results for April through June. They contained two sentences about the refunds. The company wrote that it recorded approximately $300 million US dollars as a reduction of cost of sales in connection with refunds of IEEPA tariffs. And then it wrote this, quote, the blog post related to the refunds were primarily born by the company rather than passed on to consumers through product prices, end quote. On September 10th, Nintendo of America announced a customer appreciation sale, 30% off dozens of Switch digital games and bundles, September 12th through 26th. The announcement said the sale was, quote, made possible in part by tariff-related refunds. While Nintendo absorbed most tariff-related costs, the refunds helped make promotions like this one possible, end quote. The sale has ended. So there are three statements on the record. The plaintiffs allege the costs were passed on. Nintendo's filing says customers got what they paid for at the advertised price. And Nintendo's own results say the tariffs were primarily born by the company. As of Game Files September 3rd report, judges had not ruled on the motions to dismiss in the console cases. Nintendo is not alone. Lawyers at Foley & Lardner counted more than 100 proposed consumer class actions since the ruling as of July 9th, filed in more than 30 federal districts. The next case is one in which the defendant's lawyers pointed to something that happened after the ruling. In August 2025, Sony raised the recommended US price of the PlayStation 5. Its blog post said, quote, we continue to navigate a challenging economic environment, end quote. The post does not mention tariffs. In May, two PlayStation owners sued Sony in federal court in California. Their complaint says Sony, quote, is poised to be paid twice for the same unlawful tariff burden, once by its customers through elevated prices and once by the US government through tariff refunds, end quote. Those are allegations. On August 31st, Sony's lawyers asked the court to dismiss it. They wrote, quote, paying fair market price for voluntarily purchased consumer goods is not a legally cognizable injury in fact, end quote. They called the tariff link, quote, speculative and illogical, end quote, and listed other possible factors such as inflation, currency, component costs and demand. In March, after the Supreme Court ruling, Sony announced another price increase, citing, quote, continued pressures in the global economic landscape, end quote. Sony's lawyers argued that if tariffs had caused the earlier increase, one would expect the company to lower prices once the tariffs were eliminated, not raise them again. Judges had not ruled on that argument as of Game File's September 3rd report. Microsoft made a similar argument on August 21st in a case brought in July by an Xbox owner. Its lawyers wrote, quote, there is nothing unjust about plaintiff purchasing an Xbox at an advertised price and getting exactly what he paid for, end quote. Legal experts see difficulty for the plaintiffs. Class action attorney Jonathan Shub told Marketplace, quote, there isn't really a legal obligation to reduce prices if costs decrease later in our free market, end quote. Panic, the small company that makes the Playdate handheld, said it will pass its refunds onto customers. Game File called it the only gaming hardware maker to have made such a pledge as of September 3rd. Beginning in July, companies started saying on earnings calls and in filings how much they had received and what they planned to do. Their answers do not line up in one direction. Later, the Atlanta Fed put a number on how common each answer is. Walmart's chief financial officer, John David Rainey, said Walmart had received substantially all of the $2.9 billion in refunds it was eligible for. He said, quote, >> taken a disciplined approach to investing these funds back into customer experience and price leadership. >> Walmart said it cut prices on items and rolled back prices on 11,000. Tufts University economist William Masters told Marketplace he does not expect those price cuts to last forever and called them an end of summer promotion. Amazon said it received about $600 million in the second quarter. Its finance chief, Brian Olsavsky, said Amazon is not the importer of record for most items sold on its site. Olsavsky said, quote, >> These is where we did see an increase in costs due to tariffs. We largely absorbed these costs rather than pass them on to customers. >> In a limited set of circumstances where it can trace that it passed specific import charges on, he said, Amazon will contact affected customers and refund them automatically. He said that is a little more than a third of the refunds it expects. He said the quarter included a non-recurring benefit of 15 cents a share from the refunds less partial reinvestment in member values. metadata.title: $126 BILLION in Tariff Refunds Are Going Out. Not to You.
metadata.author: Plainly Public
metadata.shortDescription:
Tariff refunds explained: who gets the $126 billion, and why it isn't you. The Supreme Court ruled Trump's emergency tariffs illegal. About $126 billion is now being certified for refunds. You paid those tariffs at the store, but the checks go to the importers. Here's where the money is going, what companies do with it, who is fighting over your share, and why you may end up paying twice, with interest.
I'm Sam. I read it so you don't have to.

Everything in this video comes from public reporting, court filings and official statements. Statements are attributed to the people who made them. Figures are the latest public numbers at the time of production and may change. This is not legal or financial advice. Sources are listed below.

Chapters:
0:00 You paid. They get it back.
0:28 How you paid a tax you never saw
1:10 Where the checks are going
1:59 What the companies do with it
2:47 The fight over your share
4:03 You pay twice
5:45 What's behind it

emergency tariffs. [music] Not directly,
at the store in higher prices on almost
everything that crossed a border.
Then in February, the Supreme Court said
those tariffs were illegal. [music]
So the government is giving the money
back. About $126 billion
already certified for payment. [music]
Here's the part almost nobody is telling
you. None of it is coming to you.
I'm Sam. Let me put this plainly.
[music]
Here's how a tariff works. A company
brings in a container of goods at the
port. [music] It pays the tax to
customs.
That company is called the importer of
record.
Then the cost moves down the line,
wholesaler, store, shelf, and at the end
of the line, there's you.
[music]
Customs says importers paid about $166
billion
under these emergency tariffs. [music]
Most economists agree a big share of
that ended up in the prices families
paid. [music]
So when the court said the tariffs were
illegal, the obvious question was, who
gets the money back? [music]
The answer is in the law. A customs
refund goes to the importer of record,
[music] the company that signed the
paperwork, not the shopper.
In April, customs opened a refund portal
called CAPE. [music] Companies log in,
list their shipments, and get the tax
back with interest.
By early October, customs had accepted
about $137 billion in refund claims and
certified about $126 billion [music] to
the Treasury for payment.
Who's in line? Reports say Ford expects
about $1.3 billion. [music]
General Motors, about $500 million.
Costco sued for its refund before the
ruling even came down.
[music] And for you, there's no portal,
no form, no check.
[music]
Now, to be fair, some companies say
they'll pass it on.
FedEx and UPS, [music] which paid
tariffs on packages for their customers,
say they'll refund those customers when
the money comes in.
Others have stayed quiet. [music]
Analysts at BOK Financial put it
bluntly.
[music]
And here's a detail that tells you who's
protected.
Some retailers, including Ross Stores
and The Gap, took tariff costs out of
the math that decides executive bonuses.
[music]
Their CEOs were paid more than $17
million each.
To be clear, that's not refund money
being handed out as bonuses. It's
executives being shielded from the
tariff hit while customers paid it at
the register. [music]
Some people are fighting for it. [music]
Class action lawsuits now target
companies like Costco and Nike, arguing
customers should get a share.
Those are claims, not rulings.
In Illinois, Governor JB Pritzker asked
the administration to send $1,700 to
every Illinois family and called for a
law forcing companies to pass the relief
[music] on.
>> You paid them. You deserve to have those
tariffs paid back to you because the
Supreme Court ruled that they're
illegal.
He's not going to do it. He says he's
going to send that money to the
businesses you paid.
We need Donald Trump to pay up for
American families $1,700
per family. That's what you're owed.
>> And on the day of the ruling, Treasury
Secretary Scott Bessent warned that
consumers might never see the money.
[music]
Here's the other side, and it's a real
argument. [music] Legally, the importer
paid the tax, so the importer gets it
back.
[music] Economists at the American
Action Forum argue that's how a refund
has to work and that lower costs will
reach shoppers over time, the same slow
way the tariff did.
The problem?
Nobody is required to prove that it
does.
[music]
And the refunds aren't done.
To see why, [music] you need one customs
word, liquidation.
When a company pays a tariff, the bill
isn't final that day.
Customs closes the books on each
shipment months later.
Usually about 10 months. That's called
liquidation.
After that, the company has a window to
protest. When that window closes too,
the shipment is finally liquidated. Case
closed.
So recent shipments get their money back
through the portal.
Old shipments that are already closed,
the system locks. Only a court order
opens it.
That's where about $11 billion is stuck
right now.
In October, customs opened a third phase
just for those and only for companies
that went to court. [music]
But the biggest number in this story
isn't the refund. It's what the refund
cost.
By law, every one of these refunds comes
with interest. [music]
Customs told the court so itself.
And that interest doesn't come from the
companies.
It comes from the Treasury, from
taxpayers. [music]
Think about that loop.
You paid the tariff once at the register
in higher prices.
Now the government is paying that same
tax back to the company that collected
it from you plus interest. [music] And
part of that interest is paid with your
taxes.
[music]
The Cato Institute estimated that while
the money waited, interest was piling up
at about $700 million a month.
That's billions of dollars on a tax that
should never have been collected.
So you didn't just miss the refund.
You're helping pay for it.
[music]
Here's what's behind it. Plainly,
[music] the tariffs were illegal. The
refunds are real. They're going to the
companies that signed the customs forms.
[music]
You paid at the register.
You get nothing back unless the company
that got your money decides to share it.
So should companies be forced to pass
tariff refunds onto customers? [music]
Tell me below.
I read it so you don't have to.
I'm Sam. [music]
See you on the next one.
>> [music]
[music]

metadata.title: Tariff Refunds Are Going to Companies. Will You See Any of It?

metadata.shortDescription:
On Feb 20, 2026 the Supreme Court ruled that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs. Under CBP's refund process, the money goes to the company that paid the duty at the border, not to shoppers. Customs (CBP) estimated $166 billion in duties on 53 million entries from about 330,000 importers. The Court of International Trade wrote on Oct 8 that more than 75% (about $126 billion, duties plus interest) had been refunded as of Oct 2. A CBP filing reported by the Daily Caller says $128.4 billion was certified and sent to the Treasury by Nov 5. CBP's own page says only the importer of record, or its customs broker, can file for a refund.

So the question is whether any of it reaches your receipt. Five ripples, each with what is confirmed, what is only reported, and what you can do: (1) the money has one door; (2) did the tariff end up in your price? (the studies disagree); (3) the carriers are the exception; (4) the courtroom; (5) what happens next.

What we do NOT claim: we are not saying companies stole your refund. Legally, the refund goes to whoever paid the duty at the border, and some companies say they will pass value on (Walmart says it will reinvest in prices; Costco says it will invest most of its refunds for members). We are not saying your prices did or did not rise because of tariffs. Not confirmed: we found no consumer settlement and no claim form as of Nov 21, 2026, and no date for the Federal Circuit argument.

Our prediction (dated Nov 21, 2026): by Dec 31, 2026, none of Walmart, Target, Costco, Amazon or Home Depot will announce cash payments to shoppers for tariff costs. We'll check it and tell you if we were wrong.

metadata.title: Sad, Beautiful, Tragic: New Section 301 Tariffs | Cindy’s Version
metadata.author: Simply Trade Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
New Section 301 tariffs took effect on July 24, 2026, creating immediate compliance questions for U.S. importers and customs brokers. Cindy Allen explains the new tariff rates, product exemptions, MFN duty treatment, HTSUS classification, tariff stacking, and forced-labor enforcement rationale behind the action.

Explore practical international trade compliance training from Global Training Center:
https://www.globaltrainingcenter.com?utm_source=SimplyTradePodcast

In this Simply Trade: Cindy’s Version update, Cindy also examines the expiration of Section 122, Section 232 carve-outs, proposed Section 338 tariffs on certain Canadian products, USMCA uncertainty, IEEPA tariff refunds, and potential tariff court challenges.

WHAT YOU’LL LEARN

• How general, country-specific, and use-specific tariff exemptions may apply
• Why tariff classification and country of origin must be reviewed together
• How MFN duty rates can affect the Section 301 tariff amount
• How Section 301 interacts with Section 232 and other trade remedies
• Why correct tariff stacking and customs entry reporting matter
• What importers should discuss with customs brokers and software providers
• How Section 338 tariffs could affect imports from Canada
• What the changing tariff environment means for landed costs and compliance

RECOMMENDED TRADE COMPLIANCE TRAINING

Develop strategies for changing tariffs and trade policies:
Trade Action Strategies Advanced Mini Course
https://globaltrainingcenter.com/trade-action-strategies/

Tariff Classification Training
https://globaltrainingcenter.com/tariff-classification/

Strengthen import documentation, entry procedures, and duty compliance:
Importing Procedures Training
https://globaltrainingcenter.com/importing-procedures/

Address forced-labor enforcement and supply-chain tracing:
Forced Labor Compliance Workshop
https://globaltrainingcenter.com/forced-labor-supply-chain-tracing/

Prepare for North American rules of origin and USMCA compliance:
USMCA Training for Importers and Exporters
https://globaltrainingcenter.com/usmca/

TRADE COMPLIANCE SERVICES

Need customized training for your import, export, brokerage, or compliance team?
https://globaltrainingcenter.com/team-training/

Need guidance tailored to your company’s trade compliance challenges?
https://globaltrainingcenter.com/consulting/

Using Taylor Swift’s “Sad Beautiful Tragic” as the episode’s lens, Cindy connects the changing tariff environment with growing uncertainty surrounding predictable trade and the U.S.–Canada commercial relationship.

TRADE GEEKS: Which issue is creating the biggest operational challenge for your organization—tariff exemptions, HTS classification, tariff stacking, customs programming, or duty refunds? Share your experience in the comments.

CHAPTERS

segments.text: Cindy Allen - Trade Force Mult Hi, today is Friday, July 24th,
2026. I'm Cindy Allen, also known as a Taylor Swift of Trade. I'm CEO of Trade Force Multiplier,
a global trade consultancy service that handles everything from those pesky 28s
and 29s requests for information and notices of action to complex trade strategies that you
need to outline for your board in this enforcement-oriented trade environment.
Welcome to Simply Trade Cindy's version where I base an international trade update
on a Taylor Swift song. It's brought to you in association with the Global Training Center.
It's good to be with you after two weeks. And unlike my muse Taylor Swift,
I didn't take two weeks off to get married and go on a fancy honeymoon.
I took time off to hang out with my three kids and play Gigi to my four grandkids,
but it is really great to be back with everyone. Today's Taylor Swift song is "Sad,
Beautiful, tragic." And I know there is a lot going on in trade. So much has happened
just in the past week when I looked back on everything. at 12:01 this morning,
Eastern Standard Time in the US, Section 122 ended. That was the 10 that was due on
all goods coming into the United States, with some exceptions, and we have seen.
The implementation of Section 301 tariffs for lack of forced labor enforcement that
the US found was harm to the US economy. So very interesting that 301 section can
be justified utilizing the lack of enforcement for another country of
their own laws. So really interesting. Let's delve into the details here.
This does cover all 60 countries. Some have 10%, some have 12.5%,
some include the MFN or most favored nation or normal duty rates within that 10% and within
that 12.5%. But some countries have that just on top of the MFN or the normal duty rates.
There are over 700 products or tariff numbers that have a general exemption. This means they
Don't have the Section 301 applied to them. And there are three criteria that they outlined in
the executive order or the notice of action in the in the FRN notification.
And that's raw materials for a domestic supply. So that would cause an issue with
domestic either supply or manufacturing. Products that cause economic-wide impact.
So this is seen to be the gas and oil exemptions that we saw,
some of the food exemptions that would have a massive impact to the economy of
the United States, or that can't be grown or produced in the United States. Now,
this is similar to a former exemption that came under a lot of fire, that goods couldn't
pre- be produced in the United States. But we did see it for some exotic fruits, coffees,
things like that. As an avid coffee drinker, I'm very happy that this will not cover coffee.
unflavored coffee only, which I found really odd, but you know,
we don't understand a lot of these actions. on top of those more than 700 product exemptions,
there are hundreds of company, country-specific exemptions or use specific exemptions. So it's
gonna be really complex to go through this and determine if the product applies or not.
There are also Section 232 product exemptions. So if you have steel,
aluminum, copper, those automotives, heavy duty trucks, automotive,
aerospace that are in the section 232, you don't have to pay the 301 on top of that.
So some good news there. Also carved out some trade agreements are also exempt. I have to say,
this is one of the most complex trade remedy actions that I've seen rolled out.
It's multiple layers. The notification itself was hundreds of pages, which everyone was
reading because it came out at the end of the day yesterday and was in effect at midnight,
1201 this morning. So a lot of us spent a lot of time reading through all of the exemptions,
reading through the text of the Federal Register notice to make sure that we
understood what applied and what didn't. And one of the things that I can tell you.
Is that I do believe that some of the trade associations will come out with a spreadsheet
or guide that will assist you as an importer, as a customs broker in applying the correct amount
of tariffs because it's going to be very complex. There are A through O annexes on this. The first
annex, of course, is those 700 plus exemptions that apply to every country, and then it goes into
country specific exemptions. And each country is referred to a different exemption list. in
the B through O phase. Some of them are applicable to only some products,
although the tariff rate may cover that tariff number may cover more than one product. So I would
Carefully examine the tariff numbers, carefully examine the text for the
country that you are buying those goods from to make sure that your product does
or does not fall in a tariff exemption. I know that the programmers also spent
a lot of time last night trying to program their systems to ensure that you're paying
the right amount of duty and that that duty is accurately reflected.
The information that was supplementally sent out after the Federal Register notice does give
customs brokers advice on how to list each of these trade remedies, in what order the tariff
stacking, as we call it, where the duty rates for each of these should be applied, so that we
can prevent some issues that we're seeing in some of the IEP or refund duties that are coming out.
in that the tariffs were not stacked properly, or that the tariff rate was
not shown on the right tariff stacking level, or that it was lumped together
inaccurately. And as I've said before, some of those AIPA tariffs when they came out,
there was not specific guidance. So I I commend CBP for giving guidance so that
the implementation could be a little bit more smooth. the 301 is thought to fare better.
In the court challenges than the previous trade remedies. You know,
we saw both section 122 and the IEEPA tariff speech challenge in court. The
122 is still ongoing. We do know that there have been some court actions that have asked
for the review of section 232 as well, but previous 301 challenges in court have not.
Been wholly successful. So this is seen to have a better legal standing. it does 301,
Section 301 does give the president clear authority to actually assess tariffs. However,
I think the lack of direct link to emo economic impacts in the United States from the foreign
adoption of forced labor enforcement and the level of enforcement could be at
play in a court challenge moving forward. Those of us in trade do expect us to be challenged like all
the other tariffs. So stay tuned. This is a very litigious administration and we do believe that
this will spawn some some court challenges in the in the future. It'll be interesting to see what
industry steps up, what countries and companies step up to actually challenge us in court.
I know it's also concerning that forced labor seems to have the same effect on
50 or more countries and that they're 12.5% and on a smaller number of countries they're
10%. And those aren't rated specific to the country's level of of enforcement of forced
labor specifically. They are just dumped into buckets. So I think that could be an issue.
very interesting, very long night for those of us in trade advising our customers
what's happening and how to go about understanding how
that impacts the products that you're importing. And for customs brokers,
all of your customers understanding where that impacts. if you are an importer and
you're reaching out to your customs broker, just know that they got as much notice as you did.
To make all of the changes to identify all of the products that are going to be assessed
this additional tariff, and that they are working as hard as they can to make sure,
